#8147. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

#8146. Musician Allie Teilz says becoming a mom made her “bigger, not smaller”

The DJ’s debut album, Come to Mommy, is a refusal to pick one version of herself, and a reminder that we don’t have to either.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 23, 2026

It’s dinnertime at Allie Teilz’s house, and the music is already on. Perhaps a film score courtesy of Italian classicist Morricone, maybe some Italian disco easing in behind it. One of the twins, age 3, is already dancing to it. The phones go in the ceramic cow on the counter for the remainder of the evening, where her almost-8-year-old likes them. There’s a projector, a record player, and a wall of VHS tapes with Yellow Submarine and The Land Before Time on heavy rotation. Teilz calls it, half-joking, a ’90s-electronics household.

She is, for the record, impossibly cool. A vinyl DJ and producer who came up in Los Angeles nightlife sharing booths with the likes of Grace Jones and Daft Punk, she now scours thrift stores and estate sales for those VHS tapes and describes herself as “a mother first and an artist second.” She is a mother of four who weaves those two versions of herself authentically into one.

We talked for an hour, and I could have gone three more. Somewhere in the course of our call she made me wish, for a second, that I could do the whole motherhood thing over again. My kids are grown and nearly grown, and I am not in the market for a redo. Still, the childhood she is building for hers, steeped in art and music and curiosity, had me calculating.

Her debut album, Come to Mommy, out now, is the sound of her reclaiming the artist within after the babies arrived. It’s atmospheric, irresistibly dance-able and laced with an electronic vibe that’s both throwback and futuristic. The title turns “come to daddy” on its head. The culture asks what Daddy wants. Teilz would rather ask what Mommy wants, and she answers without flinching. “Mommy wants joy,” she says. “She wants to have fun and dance. She wants pleasure and joy.”

Teilz doesn’t treat her kids as the thing she makes art around. She treats them as the reason her art got deeper. “Becoming their mom,” she says, “only made everything bigger, not smaller.” Motherhood taught her that “the deepest creativity can come from having very little time and knowing exactly what matters.”

There’s a surrender in becoming a parent, she says, a soul handing itself over to lead someone else through life, and for her it cracked the work open instead of closing it down. It “liberated me in creation,” she says, and gave her “a deeper well to pull from.” She has taken to calling motherhood “the highest form of art I’ve ever experienced.”

It changed what she wants to make, too. She looks at her own work through her children’s eyes now and holds it to a single north star. What do I want to see more of in the world? Certainly not  “AI art and lobotomy chic,” her encapsulation of the soulless, machine-driven work she’s watched creep in. She wants her kids to have what she had, the feeling of hearing Talking Heads for the first time and being free, the permission to flail around in  an imaginary version of David Byrne’s giant suit and stay in “that beautiful state of play.” Come to Mommy is her attempt to put that feeling back into the world, and she credits her kids as the inspiration. “They’re the greatest teachers,” she says.

Most women are familiar with the shift that happens when you become a mother. The self gets smaller to make room for everyone else, and for a while Teilz felt it, sliding toward the motherhood she’d watched other women vanish into. The mom groups where everyone gave and gave without ever taking their own needs into consideration. The careers set down and never picked back up. The inability to truly answer the question, “Who am I?” She calls out the insidious culprits that get woven into culture. “We’re indoctrinated by The Giving Tree and The Rainbow Fish,” she says, the children’s books that sell self-erasure as generosity. Make yourself a stump and you’ll be loved. Give away your sparkles and you’ll be accepted. “That’s such a dangerous thing,” Teilz observes.

For a long stretch, her own priorities became submerged. What pulled her back was simple. Boundaries. A flip phone for the hours she refuses to be reachable. She points to a line she saw online, “have boundaries or get an autoimmune disorder,” and says that her health was what finally made her stop. “My kids don’t need a mom who disappears into anything,” she says. “Even motherhood.”

Teilz builds her kids’ childhood the way she builds a record, out of specific, deliberate, slightly magical details. When her daughter earned a leader award at school and got to choose the celebration, she asked to make “ice cream mountains” with scoops stacked into a castle on parchment paper, modeled on the shop Teilz loved as a girl. Ridiculous for the sake of being ridiculous. The memories Teilz recalls most fondly from her own childhood aren’t the cruise or the big trip. They’re the one-bedroom apartment and her mom letting the kids pick a favorite ice cream before the first day of school. Now she makes the small, arguably more impactful kind of memories for her own crew.

There’s also a healthy helping of wonder. The kids get sent out to the garden to pull parsley or a tomato so their hands are involved in making dinner–she’s been teaching them to grow things from seed to fruition for years, because watching a baby artichoke push up from a seed you watered is the kind of small miracle she wants them to appreciate. Books work the same way. She still talks about a woman she once watched on the subway, reading beside her small daughter while the car churned around them, the two of them just reading, an image that stuck with her long before she had kids of her own. Now one of her proudest moments is her daughter climbing onto the couch to get lost in Harry Potter. “Stay curious about the world,” she tells other mothers. “Keep reading. Stay interested in what matters to you.”

None of this came easily. Come to Mommy was written through a brutal stretch that included a traumatic birth, one that nearly cost Teilz and one of her sons their lives, and the album is partly the record of her finding the way back. The final track, Back From the Dead, was written for the twin she almost lost. It’s her way of telling all of her kids that they can come back from the worst thing. Making art out of it was a way to process, and she says, proof to her children that you can take something that breaks you and “make something beautiful out of the ashes.”

Near the end, I painted an image for her. A mom pulls into the driveway and sits in the car a minute before going in, the album still playing. What does she want that woman to carry inside with her? Teilz didn’t hesitate. She wants her to “steal the fire” of her own passion, to think of the song she danced hardest to at her best friend’s 13th birthday, to feel held, to have a reason to dance. Mostly she wants her to feel more like herself.

Not many people tell women that the self doesn’t have to shrink to make room for mothering. Teilz spends a whole album saying it.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

#8145. Are We All Boomers Now?

While we may actually be Millennials and Gen X, it’s become clear that the kids think we are … old.

As I lay on my bed with one of my teens next to me, laughing over a Reel before we forward it to my mom, I find myself suddenly the butt of a joke. “Why do you poke your phone like that, mom? You’re such a Boomer. That’s so unc.”

I paused, hovered over the sharing airplane, and looked at the seemingly normal (to me) way that I am tapping my phone. Was I acting like an old lady? Was I “unc,” the new gender-neutral uncle-derived slang term the teens currently use to describe anyone annoyingly older than them?

After a moment of denial, I settled into the belief that my kid was actually right: I am old. No, not as old as my parents or as old as most U.S. politicians, but when it comes to the benchmarks that define age, I am decidedly more crotchety than I was five years ago.

Today, as I sit in my dining room typing this missive on the morning of my 43rd birthday (Yes, I am an geriatric millennial), I am faced with two important thoughts: Why is my neighbor’s car engine so loud, and what kind of bird is chirping in the tree outside of my window?

I pause to send my friend a recording of the bird. She replies that it is a mockingbird (likely mocking me, like my children) and I get back to work. She’s a Boomer now too, I assume. She recently invited me over to learn about plants — and take a few clippings. Wild times for the Real Housewives of Pittsburgh as we all work remotely from our messy homes.

I begin to mentally list the things that now piss me off: Overhead lighting, too many people talking at once, small talk at professional events (or anywhere), pants with a waistband and shoes without good arch support. I am furious that every movement in life requires a new app, deeply concerned about the safety of e-bikes and gas station drugs and the state of our local roads, and trialing my fourth set of cooling bed sheets. I also list the things I do not care about any longer: fashion trends, what anyone else thinks of me, and the well-earned lines and wrinkles on my face.

It’s a weird juxtaposition when you’re parenting in middle age, raising kids that are on the cusp of adulthood. In many ways I feel like I’m in the prime of my life. I’ve whittled down my friend group to the besties who can stand me, my career is satisfying and moderately successful, and I’ve finally found a hairdresser who gets me. Some days I walk down the street feeling like a million bucks — only to be cut off at the knees by a side-eye at my shoe choice from my teen daughter.

I ask my friends, my comrades in aging semi-gracefully, if they feel the Boomerness creeping up on them, too.

“For sure,” one friend tells me, “Or like how my boyfriend always talks about how we used to be able to get a hamburger for $5 or what the cost of gas used to be.” I remember… it was under a buck the day I got my license.

Another friend says her kid dissects the “unc-ness” of her text messages. Emoji choice is a dead (☠️) giveaway, apparently. So are the television shows and movies we reference as “recent.” Hold hands while I tell you this: The final episode of Parks and Recreation aired well over a decade ago; ten whole human years ago. Don’t even get me started on the OG version of SATC.

So I’ve chosen to accept my fate. In many ways, we are becoming the Boomers now. Not literally — generations are fairly well-defined, and Boomers were born between about 1946 and 1964. But in the funny, small ways that matter, many of us Elder Millennial and Gen X parents are showing our age.

After some soul-searching in my backyard inflatable hot tub, which helps with the aches and pains of old age we’ve barely touched on, I’ve decided this isn’t such a bad thing.

So I am worked up enough about e-bikes to briefly consider a run for town council? That’s because I care about the safety of kids in our community; call me Karen. I’m frustrated with the condition of roads or schools or public infrastructure? I won’t apologize for being old (or mature) enough to realize civic engagement matters. If we want to live in a thriving and bustling community, we are the adults that must create that now. We can’t decry the loss of a village if we aren’t willing to get out there and make one.

We’ve also, as a group, taken healing quite seriously. I am proud of us for this, more than anything else about our generation. While we might bitch about the cost of everything or the state of the world in those Boomerish ways, we are also a generation that is serious about breaking cycles, building new patterns, and parenting conscientiously.

We talk about our therapists in ways that normalize taking care of our mental health. We find mental health help for our kids when they need it, too. We mess up with our kids—and we apologize. We try, we screw up, we try again. Our hips and back and knees may be less flexible than they once were, but I am proud that we are trying to keep our minds flexible. Our Gen Z and Alpha kids poke fun at us and insist the way we dress is awful, but I choose to believe that they see we are working so hard.

So, to my fellow Millennial-and-Gen-X-Boomer-but-not-really-moms, pull up a supportive chair and join me. Bring your latest craft project, your current book club read, or your stack of political postcards that you need to get out before the midterms. Bring your comfy soft pants, your persistent chin hair, and your achy lower back. We will turn off the Big Lights, skip the small talk, and bitch about hot flashes while our kids make fun of us in the next room. Honestly, I think we’ve earned this.

Meg St-Esprit, M. Ed. is a journalist and essayist based in Pittsburgh, PA. She’s a mom to four kids via adoption as well as a twin mom. She loves to write about parenting, education, trends, and the general hilarity of raising little people.

#8144. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

We spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

#8143. Karla Souza Talks Narrating The New 'Thomas & Friends' Special, Mom Guilt, & More

The HTGAWM star and mom of three talks narrating the new Spanish-language Thomas & Friends special, and how she’s leaning into her latest parenting era: minivan life.

Karla Souza has accomplished a lot in her career. She famously played a law student covering up multiple murders in How To Get Away With Murder. She won two International Emmys for producing and starring in Dive (La Caída). She’s built a filmography that fluently bounces between Hollywood and Mexico. But it took a little blue engine to impress maybe the most fickle audience of all: her three kids, ages 8, 6, and 2.

Souza is the Spanish-language narrator of Thomas & Friends Railway Stories: Really Helpful Engines, a 30-minute special that kicks off a new era for the beloved franchise through refreshed character designs, three original songs, and a story about friendship, teamwork, and helping others. She’s also, as she learned after signing on, the first woman — and first Mexican woman — to narrate Thomas & Friends.

Scary Mommy caught up with the charming Souza to talk about the special, why “balance” is a myth, officially surrendering to minivan life, and more.

Scary Mommy: Your kids are 8, 6, and 2, which is prime Thomas territory. Were they Thomas fans before? Do they have a sense of what you’re doing?

Karla Souza: This is actually the first project that I'm able to watch with them, so it was very special. I was definitely chomping at the bit, wanting to be able to share something for the first time with them. They were very confused as to why I wasn't making the train sounds and why that was somebody else. There was a lot of confusion with that part of it, but I love this new chapter of being able to share these kinds of things. And it was the first thing that I did for that kind of age range.

I just find it so special to think that maybe, when they have kids, they'll be able to show old Grandma… there’s something to be said about doing projects that can live on for generations.

SM: What does it mean to you that kids can hear Thomas in Spanish, told by a Mexican narrator?

KS: I wasn't aware that this is the first time that a woman and that a Mexican woman is the narrator of Thomas and Friends. I am so honored, and I'm very excited that female voices get to guide these new generations in seeing women in these kinds of positions.

I love how Thomas and Friends has content that isn't in overdrive, as a lot of the kids' content nowadays is extremely saturated with, I don't know, stimulation is just being thrown at you. I find that this type of content is not only going to provoke imagination, but it's also going to turn on their hearts how to be a better person, how to work as a team, how to learn from mistakes in a calmer way. So it's been a great thing to watch with my 2-year-old as well as with my 6- and 8-year-old. That doesn't really get to happen as much, so I'm really grateful for that.

SM: Three kids, a career as an actor and producer, you split your time a lot between two countries. What does balance actually look like for you, or is that nonexistent?

KS: Yeah, it's not possible. I think that word is thrown around as if it were possible to have a balanced life. I mean, anyone who's near my life is like, "How do you do this?" I think the trains have systems; they're on the tracks. There are times when the train leaves. If there's a delay, there's an announcement to all the people that there's a delay. It's the same. If I didn't have all these systems and a community of people around me to support me, my husband, my family, our nanny, the school, everything, we would not be able to do this. My mom didn't work, per se, so I never saw what that would look like. So it's been a learning curve for me to understand how to juggle all of it.

There's a lot of mom guilt still there that, every therapy session, I'm trying to get to why I still feel that way. It's real, it's hard, but I will say that also the ability to see my kids watching me do something that I love, watching me impact society in a way, watching me live out my purpose, is as important as being with them 24-7.

SM: Such a good reminder that we’re not alone; we all feel like this in a way. Your youngest is 2. What difference strikes you the most about parenting your third compared to your first?

KS: My 2-year-old started saying words that were like, "Where did she hear that?" I'm like, "Obviously from us; there's no other place. This word isn't going to magically appear in her mouth. That is why she is saying that word." It's funny how you're in denial of, like, "I don't do that,” but surely we do.

I think having children is a great mirror for who you are and the work you have to do on yourself, because they call BS so quickly when we try to teach them about, like, breathwork. And yet when I get frustrated, I'm not practicing what I am trying to teach. So as much as I try to think that they aren't as perceptive, they are. They just absorb so much of how we live our lives, of what we do.

Whenever I've noticed that working on myself is actually the best way to show up for them and to model it, that's how I see it with my 2-year-old and my 8-year-old — my 2-year-old is an imitator of everything she sees from my 8-year-old. Whatever my 8-year-old wants to do, whether it's gymnastics or staying up late or reading a book, my 2-year-old goes off and does it. It just shows you how interaction and who you surround yourself with really is very important at this stage in their lives.

It’s an interesting sort of case study on life and how we are as humans and what makes us feel like we belong.

SM: Yeah, it is fascinating how it shows up like that.

But yeah, the 2-year-old obviously is the queen of the household, and my 8-year-old is as well, but the 2-year-old is coming in like a storm. She's a spitfire. So we do what she says. My 8-year-old is a great sort of... I try to not put the caretaking role on her as much because a lot of people try to have the older kids kind of become the caretakers, and I don't want to do that. But I will say she has a lovely pull towards taking care of her baby sister.

I love having that separation of years, but yeah, the 2-year-old's my last one. We just bought ourselves our first minivan, so I've given up. That's it; I'm a mom of three. I've never had a minivan in my life, and we just got one. I'm like, "All right, that's who I am now."

SM: We rented a minivan for a girls’ trip a few years ago. Five moms driving up the coast in a rented minivan; it was hilarious. But it was the first one I drove as well, and I was like, “You know what? There’s something to this. It’s super comfortable.”

KS: I know. The kids just get in and they get out, and it's just so comfortable. I feel more powerful driving it than I thought I would be. I'm like, "This is actually cooler than I thought." But yes, I've given up on the cool, sexy cars now and I'm like, "All right, I'm going to embrace it."

SM: As you should. Let's make minivans cool and sexy.

KS: Yes. Hey, you did it on a girls' trip! That's hilarious.

SM: Pivoting a bit, I saw you post that How To Get Away With Murder just marked 12 years since its premiere. Does the ending hit differently now that you’re a mom of three?

KS: Man, I am in awe of Laurel being able to be a mom at that period of her life. I'm still shocked. And I'm shocked that I, as a human being, was able to... I think I was pregnant when I did that scene on the elevator where she's having these contractions and there's a potential stillbirth. Nowadays, knowing so much more, I'm like, "I don't know how I could do that today." But I will say that at least playing to be a mom definitely prepared me in the smallest of ways, but it did prepare me to be a mom. It kind of gave me that vote of confidence because I never thought I could be a mom.

I didn't grow up with that faith of I can do it. I was like, "I still feel like I'm a child and I'm trying to parent my own child, my inner child every day." But that's why I thought I wasn't sort of made for motherhood, and look at me three kids later: here I am.

So for all the moms out there, all the women out there, who feel like they wouldn't be able to do it, I was that person. I was definitely thinking, "How can I still have a career and do what I love and travel with my friends in a minivan? How can I do all these things and still have kids?" It's possible. Does it all look the same as when I was single? No, it doesn't, but it is possible. It's tough, but that's the caveat. It's the silver lining, but yes.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

#8142. 8 Proven Steps to Deter Snakes From Your Garden – and October is the Very Best Time to Take Action

Make your yard inhospitable to snakes in fall and you'll reduce numbers next year, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve got snakes in your garden then I don’t need to tell you that it’s not the snakes themselves that are the biggest problem, but the constant worry that you might be about to encounter one. Only a quarter of native snake species in the USA are venomous and most – like garter snakes and corn snakes – are helpful garden visitors, eating rodents as well as slugs and bugs. But even if you’re happy to tolerate them as part of a healthy garden ecosystem, it’s smart to set some boundaries and deter snakes from yard areas you regularly use.

October is the very best time of the year to make your yard inhospitable to snakes, if you don’t fancy your garden becoming their permanent winter home. As fall temperatures drop to around 60°F, reptiles will start scouting out a frost-free space to brumate (like hibernating, but not as deep), so now is the time to take action. By making these areas scarce in your garden, snakes will likely move out of your yard to find somewhere to stay. Snakes are also exceptionally hungry in October as they need to store body fat to survive months of winter brumation, so removing food sources will also drive them out of your garden.

And if you need any more motivation to keep snakes out of your garden this month, know that they frequently breed in the exact same space they brumate. A typical female produces 10-30 babies, so if you don’t want a heap more slithering around your garden next summer, here’s your 8-step plan that explains how to deter snakes this fall.

Snakes like cool, damp, dark and undisturbed areas so take a look around your garden to identify probable hiding spots. If you’ve got a large yard and like to share your yard with wildlife, then by all means leave shelter in unused corners. However, in areas of the garden you frequent, clear yard clutter, trim vegetation and bag up fallen leaves. If you have a firewood stack or compost pile, consider moving them further away from the house.

When you’re clearing an area that may already be providing cover for snakes, always use tools rather than your hands. Don’t think that even leather gauntlet gardening gloves will protect you, either, as the single layer of fabric is easily pierced by a snake fang. Gloves are a smart move, but you’ll need animal-handling gloves such as these from Amazon for any worthwhile protection.

Snakes hate spending time in open spaces where they’re visible from the sky and could become easy prey. Especially in October when snakes are highly mobile, keep all grass mown to a length of 3 inches or less and you’ll strongly deter snakes from slithering across it. Be sure to trim transitional zones too, where a mower can’t reach, as these can become favored travelling routes for snakes. A pair of shears with a 90° blade action such as these lightweight Hand Grass Shears from Walmart make short work of trimming lawn edges, or use cordless clippers like this Rechargeable Grass and Hedge Trimmer, also from Walmart.

Dense shrubs provide welcome cover for snakes but it’s an easy task to trim off lower branches to expose the ground and make them less inviting. You can also prune a shrub into the shape of a small tree. Use a pair of pruners – and do sharpen them first with a tool such as a Sharpal, available from Amazon, as cuts made with sharp blades heal much quicker – to cut unwanted branches flush with the main trunk. For bigger branches, a pruning saw like Fiskar’s Power Tooth Pruning Saw, available from The Home Depot, is a better bet.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

We often mulch our garden beds in fall but a cosy, damp layer of pine straw or chunky bark chips offers snakes the ideal spot to regulate their body temperature. Use fine compost to mulch beds and borders instead, which snakes will find far less appealing. If you make your own compost then a rotary sifter such as the Mikiotto Soil Sifter, available from Lowe’s, makes short work of sieving the larger chunks out. Otherwise use a pre-made manure-free compost such as Back to the Roots Organic Compost, stocked at Walmart, as a mulch.

Bird feeders are a prime reason why snakes hang around in gardens. While they don’t eat the dropped seed itself, the reptiles are drawn to the plentiful supply of mice, voles and insects it attracts. And how many of us resume feeding garden birds in fall, just as snakes reach peak appetite?

Getting rid of this easy food source is a key part of the plan to keep snakes out of a garden. The solution is to switch to a waste-free bird food such as Kaytee No Mess Wild Bird Seed, available from Amazon. Hook a seed catcher like this hanging tray from Walmart to the base of hanging bird feeders too, to catch any discarded seed husks.

Fix any gaps that give snake access to a shed, summerhouse or your home. If you need a temporary closure then steel wool is the best way to create a sturdy, weatherproof but non-permanent barrier and bulk packs are available cheaply, such as this steel wool from Amazon. In October, snakes are highly mobile and need the heat of the sun to be mobile, so you’re far more likely to block them out of a hole than seal them in. Do your repairs in the middle of the day when the sun is at its warmest and you can be confident a snake is out basking, hunting or scouting for winter digs.

There are plenty of urban myths that promise mothballs, crushed eggshells and even marigolds deter snakes, but extensive research has proven otherwise. What a study by the USDA National Wildlife Research Centre does show to be an effective snake deterrent is essential oils that are rich in eugenol, namely cinnamon and clove. The research found that this compound irritates the snake’s scent receptor in its mouth and triggers its escape response. So if you're wondering how to keep snakes out of gaps that can't or shouldn't be blocked, here's your solution.

Add 15-20 drops of pure clove oil and the same of pure cinnamon oil to a quart of water in a spray bottle. Add a teaspoon of dish soap to help the oil bind with the water and shake well to mix. Spray this blend around ground vents, woodpiles and decking or porch voids, or anywhere else that gives access to a dark space that can’t be blocked.

Outdoors, oil disperses quickly so reapply after heavy rain or every 2-3 weeks. Once temperatures fall consistently below 50°F, it’s safe to stop as snakes will be holed up in their winter dens.

Snakes are terrified of birds of prey, and one of the easiest ways to deter snakes is to attract owls into your garden. Whether you DIY an owl box or opt for a ready-made design like the Aoibox Large Owl House from Lowe's, October is a prime time to invite owls into your yard as they're actively looking for nesting sites between September and March.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#8141. Beautiful Eastern Orthodox Baby Names and Their Meanings

Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations

Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

From Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

#8140. Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage

Home / Getting Pregnant / Miscarriage & Loss

When I lost my baby, I knew it was a day I’d never forget. And then I did.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Content warning: Discussion of pregnancy loss ahead.

I was cleaning my kitchen, pop music blaring from a speaker, when I glanced at the digital calendar on my counter. That’s when I saw it—the butterfly emoji that flutters every August 21 to memorialize the day I lost my pregnancy.

I was gutted. But this time it wasn’t because of the miscarriage. It was because I forgot. For the first time in 10 years, the date my baby’s heart stopped beating had slipped my mind.

It’s not hard for me to bring myself back to that day. At my 12-week appointment, the doctor ran a fetal doppler across my belly, searching for a heartbeat she would never find. I watched the crease between her eyebrows deepen as she moved the wand around. She tried to reassure me there could be a reason she couldn’t find the heartbeat. Still, it made sense to get an ultrasound.

I headed off to a new location. I didn’t call anyone, doing my best to will “it’s fine” into existence. I sat nervously in the waiting room, tapping my leg up and down as I listened for my name.

When it was my turn, I laid back on the table, prepped for the squeeze of cool jelly on my stomach, then watched a screen on the wall as the ultrasound tech poked around to find my baby.

And there it was. The makings of my second born lit up on the screen. Those images are always a bit tough to discern, but I could clearly see a head, a body, and four limbs. But those limbs weren’t moving, and the tech stayed quiet. She pressed buttons, took snapshots, and kept her gaze trained squarely on her computer screen. When she finished, she said, “The doctor will be in to talk to you,” then scurried out the door.

Seconds later someone else popped in and asked me to follow them to another room. I now realize I was taking up precious space near the ultrasound equipment. They’d need it for their next appointment, and the news I was about to hear might stun me in place for some time.

The moment is crystal clear in my memory even ten years later. I remember the hard plastic chair I sat in. I remember looking around the room and realizing that half of it was used for storage. There were boxes of papers and remnants of mailers alongside random supplies waiting for their real homes. Next to me, a box of tissues sat on a small table.

When the doctor walked in, he introduced himself. I don’t remember his name, but I’ll never forget his somber look when he said, “It’s not good news.” The floor falling out from beneath me. I called my husband in tears, barely able to say, “There’s no heartbeat,” then made a desperate call to my mom to share the same news.

I don’t remember how I got back to my grandmother’s house, where she was watching my 2-year-old son. I know I drove there, but the memory is hazy, overlaid with the sadness, terror and anxiety that were coursing through me.

When I arrived, I collapsed into my grandmother’s arms. “They couldn’t find a heartbeat,” I said, fighting back tears as my son watched us intently. She tightened her grip on me and let me dissolve.

I suffered a missed miscarriage—my body didn’t recognize that the baby growing inside had died. But based on its size and development, doctors were able to tell me that the heart likely stopped beating at 10.5 weeks. That’s how I came to mark August 21 as the day my baby died.

In the years that followed, I anxiously awaited both that date and my due date as they crept closer. I knew they would be hard. Over the first couple of years, I’d plan for unproductive days, knowing I’d fall back into my grief. I’d spend the morning each August 21 remembering the day I found out, going over every detail as I let the tears rain down. I’d search for signs of butterflies, which became a hopeful symbol to me in the wake of my miscarriage.

But ten years later, I was caught up in the details of a very busy life. I’m a working mom with two school-aged kids who spends much of my time chauffeuring them between playdates and sports practices.

It’s likely a good sign that August 21 no longer looms over me like a dark cloud. In those early years of letting the grief wash over me in full force, I gave my mind, body and heart the space to release its tension and ache. But forgetting the date brought its own type of grief. It was a reminder of how far I’ve come, and how far my baby never did.

Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage, but that grief has evolved. I will always wonder what that little life would have become, and why they weren’t given the chance. I will always take a moment to pause and remember the hope, joy and love I felt in the early weeks of that pregnancy, even if I need the calendar to remind me to do so.

And most importantly, I will always talk about it. With time, grief has lessened its stranglehold on my heart and emotions. What remains of my grief is more like a tool. It appears when I need to be a supporter. It boosts my voice so I can help others in the throes of their own despair.

One in 4 women will experience pregnancy or infant loss in their lifetime. I’m a 1-in-4, and I hope sharing my story helps someone else feel less alone in their pain, no matter where she is on her grieving journey.

October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. If you or someone you know is struggling with a postpartum mental health challenge after a pregnancy or infant loss, call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-9-HELP4MOMS (1-800-943-5746). This free, confidential service provides access to trained counselors and resources 24 hours a day, 7 days a week in English, Spanish, and more than 60 other languages. They can offer support and information related to before, during, and after pregnancy.

#8138. 250 Turkish Baby Names Inspired by Nature, Strength and Beauty

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even said a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

Names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

Turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

Below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design

#8137. 10 Questions Worth Asking At Your Annual Physical After Age 40, According To Doctors

They want to talk to you about prevention, prevention, and more prevention.

Between work, kids, kids’ extracurriculars, family obligations, and everything else, it’s easy, as moms, to let our own health fall by the wayside. If nothing’s bothering you, of course your annual physical is the first thing to get canceled in a week loaded with other appointments and to-dos. But doctors agree that while moms are often the last people to complain about feeling tired, rundown, or off, they also tend to wait too long to bring their concerns to a medical provider, as Scary Mommy previously reported. So, this is your sign to keep that annual physical and use it to talk to your doctor about all the health concerns that come with aging. While you might be fine now, your doctor is eager to tell you how to keep it that way.

“Cardiovascular disease is the number one killer in the United States for both men and women. In order to live a long and happy life you need to understand your risk for developing cardiovascular disease and how to combat and lower your risk,” says Dr. Colleen Reidy, DO, is a family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

“This is the blood work that I recommend for most patients,” says Reidy. “CMP will evaluate electrolytes, kidney function, and liver function. A CBC will look into your blood counts. Ferritin level will screen for iron deficiency, which can be the first sign of colon cancer. Lipoprotein a and LDL/lipid panel can give us insight into your risk for high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease. If you are obese or have a family history of diabetes, you might want to consider getting your A1C checked to rule out pre-diabetes or diabetes.”

Make sure you discuss any family history of cancer with your primary care provider while you’re at it. “Age-based cancer screening allows for early detection of certain types of cancers and reduces cancer mortality,” says Dr. Jacqueline Jepsen, family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

Your family history may influence when screening should begin and how frequently it should be performed, according to Dr. Harold Jaimes, board-certified internal medicine physician and owner of Jaimes Medical Group in Chicago.

“Always tell your doctor about any family history of cancer, especially when relatives were diagnosed at a younger age. This can significantly change screening recommendations,” he says.

“Routine colon cancer screening now begins at age 45 for most people, rather than 50. Be sure to tell your doctor if anyone in your family has had colon cancer, particularly at a younger age,” Jaimes says.

You might be at higher risk of colon cancer — and therefore require screening at an earlier age — if you have a history of radiation to the abdomen, inflammatory bowel disease, or certain types of polyps, according to the American Cancer Society.

“Age 40 is the year to start doing routine yearly mammograms. If you have dense breast tissue, then you might qualify for follow-up ultrasound,” Reidy says.

Women should stay current with cervical cancer screening, including Pap smears and/or HPV testing, as appropriate for their age and medical history, Jaimes adds. New guidelines allow for women to self-swab the vagina at home to be screened for HPV. If you’re someone who struggles with annual well woman visits, talk to your OB-GYN about this option.

Keeping up with the recommended vaccine schedule is an important part of disease prevention that boosts personal immunity and herd immunity, Jepsen says.

“The average age of menopause in America is 51 years old. However, the perimenopausal phase can last a few years and can look different in everyone. It’s good to talk to your doctor about what to look out for,” says Reidy.

Women, especially after menopause, are at risk of decreased bone density, Reidy points out. As Scary Mommy previously reported, you can maintain bone density with exercise, like strength training two to three times per week or adding walks, and even dancing, into your day-today. Bringing up osteoporosis with your doctor allows them to talk to you about any potential risk factors too.

“You might want to talk to your doctor about any chronic conditions, like celiac disease, or long-term use of steroids that might put you at increased risk of osteoporosis and warrant earlier screening,” Reidy says.

Exercising isn’t just about your weight; it turns out that your muscle mass is the best indicator of your longevity and quality of life as you age.

Most doctors recommend 150 minutes of moderate intensity exercise per week, but it’s important to talk to your doctor about what that means for you, Reidy says. Make a plan with your provider that takes into account your unique medical history, risk factors, and lifestyle.

“As we age, certain hormone levels change, and this is normal,” Jepsen says. “It is important to discuss with your doctor what signs of aging you should expect and what symptoms are ‘red flag’ symptoms, meaning you should reach out to your doctor to discuss further.”

“I remind my patients that many serious medical conditions develop silently, long before symptoms appear. Annual visits give us an opportunity to identify problems early, address risk factors, and hopefully prevent more serious illness down the road,” says Jaimes. “After all, we wouldn’t think twice about maintaining our cars to keep them running for years. Shouldn’t we give our own bodies at least the same attention?”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I think we're all big enough to admit that burning bush has spectacular autumn foliage, but there’s actually a native shrub deserves a place in the fall color spotlight... one that doesn't come with all the same problems.

As I'm sure many readers know already, burning bush is considered invasive in many states, as it can escape cultivation and spread into natural areas, where it fights with other plants (and usually comes out on top). So, yes, it's well worth looking at native shrubs that deliver that same bold fall foliage without the headache.

And is it too much to ask for more than just that? After all, I'm always drawn to plants that can do more than one job in the garden, so a native shrub that looks beautiful in fall, produces flowers for pollinators, and fruits that can feed birds? Why, it's an absolute must in my books!

So, which native shrub am I waxing lyrical about? Why, it's black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa), a native of eastern North America that is almost criminally underrated by gardeners all over the country... making something like the Viking Black Chokeberry from Nature Hills a brilliant investment for your space!

With its crimson-red to burgundy fall color, black chokeberry typically reaches around 3 to 6 feet tall and wide, making it a useful option for home gardens where a large shrub or small tree might be impractical. It can be planted in a mixed border, used in a native shrub planting, or incorporated into a wildlife-friendly landscape.

Better still? Unlike the pesky burning bush, which is primarily grown for its foliage and compact shape, black chokeberry (as mentioned already!) offers flowers and fruit, making it a standout beauty all season long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

This native shrub is a happily adaptable one, growing in full sun to partial shade and tolerating a range of soil conditions. It's also generally hardy across USDA zones 3 to 8, although I'd still be sure to check the requirements of a particular cultivar and confirm that it's suitable for your local climate.

In terms of maintenance, it generally doesn't need much intervention once established in a suitable location; just stick to the Three Ds rule when pruning as needed to keep its shape manageable. And otherwise? Well, just sit back and enjoy as its red and burgundy leaves bring the seasonal drama, its white flowers get minibeasts (including your birth month bug) buzzing, and its black berries attract birds like cardinals, waxwings, finches, robins, and more!

Oh sure, burning bush may feel more familiar, but familiarity isn't the only reason to choose a shrub. If I wanted brilliant fall color with the added potential to support local critters, black chokeberry would be at the top of my list... especially if I didn't want to land myself in hot water for planting an invasive beast of a shrub!

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#8135. The 14 Best Winter Comfort Foods That Aren't Soup

Warm, satisfying, delicious dishes you can chew.

I’m going to be vulnerable with you here: I don’t like soup that much. I know! I know. Burn me at the stake. Soup can be delightful and certainly has its place, but for me, soup will never satisfy in the same way as, I dunno, any other warm and savory food you can chew. If you’re with me, then you also probably look forward to your favorite winter comfort foods that aren’t soup. From pastas with savory sauces to giant pots of piping hot chili, these are some of my favorites to fall back on all throughout the coldest season of the year.

It’s hot, cheesy, carby, and filling — yep, Damn Delicious’ creamy beef and shells is a bona fide comfort dish. It’s essentially a homemade version of Hamburger Helper, and it’s one your family will ask for again and again.

Chili is the ultimate comfort meal, in my opinion. All The Healthy Things’ recipe is super easy — just brown your meat, dice your veg, and dump everything into the slow cooker for five to six hours on high or seven to eight on low. The best part of chili is adding all your favorite toppings, so don’t forget the avocados, cheese, and crushed Fritos.

Laughing Spatula’s cheesy chicken and broccoli casserole is so good when you’re feeding a crowd, and it’s particularly easy to make if you have some leftover chicken breasts lying around that you need to use up. Serve it with some garlic bread for maximum comfort.

Shepherd’s pie is one of those dishes I love but always seem to forget about when I’m planning what to make for dinner. Princess Pinky Girl’s version is super simple and uses instant mashed potatoes to speed things up, and overall is a surprisingly affordable meal for how many servings it yields.

When I think about the effort that goes into making a homemade soup, I think... what if I put the same amount of effort into something made of pasta instead? Averie Cooks’ homemade lasagna is such a great comfort meal for wintertime. It’s hot, saucy, cheesy, and just everything you could want.

If you were also introduced to beef bourguignon in the movie Julie & Julia, you were probably intimidated out of ever trying to cook it for yourself. Laughing Spatula’s version is much simpler because it’s made in the slow cooker and doesn’t require so much time and attention. You still get all the savory, herby deliciousness, which is what matters.

Dude That Cooks’ yellow fish curry feels nostalgic for me; when it was wintertime in college, I’d hit up the local Indian restaurant for yellow curry quite a bit. If a solid, spicy curry is what warms your bones best, you’ll be very happy with all the authentic flavor of this recipe.

Something about eating like I’m at a medieval tavern comforts my soul — the thought of crusty bread, a hunk of cheese, and a roast chicken feels like a balm against the winter cold. All The Healthy Things’ recipe will help you make a flavorful bird that’s done all the way through (and you should definitely eat those carrots in celery when they’re done — yum).

Chicken and dumplings is the comfort food in the South, and if you’ve never tried it, I urge you to make Princess Pinky Girl’s version. It’s a delicious, creamy chicken base with floating, fluffy dumplings bobbing throughout, and it’s ready in 30 minutes. Ugh, it’s just so good when you’ve been out in the cold all day.

Mac and cheese but make it seasonal? Twist my arm... Feel Good Foodie’s recipe for pumpkin mac and cheese is incredibly simple and requires very few ingredients. You could definitely toss in some chicken and broccoli to make this a more filling meal-in-a-bowl too.

Fried rice topped with a runny egg is a top tier comfort food. Damn Delicious’ version, kimchi fried rice, is even more delicious than your average bowl and you know the spice will help clear your sinuses and warm you up too.

I love an Averie Cooks’ recipe when I want to get maximum flavor out of minimal time spent in the kitchen. Her slow cooker Tuscan chicken offers just that, with a creamy, comforting Parmesan and sun-dried tomato sauce that’ll have you coming back to the Crockpot for seconds.

When nothing else sounds good, enchiladas always do. They’re hot and melty and cheesy and saucy and just...comforting. Simply LaKita’s are more exciting than your usual chicken or ground beef enchiladas. Hers are stuffed with chorizo, sweet potatoes, and a little bit of spinach, so you’re still getting your veggie servings in, don’t worry.

Welp, time to go drag my slow cooker back out again.

This article was originally published on Dec. 17, 2025

#8134. 6 ways to make homework less of a battle when your kid has ADHD

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A child psychiatrist on getting through the after-school hours without a standoff.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Tonight’s homework is a single worksheet. It’s been 50 minutes. Your kid has sharpened every pencil in the house, visited the bathroom twice, and is now face-down on the floor insisting it’s impossible. You can feel your patience slipping by the second.

If homework battles turn your evenings into a standoff, you’re far from alone, especially if your child has ADHD. About 1 in 9 US kids have been diagnosed with the condition , and the American Academy of Pediatrics says it can profoundly affect a child’s academic achievement. For families managing ADHD, the after-school stretch is often the hardest part of the day.

There’s a reason those hours are so trying. By the time a child with ADHD gets home,  they’ve spent “six or seven hours working harder than their classmates to sit still and focus,” says Michael Morse, MD, a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist who directs the ADHD & Anxiety Center at Alvord Baker and is an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University. That effort is used up, and for many kids the medication has worn off too, so “the after-school brain is often a tired brain.”

The resistance usually isn’t a matter of defiance. Executive function, the set of skills needed for getting started, planning and keeping track of steps, develops more slowly in kids with ADHD. That’s why a child can freeze in front of an assignment they’re fully capable of completing, and why the thing that helps is making the first step smaller rather than pushing harder.

The worst time to start homework is the moment your child walks through the door. The school day has already drained the same systems homework demands, so Morse suggests framing the immediate after-school window as a time to refuel. “A snack with some protein comes first, because after-school hunger makes both focus and mood worse,” he says. Movement comes next, whether that’s riding a bike or walking the dog, which burns off the day’s tension and helps many kids with ADHD settle. Make the break predictable with a clear end, and pick a consistent homework time that comes after the break and well before your child is too fried to think.

Most importantly, hold off on screens. “The transition from screens to homework can be particularly painful,” Morse says, so it’s usually easier not to turn them on after school at all.

“A task feels too big when a child can’t see where it starts,” Morse says. Many kids with ADHD freeze in front of a big assignment because their brain can’t break it into steps on its own, so the task is to shrink the first step until it feels easy.

Say a book report is due in two weeks. Sit down together and have your child break it into pieces: choose the book, read one chapter, jot notes on the main character. Then put each piece on a calendar so the deadline isn’t, in Morse’s words, “a cliff at the end.” For a single night’s work, 10 math problems can become two sets of five with a break in between. And when your child finishes a piece, say so out loud, since that small win makes the next one easier to start. (Younger kids need the pieces smaller and the check-ins more frequent.)

“Players usually appreciate coaches who run laps with them,” Morse says. He encourages parents to be “a coach and a model, not an enforcer.” In practice that can look like sitting at the kitchen table with your own work, while your child does theirs. A calm adult nearby helps many kids with ADHD get started and keep going. What a coach doesn’t do is finish the work so it comes back perfect, “because then the teacher never sees what the child can really do,” Morse says. The job is to help plan the night and praise the effort while leaving the outcome up to your child.

When homework turns into a power struggle, handing a little control back to your child can often defuse it. Offer two options you’re happy with either way, like “Math or reading first?” or “Before dinner or after, but before screens.” “A choice gives a child some control,” Morse says, which can take the fight out of the room before it starts. (If homework is still a daily battle no matter what you try, Morse notes a tutor can often take the coaching role with less friction than a parent.)

Some nights, the right move is to stop. “A parent should call it when the homework is no longer teaching anything or when substantial conflict emerges,” Morse says. If your child is in tears, exhausted or stuck on the same problem despite your help, more pushing won’t produce learning. “It mostly produces a worse night and a child who dreads the next one,” he says. When you stop, have your child’s back by sending the teacher a short note about how long they worked and where they got stuck. Most teachers would rather know.

“Your relationship with your child is more important than any assignment,” Morse says, and that relationship is what carries a kid through years of school. Kids with ADHD already hear a lot of criticism, and “if homework turns every evening into a battle, home stops feeling like the place where they’re accepted.”

Some homework problems are too big to solve at the kitchen table. “I’d start advocating when the problem looks bigger than effort,” Morse says. Watch for homework that routinely takes far longer than the teacher intended, work your child understands but can’t get written down or turned in, or nights that keep ending in tears. Those point to a gap between what the assignment asks and what your child can do right now, and pushing harder at home won’t close it.

Start by telling the teacher how long the work is actually taking. Some kids need more formal support through a 504 plan or an individualized education program, the school plans that put accommodations in writing. This matters especially for girls, Morse says, “whose late-night effort can keep their grades up and hide how much they’re struggling.”

As kids get older, Morse’s advice is to hand over the wheel gradually, with middle school as the moment to watch, when additional teachers and long-term projects arrive just as parents tend to step back. Teach your child to use a planner, check in briefly each evening, and let them take on more as they show they can. The long-term goal is teaching a kid which tasks will always need a system or a helper, because “knowing when to ask for help is one of the most valuable skills a teenager can carry into adult life.”

That need goes well beyond ADHD. Accountability partners and body doubles, “people whose quiet company helps you start and stay on task,” work for nearly everyone. “Not everyone knows to ask,” Morse says.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

150 boy names and 150 girl names, filled with history, beauty, and qualities a child can grow into.

Choosing a baby name can begin with sound, family tradition, or a meaning that catches you at exactly the right moment. Some names feel strong and grounded; others bring to mind light, tenderness, wisdom, or the beauty of the natural world. Then there are the ones that simply sound right when spoken aloud.

Muslim baby names draw from a rich range of languages, histories, and naming traditions. Arabic and Quranic choices appear here alongside other names found within Muslim families and communities. Some are familiar favorites, while others may offer something less commonly heard.

Meanings and English spellings can vary between languages, regions, and transliteration styles, so it is worth checking the pronunciation and cultural context before making a final choice. Ahead, find 300 Muslim baby names and the meanings connected to them.

Ihsan – Excellence; kindness; beautiful conduct

Tahsin – Improvement; enrichment; beautification

Delara – Beloved; one who delights the heart

Layan – Softness; gentleness; comfortable living

Rayhana – Fragrant basil; sweet-scented plant

A beautiful meaning is an important beginning, but a name also lives through pronunciation, family history, and the culture in which a child will grow. Say your favorites with the family name, write them down, and ask relatives how they sound in the languages your child may hear at home.

Often, the right choice is the one that feels natural when spoken and holds something your family hopes to pass on.
