#8121. Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

What Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

She doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

Even the loveliest flowering ornamentals can cause problems if left to self-seed. Fall is the time to remove these key bloomers before they take over your backyard

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Self-seeding flowers initially seem like a delight, particularly in a cottage garden border. There’s an effortless charm to volunteer blooms filling bare gaps between perennials, softening hard edges, and lending an organic, spontaneous feel. However, what starts out as a free-flowering companion can sometimes become an aggressive garden interloper. Left unchecked, enthusiastic self-sowers can quickly wind up in walkways, lawns, vegetable patches, and even your neighbors’ yards.

As their blooms fade, seed heads get ready to burst, scatter, or get carried away by animals to fill new areas. Once the seeds disperse, you’re facing a lot of cleanup in spring. The real danger with these prolific self-seeders lies in their competitive vigor. When permitted to drop seeds in fall, they naturally get a head start on anything you might add in spring, hogging nutrients, and casting shade over slower-growing sunseekers. So fall is an important time to keep key self-seeding flowers in place.

By intervening now to deadhead mature capsules, sever seed stems, and clear away dropped seed heads, you prevent billions of viable seeds from ever hitting the soil. And if there are any standout heirloom varieties you want to keep, you can save their seed for controlled sowing in spring, keeping all the beauty while sparing yourself lots of backbreaking pulling and digging next year. Here are the key culprits you need to control now, with insights on what to do with seed heads so you can still continue to enjoy them on your terms.

Some self-seeders are more aggressive than others, so you need to focus your efforts. Try the strategies that work best for your climate, yard and gardening goals, as well as your USDA hardiness zone. In colder zones 3-5, severe early frosts can sometimes halt late-forming seed heads before they mature. In milder southern and coastal regions (6-9), extended warm falls can give plants weeks of extra time to disperse seed capsules, making rapid intervention vital. Wind patterns and heavy rain can also transport tiny seeds across garden beds in a single afternoon.

The primary defense is regular deadheading. While removing spent flowers in summer promotes reblooming, autumn deadheading is about containment. As petals drop and seed heads swell, snip them away before they turn dark brown, dry out, or split. Always carry a deep bucket or paper sack with you. Tossing cut seed heads onto the ground or moving bare stems across the yard will inadvertently broadcast thousands of seeds hither and yon. Bag up seed heads and discard them in the household trash, never into home compost heaps, which rarely sustain the high internal temperatures required to destroy persistent weed seeds.

Not all self-seeders deserve eviction, however. Native wildflowers like purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) and native black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) produce sturdy seed cones that feed foraging goldfinches and native songbirds through winter without becoming overly thuggish. Choose this option for an area where you don’t mind some seed dispersal or with flowers that are less aggressive.

Additionally, selective seed saving is a great way to hang onto more unusual or heirloom bloomers. Harvest mature, unopened seed pods on a dry sunny afternoon. Use snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips, available from Amazon, to remove the heads. These spring-action blades give targeted deadheading without dropping loose seeds. Spread your collected seeds on paper towels to cure, then store them in labeled paper envelopes in a cool, dark drawer for measured sowing next spring.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With their feathery foliage and cheerful daisy blooms, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) add delicate color and movement to beds and borders. However, beneath their dainty features lies a fierce capacity for uninvited propagation. A single plant can produce dozens of flower heads from midsummer through frost, each maturing into a cluster of needle-like seeds with barbed tips that catch on fur, gloves, and clothing.

To prevent cosmos from transforming into an unruly forest next year, inspect the fading flower heads now before the central florets turn black and stiff. Cut off spent blooms while the seed heads are still green or pale tan, or shear the entire plant to ground level once the first frost blackens the stems. If you wish to save seed, snip off a few brown heads on a dry day, strip the spiky seeds into paper envelopes, and store seeds in a cool, dark drawer for sowing next spring. For a good storage tin, try the Pethiy Green Storage Seed Tin, available from Walmart, which I love for its rustic appearance and enduring, airtight reliability.

Also known as cleome, spider flowers (Cleome hassleriana) produce spidery floral globes with extra-long stamens for brilliant late-season drama in borders. Yet few cottage annuals reseed with as much ruthless efficiency. As petals drop along the lengthening flower stalks, they leave behind long, slender, bean-like seed pods held on wiry pedicels. As these mature from green to brown, they dry out, crack open, and fling dozens of seeds across the yard.

Tackle your cleome before the seed pods reach the brittle stage. However, take care, as mature stems develop sharp spines and sticky hairs. Wear heavy gauntlet gloves and long sleeves. If you need a good pair of long-lasting gauntlet gloves, I love the Womanswork Arm Saver Garden Gloves, available from Anthropologie, with their gorgeous floral pattern and comfy fit. Snip off those green pods and bag them, or sever the entire stalk. If you love their height, keep a few ripe, unopened pods in a paper bag to dry, ensuring you dictate where they grow next season.

Pretty, delicate forget-me-nots (Myosotis sylvatica) are cherished for their sea of sky-blue flowers, creating a romantic underplanting beneath tulips and flowering shrubs. However, their common name carries a double meaning: if you forget to remove their seed heads, you will spend years pulling up unwanted seedlings from rockeries and paving cracks. Each spent flower produces tiny nutlets with barbs that cling to animal fur and shoelaces, scattering those seeds far and wide.

Ideally, it’s wise to deadhead right after flowering, but this month is the deadline to scout your beds for lingering plants that set seed during late summer. Rake through mulch with a hand cultivator to expose any dry, brown seed clusters that escaped summer snipping. Sever any remaining seed stems, bag the debris, and apply a 2-inch (5cm) layer of clean mulch where needed. Go for an organic wood-based option such as team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon. This smothers new seeds by depriving them of the sunlight and winter chilling triggers they need to germinate in spring.

Revered by landscape designers for its airy stems topped by vivid violet and pinky-purple blooms, Verbena bonariensis (aka tall verbena or purpletop vervain) is a pollinator magnet that butterflies adore. However, in zones 7-10, this designer darling can be an invasive self-seeding powerhouse. Just a single plant produces tens of thousands of dust-like seeds capable of surviving freezing winters. These germinate with wild abandon in spring.

The challenge lies in how easily mature seed heads shed. The moment the blooms turn from purple to a dull brown, the tiny seeds loosen and scatter at the slightest brush of a breeze or sleeve. Cut back the flowering stems now, while flower clusters still hold a hint of lilac, or cup a bucket beneath the stems as you snip to catch dropping seed heads. Use wipes, such as Clorox Disinfecting Wipes 3-Pack from Walmart, to protect your snips and shears from clinging micro-seeds. Bag cut stems immediately to prevent contaminating lawn edges.

This vintage cottage garden annual is admired for its blue, pink, and white blooms nestled within a fluffy ruff of misty green bracts. Following bloom, love-in-a-mist (Nigella damascena) flowers transform into intriguing striped seed capsules that look like paper lanterns. While these pods look stunning in dried floral arrangements, it’s risky to leave them in the garden. Once they burst, they will shed hundreds of seeds across your yard like demented pepper shakers.

So, as soon as you see their green lanterns developing dark striping and they start to feel papery to the touch, harvest them with snips before the top horns split. Cut the stems long and tie them upside down inside a paper sack. The seeds will drop into the bag as the capsules dry. Save these in airtight tins for controlled springtime planting. If you need seed-saving envelopes, Artrylin Self-Seal Seed Envelopes (150-Pack) from Walmart are great for labeling, dating, and organising your seeds.

Also known as pot marigold, calendula (C. officinalis) is a hardworking cool-season annual that brightens borders and edible gardens, and continues blooming late into fall. However, each spent bloom forms a dense ring of seeds with hooked backs, which cling to tools, garden clothing, and pet fur, hitchhiking to new corners of your yard. If left undisturbed, fallen seeds create thick mats of seedlings that can choke out early spring bulbs. Deadhead those spent blooms the moment the petals wilt, snipping just below the green seed ring before it gets rigid.

If self-sown seeds have already scattered across the topsoil, lightly skim the surface with a hand rake to collect the seeds. Then cover the area with compost or shredded bark mulch to prevent early spring calendula germination. If you fancy adding some compost but don’t have enough of your own, The Home and Country USA Store do lovely little Mushroom Compost Pails from Amazon, to help you create a good soil blanket after sorting out your seed heads.

Few annuals provide the explosive vigor of the Mexican sunflower (Tithonia rotundifolia). Reaching 6-8 feet (1.8-2.4m) tall with brilliant orange blooms, it can draw monarchs and hummingbirds from miles around. However, that size poses a major problem when it self-seeds. Spring volunteer seedlings grow with ferocious speed, quickly developing thick stems and umbrella-like leaves that cast deep shade over surrounding perennials and crops.

By October, spent blooms transform into dark seed heads packed with dozens of stiff, pointed seeds that shatter outward at the slightest bump. Cut fading flowers back promptly before the centers turn dry and brittle. Once frost claims the foliage, chop down the hollow stalks and take them to the municipal waste. If you need strong debris sacks, Lowe’s Heavy Duty Debris Bags hold coarse stalks and seedheads securely for curbside yard disposal. Never toss mature heads into your home compost, or you will see hundreds of giant seedlings in beds next season.

Self-seeding can bring dynamic energy to the landscape, but if you want to prevent unwanted thuggish invasions (and all the gardening chores that go with that) then take timely fall action. The trick is deciding which flowers to allow to spread, which to manage, and how extensively to manage them.

By snipping off ripe seed heads and clearing away loose seed clusters, you can eliminate hours of weeding next spring. It might take a little trial and error, but don’t ignore your self-seeders or you might well regret it come spring. Harvest the seeds you want to keep, dispose of the rest, and enjoy a beautifully balanced and better behaved space next year.

October 16th has been recognized as National Feral Cat Awareness Day since its creation by Alley Cat Allies in 2001. Here at Catster, we believe it takes more than just one day to make a difference, and thatâs why weâre joining Mission: Meow in campaigning to make October National Feral Cat Awareness Month: a time to learn more about feral and community cats and the challenges they face.

These cats may live outdoors and have limited contact with people, but they are still an important part of many communities and deserve care and compassion.

Feral cats are unsocialized domestic cats who typically avoid close human interaction. Some were born outdoors, while others may have become feral after living without regular human contact. Community cats can also include friendly strays and other free-roaming felines who rely on outdoor resources.

One of the most widely used approaches for managing feral cat populations is trap-neuter-return (TNR). Through TNR programs, cats are humanely trapped, spayed or neutered, vaccinated, and returned to their outdoor homes. This can help prevent litters while allowing cats who arenât comfortable living indoors to remain in familiar surroundings. Through surgical sterilization, TNR reduces feral cat numbers without culling or disrupting cat colonies.

National Feral Cat Awareness Month is also an opportunity to learn how to safely interact with community cats, support local TNR efforts, and recognize when a cat may need additional help.

Catster has compiled its resources on feral cats, TNR, community cat care, and related topics to make it easier to find reliable information and learn more about helping cats living outdoors.

And while I love making our house look festive around the holidays — from our every-expanding lawn graveyard in October to cozy accents and twinkly touches for a winter wonderland — each year I’m reminded that the homes with the most impressive displays are all about the lighting. You know what I’m talking about: they’re the ones your kids excitedly point to, eyes glazed over with awe-struck longing, and sigh, “Why can’t we do that?”

Well, now you can — and you don’t have to be a professional lighting tech (or even close!) to do it yourself. Govee teamed up with horror icon Sarah Michelle Gellar as part of its “Turn Up The Spooky. Slay Halloween” campaign, helping you to transform your home into a delightfully haunted house using colorful lighting and atmosphere — they even co-created a short film, Turn Up the Spooky, on the subject. The crux of Gellar’s advice? Don’t feel like you have to go overboard in order to have the most festive house on the block.

“Instead of covering every inch of the exterior in light, choose one architectural or landscape feature to be the focus, such as the roofline, a tree or the front facade,” Gellar advises. “Leaving some areas darker will make the lit areas feel more dramatic.”

That same focus on contrast and shadow comes to life in Last Light, an original short horror film made with Ryan Connolly, founder of the DIY filmmaking channel Film Riot. In a companion how-to video, Connolly takes viewers behind the scenes of Last Light, breaking down the practical lighting tricks and creative techniques used to build its haunting atmosphere. From playing with color and contrast to using shadows for dramatic effect, the video offers inspiration for bringing a little Hollywood-style Halloween magic to your own front yard — no professional crew required.

Inspired to give your own home the Hollywood horror treatment? Both Gellar’s and Connolly’s techniques are surprisingly simple to recreate at home. Set the mood along your roofline with the brand’s Permanent Outdoor Lights Prism, add pops of color with the Outdoor Clear Bulb String Lights, and cast a dramatic wash across exterior walls with the Outdoor UpDown Wall Light.

For peak spooky, try placing a white sheet over the inside of a window and shining red light toward it from within, accenting the mood with glowing contrast lights under your roofline. Or pick a main lighting color scheme for the entire house, like jack-o-lantern orange, and use an accent color near the entryway, to make the whole display feel that much more dramatic.

Another pro tip: Don’t forget the shadows! Choose one decoration or part of the house to spotlight, then let the surrounding area stay dark. A single well-lit skeleton can somehow feel scarier than a whole yard of brightly lit ones. Don’t ask why — I don’t make the rules.

#8114. I Was Treated for Depression for Years. Nobody Asked About ADHD.

I wish I had been more curious to find deeper answers sooner.

I started taking antidepressants in my late teens. One didn’t seem to change much, so I tried another. I kept asking for help, taking the medications I was prescribed, and waiting for the point when everyday life would stop feeling like a group project I was somehow doing alone.

Some of those medications were incredibly difficult to come off of. And after all that effort, I was still exhausted. Still overwhelmed. Still wondering why things that looked ordinary from the outside took so much out of me.

I thought I was depressed. Anxiety seemed possible, too. Those explanations made sense with the information I had, so I kept trying to get better within them. When treatment didn’t change the parts of life I was struggling with, I didn’t think, Maybe there’s another question to ask. I thought, What the hell is wrong with me?

Then other people in my family were diagnosed with ADHD, and I began looking at my own history differently.

I want to be clear: A family diagnosis didn’t diagnose me. It made me curious. For the first time, I wondered whether what I’d understood as depression had been ADHD all along — or whether ADHD explained the difficulties that treatment had never touched.

The picture of ADHD I’d grown up with was a little boy who couldn’t sit still. I didn’t know to look for a woman who could appear to be holding it together while privately using every last bit of energy to do so.

A finished task looks like a finished task. You can’t see how long it took her to start it. An appointment she remembered looks like an appointment she remembered. You can’t see the reminders. A mom who gets everyone through the day looks like a mom who’s managing. You don’t necessarily see her sitting afterward, wondering why it took absolutely everything she had.

That invisible effort can become your normal. You assume everyone is working this hard behind the scenes. Then you blame yourself for needing so much effort in the first place.

I now host Chaos & Caffeine, an ADHD parenting podcast, and I’ve talked with ADHD specialist Dr. Jennifer Dall about ways ADHD can be missed in women. We discussed masking, burnout, emotional overwhelm, and the maddening experience of being unable to begin a task you genuinely want to do.

If you’ve never experienced that last one, I know how it sounds. Just do the thing. Thank you. Incredible idea. Why didn’t I think of that while spending half the day wanting to do the thing?

From the outside, difficulty getting started can look like laziness. Doing everything at the last minute can look like a bad habit. Being worn out after a day of keeping up can look like someone who needs to manage stress better. Over time, those judgments get inside your head. You stop describing what’s happening and start describing yourself as the problem.

Dr. Dall and I also talked about hormones. Puberty can make ADHD symptoms harder to manage or more noticeable. Later hormonal changes — during pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause, and menopause — can affect how a woman experiences symptoms or how well her old coping strategies work. That conversation made me think about how young I was when I first sought help, and how much of my history I had never known to bring up.

I’m not saying every hard moment in my life was ADHD. Depression and anxiety are real, and they can exist alongside ADHD. Antidepressants help many people. I can’t go back and declare that everyone who treated me got it wrong.

But I can say this: I kept asking for help because something wasn’t getting better. I wish that had prompted more curiosity about what was still happening in my daily life.

If this sounds painfully familiar, please don’t use my story to diagnose yourself or stop taking medication. Some antidepressants need to be tapered with a prescriber’s help; I know firsthand that coming off certain ones can be hard. Instead, tell a qualified clinician what treatment hasn’t changed. Describe the tasks, the time management, the overwhelm, and the effort it takes to look fine. Talk about what you remember from childhood and whether ADHD runs in your family. Ask if a fuller evaluation makes sense.

You don’t have to walk into an appointment knowing the answer. You’re allowed to walk in saying, “Something still isn’t adding up.”

That’s what I wish someone had told me when I was younger. I wasn’t failing at getting better because I still needed help. I was trying to explain a struggle I didn’t yet have all the words for.

It took diagnoses in my family to make me ask a different question about myself. If another woman has spent years following a treatment plan and still quietly wondering why life feels so damn hard, I hope someone listens when she says it isn’t working. And then I hope they ask what else might be going on.

Danielle Kelly is the host of the ADHD parenting podcast Chaos & Caffeine, which reaches thousands of families each month and was recently named one of the Best Kids With ADHD Podcasts of 2026 by PodRanker.

We all dream of a perennial that keeps the garden looking good long after summer has packed its bags, don't we? You know, the kind that keeps producing beautiful flowers just when you think the growing season has nothing left to give.

It's fair enough; as temperatures dip and fall settles in, even the prettiest garden can start looking a little lackluster. The summer blooms start fading, the flower beds lose their sparkle, and you're probably wondering whether it's time to call it a year.

Thankfully, there's one unusual perennial that can bring a welcome splash of late-season color just when you need it most... and, despite its rather unflattering name, it looks seriously beautiful while doing it.

The toad lily (Tricyrtis), a shade-loving perennial with intricate, orchid-like flowers covered in colorful spots. Blooming in late summer and fall, it offers a surprisingly exotic display at a time when many other plants are winding down.

And despite its rather unflattering name, this little-known garden gem has plenty going for it. With delicate blooms that look more at home in a tropical greenhouse than a shady backyard, the toad lily is the sort of plant that makes you stop, take a closer look, and wonder why you aren't growing it already.

Let's get one thing straight: the toad lily isn't actually an orchid, no matter how much it might look like one. Rather, as the name suggests, it's a member of the lily family, and its botanical name is Tricyrtis.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Depending on the species or variety, the blooms may feature white or pale lavender petals, deep purple freckles, and contrasting yellow or purple centers. Some have a star-shaped appearance, while others look more like tiny funnels. Either way, though, their delicate details are best appreciated up close, rather than from the other side of the yard, as they look almost as though someone has taken a miniature paintbrush to every flower.

In other words, this isn't just another pretty perennial that relies on enormous flowers to make an impression; it's all about the details. And those details are exactly what make it such a charming addition to a shady garden.

Spring and summer get most of the attention when it comes to flowering perennials. By the time fall rolls around, many gardeners are left with attractive foliage, fading blooms, and a growing collection of plants preparing for winter.

The toad lily, however, usually begins flowering in late summer or early fall, with some continuing into October and, under favorable conditions, even November. (The exact timing depends on the variety, local climate, and when the first hard frost arrives in your USDA Planting Zone).

If you're looking for a plant that helps bridge the gap between summer color and the quieter months of winter, then, this is one of those flowers you've never heard of that's worth considering, especially as many varieties prefer partial to full shade, making them particularly useful beneath trees, along woodland borders, or in those awkward shade garden corners where sun-loving flowers struggle.

Despite their exotic appearance, toad lilies aren't especially demanding when planted in the right conditions. Pop yours somewhere it won't get too much direct sun, as this can scorch the foliage (particularly if the soil dries out), and keep the soil consistently moist.

That being said, make sure excess water can drain away because, while moist soil is good; persistently waterlogged roots are another matter. Many toad lilies spread gradually through creeping underground stems or rhizomes, forming attractive clumps over time, so they appreciate a bit of space, too.

There's something especially satisfying about discovering a fall flowering perennial that offers something different from the usual lineup of autumn mums and asters, especially one that brings delicate orchid-like flowers, attractive foliage, and a welcome burst of color just when the garden might otherwise be winding down.

Honestly, if anyone asks why you've planted something called a toad lily, simply invite them over for a closer look. Once they see those extraordinary little blooms, the name might be the last thing on their mind.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. Or, since we are lovers by nature, it might be better to say we just donât like catsâat least we say it that way in public. But if you are in the canine fan club, as most men should be, you know the unarticulated raison d'Ãªtre of a dog person is that we hate cats. Or should at least say so among ourselves.

Naturally, we have childhood stories aplenty. You know the kind: they begin like âI sat there with Sally, we sat there we two,â as the good doctor who taught us our phonics would render. But, mostly, itâs cats or dogs, one or the other. Dogs are for guys, cats are for girls, right?

I grew up with Piper and Smokey, a black standard Poodle and a German Shepherd. Later came Corky and Maggie, a Miniature Poodle and a yellow Lab. And Lassie, a Collie (of course); my dadâs and my best friend at the time. Dad, a physician, took her to work every day; his patients would bring her treats and toys. When Lassieâs hips gave out toward the end, he still took her to work every day, carrying her up to his second-floor office where she would lie in the hallway all day, loving the patients who would come by to pet her and wish her well. When she just could not go on anymore, Dad taught me about the end of life and a dog. The pain, Dad said, was the important thing: âItâs okay for them to be sick and dying on their own time, just so long as they are not in pain.â And then, one night, it happened. Lassie went to sleep.

My favorite, though, was Dagny. Dagny is her own special story; I cannot tell it here, but she was the best friend I ever had, and after fifteen years of perpetual motion, I took my Dadâs lesson to heart and applied it to Dagny. I think that was the best I could do, and the best for Dagny, too.

This brings us to my conversion. I knew I could never own another dog; I just couldnât replace Dagny. But one day, I noticed in my backyard a tiger-striped cat, just sitting under one of my lemon trees. I thought, âHuh,â and not a lot more of it. She was there the next day, and the next, and the next. I called her âDanielle Striped Tigerâ after one of Mister Rogersâs puppets. Then I noticed the two kittens. They looked like brothers â same coat â and they were playing in the yard as Danielle watched.

My friend, Gay, the greatest friend cats will ever have, told me: âDanielle is their mother, and she was camping out to see if it was a safe place for them to frolic.â She added, âNow you must put some food and water out for them.â

Excuse me? Are you new here? What?!! Iâm now going to be feeding cats?!! Iâm going to be buying cat food now?

My friend Hugh had a cat like this, and he informed me that yes, Gay was quite right; this was the duty of a gentleman. It is the code of honor, decency, and kindness.

One of my favorite laws in all of Judaism is a Talmudic take on a statement from Deuteronomy: we are all obligated to feed our animals in the morning before we feed ourselves. I was scrupulous about this law with Dagny â maybe the only religious law I was scrupulous about!

Then there is a Chasidic tale of a Rabbi who bought a horse, not that he rode or needed a horse, but just so he could fulfill this law. And it struck me: with Dagny no longer with me, these cats were gifts from God to help me continue to fulfill this order.

So, I had three cats. And they needed names. No problem. In his poem, The Naming of Cats, T.S. Eliot said every cat has three names:

the name he is known by in the community, and

the name nobody knows: the name the cat knows for himself alone, how he thinks of himself.

âWhen you notice a cat in profound meditation, the reason, I tell you, is always the same: His mind is engaged in a rapt contemplation of the thought, of the thought, of the thought of his name: His ineffableâ¦Deep and inscrutable singular name.â

So, I now had Alonzo and Aloysios, and Danielle. And cat food. Lots of cat food. Alonzo would eat in front of me; Aloysios and Danielle would not. Fine, what did I care? I was just fulfilling Gay, and Hughâs, and Godâs commandments. And I told myself: these cats would never come in the house; I would not be a cat guy. I was a guy with three feral cats, thatâs all, just doing the right thing by them.

There is some sort of telegraph, I guess, invisible to the human eye, and soon the word went out: âFree food!â

Soon, âBad, Bad, Leroy Brown,â a beast of an ugly thing, started coming around. Evidently, cats also arenât familiar with the concept of âthe tragedy of the commonsâ, for they talk. They talk in the community, they gossip like ladies at a mahjong game, and now, there are âJellyâ and âBeans.â

And Iâm now buying more food and getting less sleep. I have no idea what there is for them to discuss, but discuss they do; loudly and at length. I have no idea why they need to do it in my yard, and yet, they do. I have no idea why they need to reenact Dick Van Dykeâs performance from Mary Poppins on my roof every night, but every night, they do.

Growing up, my sister had âMittensâ â all black, white paws,feral, never in the house â and Mittens knew that âloose lips sink shipsâ. Every night my sister fed her, and only her. There were no others. Mittens knew how to keep a secret.

Mine? They seem to think this is a charitable soup kitchen. There are a few others here and there, including a soon-to-be-regular, I think: all white with black rings around the tail. And can you help me with that name? I know weâre gonna need one.

But hereâs the thing: we cannot let the dog-loving community or the rest of the men in the world know. #8111. Whimsigoth Decor & Witchy Gifts To Use Year-Round

From a serpent rug to a whimsigoth-coded jacket, we have every intention of using these bewitching pieces all year.

It happens almost ritualistically every year: On Nov. 1, homes across America are de-gothed. Un-Halloween’ed. The plastic skeletons go back in the attic, and the orange string lights get stuffed in a garage bin until next fall. But for those of us who love a little magic in our everyday lives, packing it all away can feel kind of... sad?

So, we’re eschewing the idea that you can only embrace your witchiness once a year. The secret is choosing things that feel more whimsigoth than kitschy (though there’s a time and place for kitsch, too!). We’re reaching for moody botanicals and celestial motifs and apothecary-style glass. These are pieces that look right at home next to a cauldron in October but are pretty enough to keep out in March, and the same goes for what we’re wearing and how it makes us feel: a gothic perfume, a perfect witchy nail polish, pointed-toe shoes that feel a little wicked.

We rounded up the finds that make us feel bewitched all year long, from a snake-adorned rug to a notebook that feels plucked straight from an enchanted fairytale. And nope, we don’t have any plans to pack them away once the moon sets on spooky season.

When I redid my home office, I knew I wanted it to give Practical Magic energy. This gorgeous, gothic-glam rug anchors my entire vision for the space. The snake-and-floral design by Martyn Lawrence Bullard for Ruggable feels moody and luxe, and its machine-washable, stain-resistant fabric means it’ll hold up to my very real, not-always-luxe life as a busy working mom. I’m so obsessed with it. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This adorable notebook lives on my desk year-round because it is exactly the kind of beautiful, nature-forward aesthetic I want surrounding me every single day. The illustrated mushroom cover is rich, detailed, and has that perfect witchy botanical vibe that feels equally at home in October as it does in March. The A5 size is ideal for a nightstand, a coffee table, or a desk without taking over the whole space; the paper quality is thick and lovely, and it is the kind of object that makes people pick it up and comment on it every time they see it. The Halloween decor that is really just gorgeous everyday stationery that happens to have a very good autumn energy! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

In fall, I'm obsessed with wearing witchy perfumes — and this year Granado has put out a pair of "gothic, fruity" scents that I am obsessed with. My favorite is their fig scent, which smells so beautifully of the deep, mossy woods and fall harvests of dark fruits. Along with the main fig note, it smells of rose, date, labdanum, and cedarwood. I want to bathe in it. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

I very much treat books like art in my house, using them year-round to create little vignettes. So I could not resist adding a few “spooky” books to my library. A clothbound edition of Frankenstein featuring an anatomical heart pattern, stacked with Dracula, or a black-edged copy of The Haunting of Hill House? It’s moody, it’s witchy, it’s gorgeous... especially paired with a couple of antique candleholders or dark crystals. It definitely delivers the gothic library look I love. — Julie Sprankles

This particular Nautilus Puzzle has earned its place in my fall decor and activity rotation because it's just too pretty to put away. The Nautilus wooden puzzles are laser-cut with the most intricate, unexpected whimsy pieces hidden throughout that make the whole experience feel like discovering little surprises as you go, and the Japanese Bridge image is absolutely stunning in those deep greens and golds that feel made for autumn. The 237-piece count is the perfect weekend afternoon size where you feel genuinely accomplished when you finish without losing your mind over it, and the wooden pieces have a satisfying weight and quality that makes regular cardboard puzzles feel like a downgrade forever after. Fall cozy activity that doubles as a beautiful display piece while it is in progress! After I finish these, I put Mod Podge all over them and frame. — Katie Garrity

This is the perfect shade for witch nails — and honestly, I will not stop wearing this color even after spooky season is over. Love it on my toes, too! — Sarah Aswell

I mean, does this not look like something a witch would keep on an old wooden shelf next to her jars of dried herbs and tinctures? The amber glass vessel has that old-world apothecary vibe that looks so pretty lit or unlit, and the tobacco and patchouli scent makes my house smell so cozy and maybe just a little mysterious too. When it’s burned out, I’m going to clean out the jar and use it to hold matches on my mantel, which seems just as witchy and whimsical. — Julie Sprankles

I’m buying these for my daughter because Monica + Andy’s Halloween pajamas are exactly the kind of whimsical, quality set that feels special rather than just a cheap seasonal find. The organic cotton is incredibly soft, the prints are genuinely cute without being overwhelming, and the fit is generous enough that she can wear them through the whole season without growing out of them in three washes. The Halloween tradition starts the moment they go on and immediately becomes a non-negotiable part of the season! — Katie Garrity

I love these witchy candles! They come with crystals in the wax and a blend of essential oils, all chosen for a specific purpose. I love the Defense candle, which mixes smoky quartz and cedarwood, among other scents, to create a protective shield around you. So fun, and definitely fun year-round and not just around Halloween. — Sarah Aswell

These claw clips have full witchy fall energy. The Philocaly acrylic clips come in deep jewel tones, smoky neutrals, and rich autumn shades that look like they were designed specifically for the season, and the clear acrylic has a quality and weight that makes them feel like actual accessories rather than just functional hair tools. They hold an entire head of hair all day without snapping, slipping, or breaking, which means your messy bun stays exactly where you put it through every haunted hayride, apple picking adventure, and cozy bookstore visit on the fall agenda. — Katie Garrity

This is the most witch-coded leather jacket I have ever put upon my shoulders, and I am here for it! This is so fun and feminine while being just a little bit quirky, and I do not want to stop wearing it even after spooky season ends. I love wearing it with a belt or pairing it with the (also witchy) black satin skirt that Quince sells, too. — Sarah Aswell

I’m clearly a huge fan of decor that pulls double duty, like this beautiful little incense burner. The glossy black ceramic dish features a celestial star design, with a gold crescent moon right in the center to hold an incense stick. It’s also perfect as a tiny trinket dish for tossing your rings in at the end of the day! And at under $20, it (a) looks much pricier than it is and (b) is such an affordable dose of witchy charm. — Julie Sprankles

For the witchy fall vibes guide, this sweater is doing everything right — the oversized hooded zip-up silhouette is cozy and effortless in a way that reads as intentionally mysterious rather than just comfortable, and the rich fall colorways are exactly the kind of moody, autumnal palette that makes any outfit feel like it has an aesthetic. It is SO soft, has a relaxed fit, and the kind of piece you throw on over literally anything and immediately look like you have your whole fall wardrobe figured out. — Katie Garrity

This Kwendy collab is technically one of Magenta’s Halloween collections, but let me tell you — these mugs are way too pretty to retire on Nov. 1. The rich auburn color and shining gold wrap of celestial illustrations are meant to be enchanting and, well, I’m enchanted! Inspired by creator Wendy’s love of “mystical oddities” and “apothecary treasures,” it’s just the perfect vessel for my morning lattes and teas. I’m deeply unwell with obsession over this entire collection, tbh. The quality and artistry are stunning. — Julie Sprankles

I got a witchy bra set this month, thanks to Knix's new limited-edition A Court of Thorns & Roses collection, and I will not be taking it off year-round. Are you really living until you have a pair of period underwear with constellations on it? I need more reasons to look forward to my period. And YES, I got the matching boxers for my partner. — Sarah Aswell

I truly believe every room in the house deserves a bit of witchiness, and this pillow brings that to my living room. It’s black cotton velvet with gorgeous embroidery and a contrasting fringe border, so it reads as elevated gothic glam. I like that it works so well for Halloween, but then for the rest of the year it serves as a cheeky reminder that being a little bad can feel really good sometimes. — Julie Sprankles

I was looking for something to finish off all of my witchy looks, and then I found these: black pearl earrings that bring my spooky self to a perfect 10. There is something so beautiful and magical about a black pearl, and these earrings are understated but send a strong message of witchiness that is not surpassed. These are also responsibly sourced from Tahiti, so no danger of bad karma or curses. — Sarah Aswell

I currently have this lantern on my entry table, and I feel like it gives my foyer just the most delicious pop of fairy-tale forest energy. It’s etched black metal with intricate forest cutouts and a golden interior, so a lit candle inside casts flickering shadows and such a cozy glow. Oh, and there’s a bonus that brings me immense joy: When I blow out the candle, the smoke drifts up and out the top opening like a chimney in a storybook cottage. — Julie Sprankles

Every witch needs her potions, right? One of my favorite things about being a tea drinker is the ritual of it, and Dona’s tea concentrates genuinely make that ritual feel extra special: You mix the concentrate with milk, then heat it, steam it, or pour it over ice. This lineup (Masala Chai, Cardamom Rose, Turmeric) seems like it would be right at home in an apothecary! I like to sprinkle some spice on top of mine and then enjoy my oh-so-yummy latte out of an oversized mug. — Julie Sprankles

Launched just in time for Halloween, you cannot get more gothic and witchy than this perfume. The notes include cypress, black peppercorn, rose, saffron, Peru balsam, smoldering frankincense, leathered woods, and musk, and I can't wear it without feeling like I'm wearing a black floor-length gown and running through the woods toward an abandoned church. I will not stop wearing this on Nov. 1, no way. — Sarah Aswell

I’ve always thought pointed-toe shoes inherently feel a little witchy, so, naturally, I packed these perfect Rothy’s flats for my recent trip to Salem. The tortoise knit is a fun take on fall’s animal-print moment, and the roomy toe box and cushioned insole kept my feet happy while I wandered the witchiest streets in America. Safe to say I will be wearing these everywhere all year long. — Julie Sprankles

Still not sure how to make the whimsigoth style stick? We asked a practicing Witch, an interior designer, and an event strategist for their best advice on keeping the magic alive.

#8110. Why Do Moms Feel Like We Need Permission To Sleep?

A recent survey found that half of moms would rather sleep than have a spa day. So why is it so hard to give ourselves permission to rest?

My husband can fall asleep anywhere, anytime. Once, we took a day trip to Sedona, Arizona, and he fell asleep sitting on a rock. It’s a talent. And the amazing thing is... the kids actually left him alone. Me, on the other hand? I can be missing for five minutes, and they have spidey senses. I can’t remember the last time anyone let me nap without pouncing on me within a few minutes of trying.

And here’s another thing: I often sacrifice sleep for productivity. I can be exhausted at night, but if I haven’t accomplished everything on my to-do list, whether it’s remembering to email one of my kids’ teachers back, loading the dishwasher, or prepping for tomorrow’s interview, I’ll stay awake until it’s done. When my head finally hits the pillow, my mind often keeps spinning through tomorrow’s to-do list.

Apparently, I’m not the only mom doing this.

Naturepedic, an organic sleep wellness brand, recently released a survey of 1,000 U.S. mothers ages 25–45 with children under 18 living at home. Of those surveyed, 90% of moms said they struggle to quiet their busy minds at bedtime, and 48% get fewer than seven hours of sleep, with moms of kids 2 and younger averaging about 5.9 hours.

What’s even bleaker: 62% of moms feel they need someone else’s formal permission to prioritize their own sleep without feeling guilty.

Naturpedic calls this the "sleep permission gap," the disconnect between knowing we need rest and actually allowing ourselves to get it. But why are we treating sleep like a privilege we have to earn rather than a basic human need? And how do we stop this sad, nasty little habit?

Although more men are stepping up to help with household duties, unequal household responsibilities, limited support, and parenting demands can still play a role. For moms, who rarely get a break, this pressure can build up. Getting a juicy eight or nine hours of sleep? Somehow, that can feel oddly gluttonous, or like we’re wasting precious time.

"We live in a society where we increasingly measure a person's value by how much they do and how much they produce," says Lorena Bernal, founder of Live Love Better and author of It Starts With You.

She says mothers can feel selfish or lazy when they choose to rest instead of doing something for their families, adding that “in a way, mothers can feel too needed to switch off.”

For moms, nighttime is also often our only chance for “quiet time” or to catch up on things we’ve been putting off. I end up sitting on the couch a little longer, bingeing social media reels for five or 10 minutes because I don’t feel I have time to watch an actual TV series.

But this habit can also stretch to the point where I ask myself why I keep putting off sleep to Google something stupid, like how long Zac Efron and Vanessa Hudgens dated in real life (don’t judge: my daughter just discovered High School Musical).

Emily Krushefski, a licensed professional counselor and CEO of Emotional Innovations, says self-blame also serves an unexpected psychological purpose: a sense of control. In our heads, we might decide we're exhausted because we didn't manage our time well enough. She says we think that if we become more organized, productive, or disciplined, we can fix the problem.

I can relate, as I’m prone to staying up late to make the next day “easier,” which only deepens my exhaustion. "The illusion of being in charge of these complex and unrelenting demands provides a sense of agency," Krushefski explains.

She gives voice to what many of us mothers feel — that we juggle too many expectations for our families while managing our careers, other relationships, and the lovely, never-ending household responsibilities. "Sometimes the problem isn't that nobody will let us rest," says Bernal. "It's that we have become so identified with being the person who takes care of everything that we struggle to give ourselves permission to put it down."

When researchers asked what would help the mothers surveyed sleep better, 59% said someone taking over household chores, while 58% said being allowed to sleep in.

My only question is: Sleeping in? What’s that?

After years of waking up to care for babies and young children, our brains can become accustomed to nighttime vigilance, and that pattern can be hard to break as kids get older.

My kids are getting older, but I still wake consistently throughout the night. Similarly, I find that when I’m super busy, I just can’t shut off my brain when I get to bed, even if I’m exhausted. Krushefski explains that the mental load of managing a household can cause rumination, repetitive thoughts that are hard to interrupt. Our brains keep scanning for the next thing we've forgotten or need to accomplish.

Bernal likens it to a computer with too many windows open. “Each window has a different program running: the children, work, something you need to organize, a conversation you had, something you forgot to do, something you’re worried about, tomorrow’s schedule. You may have physically stopped, but all those programs are still running in the background,” she says.

“Your sleep drive builds all day, but your stress response can override it,” explains Dr. Shelby Harris, a board-certified behavioral sleep medicine specialist and psychologist with BetterSleep. “Over time, the brain can start linking bed with worry.”

We're expected to do everything for everyone, and we're still preached at about self-care. It's almost comical.

But we do have to learn to prioritize sleep. It's essential to our well-being. Chronic sleep deprivation can affect our attention, memory, emotional regulation, and decision-making, and can put you at a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease, says Harris.

One basic way to make more time for sleep is to be honest about which responsibilities are really urgent, and which can wait, Bernal says. When we do too much for our families and don't let them practice independence, it’s to our detriment and theirs. I've recently worked harder to get my kids to do their own laundry, help pack their lunches, and clean up after dinner. These are essential life skills they need for adulting anyway, and they shouldn't all fall on me!

Harris suggests spending 10 minutes earlier in the evening writing down what's on your mind, along with a next step for each item, to help take the pressure off bedtime. Dr. Joseph Dzierzewski with the National Sleep Foundation recommends getting out of bed if you've been lying awake for about 20 minutes and sleep doesn't feel close. Because the harder we try, the more it will evade us.

“No amount of sleep strategies can compensate for an absence of sleep opportunity,” warns Dzierzewski. In other words, we can try all the bedtime routines in the world, but if we don't have enough time to sleep, what's the point? For families with a partner or other support, Dzierzewski strongly recommends sharing nighttime responsibilities so each caregiver gets an uninterrupted stretch of sleep.

For persistent insomnia, it may be time to see a doctor to protect your health.

As Bernal beautifully puts it, “Sleep shouldn't be the reward you receive once you have done enough. Sleep is part of what allows you to live, love, think, work, and care for others in the first place.”

#8109. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Cat Refuses to Eat Wet Food! (October 5, 2026)

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

I feed my 7-year-old, neutered indoor male cat, Sigi, canned food and dry kibble. He prefers the kibble and leaves most of his wet food. I have tried three different brands, and he holds out until I give him the dry food.

I prefer the ingredients in the wet food to the kibble, which is the same brand as one of the canned foods. He has maintained his weight, and heâs not skinny. I do give him some treats in the evenings.

It sounds like Sigi has made his position very clear: kibble wins, and apparently, he is prepared to negotiate accordingly! The reassuring part is that he is maintaining a healthy weight and body condition. While it makes perfect sense to prefer the ingredients and higher moisture content of canned food, the most important consideration is that his main diet is complete and balanced, meaning it has the appropriate number of calories and all the nutrients he needs to maintain his body.

Wet food does have an advantage because it provides considerably more moisture and usually fewer calories per gram than dry food. For a neutered indoor cat like Sigi, keeping portions measured is especially important because these cats need fewer calories. I suggest measuring his daily kibble rather than allowing unlimited grazing, as this also helps you learn what he normally eats and notice any changes in appetite sooner. It is important to remember that those evening treats count toward his calorie intake and shouldn't exceed 10% of his daily allowance.

For cats eating a primarily dry-food diet, drinking plenty of water becomes a priority, and there are several ways you can encourage Sigi to spend a little more time at the water bowl each day. Providing multiple water sources in different locations gives cats a choice of drinking spots, which might vary throughout the day, depending on activity in the house. Ceramic or stainless steel bowls are more hygienic than plastic and provide a fresher taste that cats prefer. Many cats prefer to drink from moving water, so a cat drinking fountain is another great idea.

If you would still like to increase his wet food, you could make the transition very gradually rather than turning dinner into a battle of wills. Try warming a small amount of canned food to enhance its aroma, adding a little warm water, or experimenting with different textures. You could also try a nutritionally complete and balanced fresh food formulated specifically for cats.

Some cats find the aroma and texture of fresh food more appealing, so it can be another option to explore rather than trying to convince Sigi that canned food is the only acceptable alternative to kibble.

Most importantly, avoid trying to out-stubborn a cat by withholding his preferred food until he gives in. Cats that eat too little for several days can develop serious health problems, including hepatic lipidosis. The goal isnât to win the wet-food argument, but to find a nutritionally appropriate diet that Sigi actually enjoys eating. Wet or fresh food would be a nice addition, but mealtimes do not need to become a battle.

With cats, sometimes a little compromise goes a long way!

#8108. Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.

“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”

“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.

According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.

The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:

Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

#8107. Why Does My Dog Always Steal My Spot? The Reason Will Warm Your Heart

Experts break down the intentions behind your pup’s habit.

Being a dog owner can be extremely rewarding. In many ways, it’s like being given an adorable, cuddly, playful roommate whose main goal in life is to love you unconditionally. I mean, that’s the dream, right? But like with most things, it can also come with a few notable challenges: the main one being their inability to verbally communicate with you. If I had a nickel for every time I wished I knew what my dog was thinking… well… let’s just say I’d be in a different tax bracket by now. It can be frustrating not to know what is going on in those furry heads of theirs, not just in regard to how they’re feeling physically, but on a behavioral level as well. One example that immediately comes to mind is my own dog’s peculiar habit of stealing my spot on the couch as soon as I leave it.

For a little bit of background, my dog’s name is Luna. She is an 8-year-old yellow lab who loves to snore, wag her tail in a helicopter motion, hoard tennis balls and never give them back, and, yes, steal other people’s seats on the furniture. It doesn’t matter if she’s sitting in a similar spot to us, or even right next to us; she will proceed to take your seat the moment you get up to get a snack or use the bathroom or simply grab a nearby blanket. It’s equal parts frustrating and amusing. What exactly is making her do this? As much as I wish my dog could answer that question for me directly (and believe me, I have wondered if she is secretly a human trapped in a dog’s body due to some sort of Beauty and the Beast-style enchantment, but that probably isn’t the case), the habit has inspired me to seek answers elsewhere.

Since I’m sure my dog isn’t the only canine committing furniture theft, Scary Mommy reached out to a few experts to get their insight on what your pup’s real motive may be, and the reason is actually pretty heartwarming.

Right up front: Take comfort in knowing your dog isn’t doing this to upset you. In fact, they love you so much that this is simply an attempt to feel closer to you. “First, your body has warmed the spot, so your dog gets a cozy temperature-controlled bed instantly,” celebrity dog trainer Chrissy Joy shares with Scary Mommy. “Second, your scent is concentrated there, and familiar human scent can be comforting and reassuring to dogs.”

Tracy Murray, dog expert and founder of Saving Fido Dog Walking, echoes this sentiment, explaining that it’s all coming from a place of love. "Warmth is a big part of it,” she admits. “In general, dogs are drawn to heat, and the spot you just left is prime. But it's not just about the warmth, because otherwise they'd be equally drawn to a patch of sun on the floor." Murray adds, "A dog uses their nose like we use our eyes, so the fact that the spot smells like someone they love is awesome. Taking over your place is like sleeping on a pile of your clothes."

And for those of you who worry your furry friend is doing this to establish themselves as the alpha over you, fear not. "The dominance idea has been pretty much debunked,” Murray continues. “With my background in psychology and years working with dogs, what I see is a dog who wants to be close to her person, not one trying to overtake or outrank them."

Just when you thought that little furball couldn’t get any sweeter!

On the other hand, it’s also possible that you yourself have accidentally encouraged this behavior without realizing it. “Another possibility is that stealing your spot has become a learned behavior,” licensed veterinarian Dr. Sarah-Jane Molier explains. “If you react gleefully or offer your dog attention when they jump in your spot, this is a form of ‘positive reinforcement.’ In other words, your dog has learned that stealing your spot gains them positive attention.”

Basically, the main takeaway here is that your dog is just as obsessed with you and you are with them! They want to be wherever you are (or were), and you can’t help but snuggle them for their thievery. So the next time you get up from your comfortable spot on the couch and come back to find it’s been taken over by a hairy, slobbery, wet-nosed seat-stealer, just remember that it’s their way of showing how much they love you.

And, you know what? I guess I can live with that. Luna has already stolen a big piece of my heart. I suppose she might as well have my spot on the couch too.

That troublesome tree might be yours, but removing it isn't always your decision. A few important checks could save you a costly mistake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As homeowners, we tend to be proud and possessive. My house, my lawn, my trees. But don’t make the mistake of thinking you can chop down those trees just because you feel like it. Owning a tree doesn’t necessarily give you the unrestricted right to remove it.

We tend to think of trees and plants as our personal property, and in many cases that is true. If you plant a hydrangea bush on property you own this year, you can take it out the following summer. The same goes for a rose bush or a cherry tree. But that principle doesn’t apply to every single tree. In fact, removing trees without doing your research can leave you open to legal liability.

Some trees are legally protected under a variety of laws, ranging from municipal ordinances to HOA restrictions to environmental and wildlife protections. As a former attorney, I advise on issues like this in my Gardening Lawyer series. Read on for the whole scoop.

Everyone knows that certain animals are protected by national and state laws in this country. The animals are often endangered species, such as whales, dolphins, and manatees, protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. But many people don’t realize that laws also protect some types of trees. Most protections are at a local level, but a few national protections exist too.

Laws relating to tree removal are generally handled at the city or county level. Local municipal ordinances may require a homeowner to obtain a permit to remove a mature tree or a protected species. The types of trees most often protected include heritage trees or native species.

If your property is part of a Homeowners Association community, your landscaping rights are governed by HOA rules, also called CC&Rs – Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions. These rules can forbid tree removal without approval by the HOA architectural committee. And this doesn't depend on whether your town requires a permit.

Property laws may also affect your right to remove a tree. If the tree is planted in the center of your yard, property laws probably will not be a concern. But if the tree trunk sits on the property line, it is jointly owned, and you and your neighbor must agree before you can remove it.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Finally, you’ll want to check both federal and state environmental rules before taking out a tree if you live in an environmentally fragile area like a wetland. This can also be an issue if the area is a site where birds nest.

If you are asking this question, you are fairly new to a Homeowners Association (HOA). Yes, if your home is part of an HOA, you agreed to follow the CC&Rs.

Most HOAs require you to request and obtain board approval before pruning or cutting down a tree on your property. The Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions are legally binding rules that are part of the price you pay to be part of the HOA. The administration has every right to stop you from cutting down or even trimming a tree on your property if the action violates the community's recorded CC&Rs.

There are those risks you can’t afford to take but also risks you can’t afford not to take. The choice is always yours – to follow the laws or to close your eyes to the legalities and chop chop chip. (I mean, George Washington cut down a cherry tree and look how far he went!) But know your risks before you decide.

The average fine for cutting down a tree in a city without getting a permit is $10,000. That’s the fine in San Francisco too. In NYC, it’s $15,000. In Visalia, California, cutting down a protected valley oak without a permit is a cool $20,000.

What about HOA fees? Homeowners Association fees vary from one HOA to the next. But they typically charge administrative fines of up to $1000 plus tree replacement costs that run into the thousands of dollars. If the tree is in a protected common area or protected by local laws, fees can go up quickly to over $20,000.

If you cut or damage trees on federal public lands without federal protection, you can face criminal fines or up to one year in prison. Municipal and county governments impose direct administrative fines of up to $10,000 per tree for removing protected or wetland-adjacent trees without a local permit.

It would be nice if a homeowner could contact one agency to determine whether a tree is protected. But alas, that is not the case. You’ll have to do a little research or hire someone to do it for you. Here are some tips to get you started.

First, consider the tree's origin. Did you buy it as a young sapling from the garden store? That probably means that it is not an endangered species. Is it still a young tree, slender and only half its full height? You probably won’t be impeded by city permitting requirements, since these often apply only to mature trees of a certain height and girth. A call to city hall can confirm this.

Second, is your home part of an HOA community? If not, HOA rules won’t apply. If so, you'll likely have to jump through hoops, so review the CC&Rs.

Third, is the tree on the property line? If not, you won't need the neighbor’s permission. If so, you’ll need to arrange a conversation about the tree. Put any agreement in writing.

Fourth, is your tree on a public right-of-way or sidewalk strip? You will probably need a permit to remove it. Ask your town’s City Hall.

Last, is your property part of a wetland, a riparian buffer, or a bird nesting zone? You may not know. If you aren’t sure, start by asking your City Forester or Urban Forestry Department for direction.

Every rule has exceptions. Many local governments allow you to remove a tree without a permit if it is dead, severely diseased, or dangerous. For example, if the tree is leaning or uprooted and poses an immediate threat to your home or to passersby, the odds are good that you can remove it. Call city hall first to confirm.

This is probably also an exception in HOA restrictions. Read your CC&Rs or just call the office and ask.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.
