#8105. The Sloppy Truth: Why Dogs Love Licking Faces

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog licking a person's face can be sweet, funny, or decidedly unpleasant, depending on the timing and the recipient. It is also one of those everyday dog behaviors that can leave people wondering what is actually going on.

Dogs use their mouths to explore and communicate with the world around them, so a face lick can have several different meanings. Sometimes it is a social gesture. Other times, a dog may simply like the taste or be looking for attention.

Understanding the reason behind the behavior can make those enthusiastic kisses a little easier to interpret.

One of the simplest explanations is that dogs lick people because they enjoy being close to them.

Licking can be part of normal social behavior for dogs, so they may use it when interacting with someone they feel comfortable around. That does not necessarily mean every lick is a deliberate declaration of love, but it can be part of a dog's way of showing friendliness and connection.

Some dogs are simply more enthusiastic about this than others.

A face lick can also be a very effective way for a dog to get a reaction.

If licking someone's face consistently results in talking, petting, laughter, or even being gently pushed away, the dog has still received attention. Over time, a dog can learn that licking is a reliable way to get a person's focus.

That can make the behavior particularly persistent. What starts as an occasional lick can become a regular habit if the dog discovers that it works.

Human skin can taste interesting to dogs, particularly after someone has been eating, sweating, or using something on their skin that has an appealing smell or taste.

Dogs experience the world heavily through their senses, and their mouths are one way they investigate things. A dog that seems especially interested in licking a person's face may simply find something about the skin appealing.

It is not necessarily a complicated message. Sometimes a face just tastes interesting.

Dogs communicate in plenty of ways that humans do not always recognize, and licking can be part of that communication.

A dog may lick a person as a friendly gesture or as a way of interacting during a social moment. The rest of the dog's body language can provide clues about what is happening.

A relaxed dog that approaches willingly and seems comfortable is likely having a very different interaction from a dog that is tense, nervous, or trying to avoid a situation.

Looking at the entire behavior rather than focusing on the licking alone can make the meaning easier to understand.

Dogs are remarkably good at noticing what gets a reaction from the humans around them.

If a dog licks someone's face and receives affection in return, they will remember that interaction. That can encourage the behavior to happen again, particularly when the dog is looking for attention.

This can also explain why some dogs seem determined to keep licking even after being told to stop. From the dog's perspective, the behavior may have worked many times before.

Itâs one thing to allow a dog to lick a person's face if everyone involved is comfortable with the arrangement, but it is also perfectly reasonable not to enjoy this type of interaction.

Not only can being licked by a dog feel unpleasant to many people, but there is also the risk of spreading certain parasites and diseases, and the uncomfortable question of âwhat were they licking before they licked you?â

Dogs can be redirected toward another activity if face licking becomes excessive. Offering a toy, asking for another behavior, or simply moving away can help prevent licking from becoming the dog's default way of getting attention.

Laughing, pushing them away, or squealing are likely to be interpreted as positive reactions to a dog, and youâre much more likely to make the right impression by simply standing up and walking away.

It is also worth paying attention to the circumstances. If a dog suddenly starts licking much more than usual or the behavior comes with other unusual changes, that is different from a dog that has always been an enthusiastic licker, and you should look for other physical and behavioral clues.

A dog may lick a face because it is being friendly, looking for attention, enjoying the taste, or simply interacting in a way that has become familiar. The behavior can mean different things depending on the dog and the situation.

That is part of what makes dog behavior so interesting. A lick that looks like a simple gesture can be the result of several different motivations from the dog's point of view.

And for dogs that have discovered that face licking gets an immediate reaction, there may be an even simpler explanation: it works.

They joined forces with Mission: Meow board member Dr Matt McGlasson, Gatos Callejeros United & Urban Panthers to host a free spay/neuter event paired with a cat pantry providing food, litter, toys, and other essentials to cat families in an underserved community. That became the very first Feline Fix Fest.

This year, Feline Fix Fest is heading to Miami.

Alongside Street Cat Clinic, Little Beansâ Hope Rescue, and Hearts for Paws, Mission: Meow is hosting Feline Fix Fest 2026 on October 17-18, offering free spay/neuter services and a free pet pantry.

#8101. 17 Books Scary Mommy Editors Absolutely Devoured In October 2026

From new Kingsolver to a Booker-shortlisted Strout!

Some months the book gods really smile down on us, and October was one of those months. What did we read? We thought you'd never ask. We got our hands on Barbara Kingsolver's first novel since Demon Coppherhead, for one. There's a Booker-shortlisted title from Elizabeth Strout that we're dying to discuss more. And we obviously couldn't leave out the new Emily St. John Mandel book already being adapted for TV that, not surprisingly, is every bit as good as everyone says it is. We rounded it out with a historical shipwreck, some radium poisoning, a Grim Reaper romance, and a few old classics particularly well-suited to spooky season. I mean, c'mon... can you really ask for a better spread than that?

Most of the books on this list have already been released, making them TBR-ready. A few won't hit shelves until next spring, but we can confidently say they're 100% worth preordering. Trust, every book on the list has one thing in common: our team couldn't put it down. Here’s everything we couldn't put down and definitely couldn't wait to recommend this month.

The romantasy genre is pretty oversaturated right now, and it can be difficult to find a book that feels truly original. The magic system Dylan has invented feels completely unique. In this world, when your soulmate is born, a golden ring appears around your finger. A red one appears when your sworn enemy, the person who will cause your soulmate's death, is born (or maybe you're born with both already in place). Our main character is a reaper, someone the rich pay to eliminate their sworn enemies for a hefty fee. But what will she do when she gets an assignment that doesn't align with her moral code? — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

Author Andrew Sean Greer describes his latest book as a "charm novel," and it's so fitting for how I felt while reading it. In the novel, we meet our protagonist, who has landed his first real job cataloging items for a Baroness in the Tuscan countryside. While there, he is folded into life at the estate and meets a colorful cast of characters... but he can't quite figure out what's going on around him (and it's not just because of the language barrier). I laughed out loud multiple times during this delightful book, and I'm glad that it will be there for me to reread in the future. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

I won't lie, this book took a bit of pushing through at first. Much like ACOTAR, I assume you're going to have to read the next book or two in the series to fully understand what's happening and why in Book 1. Even though I felt a little clueless for much of it, I love the love and yearning Lee writes here, as well as the atmosphere of the book. I look forward to picking up the next installment and going "ohhhhh" a lot. — Katie McPherson

This book broke me open in the quietest, most devastating way, and I cannot stop thinking about it! Shortlisted for the 2026 Booker Prize and a Barack Obama summer reading pick, it follows Artie Dam, a 57-year-old history teacher in coastal Massachusetts who appears to be living a perfectly decent life while quietly drowning in isolation, and he soon learns a secret he cannot even speak out loud. Strout does what she does better than almost anyone — she takes the ordinary and makes it feel unbearably significant, and the Booker Prize judges called it an example of a new genre they named “radical normalcy,” which is exactly right. It is a short book that will sit with you for a very long time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

Ross is such a beautiful writer, and A Bittersweet Spell is no exception. This book has all the eldritch mystical scene-setting you could ever want; I don't even drink hot tea and I was craving a cup of the stuff every time I read another chapter. The characters feel genuine and fresh (no brooding shadow daddy stereotype here). As always, Ross' magic system is novel and fascinating, and the mystery at the heart of the story unfolds in a very engaging way. Side note: I was literally picturing Brendan Fraser as Lorne and Rachel Weisz as Avalene throughout my read, and honestly, I recommend you do the same. — Katie McPherson

From the author of the epic The Love Songs of W.E.B. Du Bois comes a collection of essays and sketches about what it means to be a Black woman living in America today. I loved the diversity of the writings contained in this book, from freeform poems to deeply researched essays to personal writings about the author's life. This is an incredibly important book from one of our best living authors, and I learned from it as much as I enjoyed its stellar writing. — Sarah Aswell

I am a huge sucker for historical non-fiction about shipwrecks (niche, I know!) and this is one of the best ones I've ever read. David Grann is the GOAT of these types of intricately researched books (Lost City of Z and Killers of the Flower Moon are both excellent), and this is no exception. It follows the very, very doomed journey of the ship The Wager, through the eyes of several of the people aboard, and we get everything that is good about these books: being stranded on an island, getting scurvy, mutiny, and murder. — Sarah Aswell

From the author of Station Eleven comes her most ambitious, mind-bending novel yet. It is 2031; America has fractured, California has declared itself a republic, and for the first time in weeks, the curfew in Los Angeles is lifted. There's a party that everyone gravitates to, but midway through the night the host disappears, guests appear to be in two places at once, and Ari Waker, freshly out of prison after 18 years, is left haunted by the night for years to come. It is already a New York Times bestseller; it is being adapted for television by Mandel herself, and reviewers are calling it the culmination of everything she has ever written. The kind of novel you will be desperate to talk about the second you finish it! — Katie Garrity

Barbara Kingsolver is back with her first book since Demon Copperhead, and it's a good one! This is less epic and more narrow in scope, but no less beautiful. In it, we meet Livia, a rural farmgirl who happens to have an incredibly rare ability to play the piano. She goes to college against her mother's wishes, only to have her life altered in unimaginable ways. This book is about the big things: life, love, and art, and it is very, very moving. It also has a playlist of piano pieces that go along with the book — so fun! — Sarah Aswell

B.K. Borison is a NYT bestselling author who simply does not miss, and Grim Tidings is already being called her best book yet. Darcy Moore is a Grim Reaper who is absolutely done with death, so she decides to save her next assignment instead of collecting him, which puts her directly in the path of Gabriel, a skeptical Guardian Angel protecting his little corner of the world as his wings depend on it. It is a grumpy-x-grumpy enemies-to-lovers romance with Halloween vibes and real emotional depth — reviewers are reporting full-on crying on public transportation, which is always the highest possible endorsement. If you loved Good Spirits, you will absolutely devour Grim Tidings! — Katie Garrity

This book has a Young Readers Edition, and it's a great option to read along with your middle-grade kid! My daughter and I devoured our copies and had so much fun talking about it together, even though the story is sad and shocking. This is a non-fiction book about the young women who worked in factories during the early 1900s, painting radium onto watch faces and airplane equipment. A huge number of them got radium poisoning — and many lawsuits followed. This book is about workers' rights and women's rights, but it's also about survival and perseverance. — Sarah Aswell

I just got back from Salem, where I toured the actual House of the Seven Gables... and I spent most of the tour wishing I’d finished the book beforehand! So I made it a point to remedy that immediately. Hawthorne’s 1851 novel is about a family slowly rotting under an ancestral curse, which is all the more fascinating when you consider that his own great-great-grandfather was a judge in the Salem witch trials who never repented (Hawthorne’s cousin, Susannah Ingersoll, was one of the house's owners). Fair warning: The prose here is very 1851 and takes some patience, but the history underneath it is worth it. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

After I heard Ann Patchett's glowing review of this book, I had to pick it up, and let's just say she was right. This book is about a young man in the far reaches of Scotland (an isolated island, to be exact) who leaves his life of sheep-raising and weaving to go to fashion/textile school. When he returns to care for a sick grandmother, he clashes with his dad about his lifestyle... but that's only the beginning! I know this lovely and difficult book will be in my top 5 reads for 2026. — Sarah Aswell

I picked up this box set because I wanted to re-read Carrie before Mike Flanagan’s new Prime Video series, then realized I’d somehow never read The Shining or Salem’s Lot... the first of which I have extra motivation for since I stayed at The Stanley, aka the hotel that inspired it, last year (clearly have a thing for reading books about places I visit!). All three are just classic early Stephen King and the set is beautifully designed, making this an easy gift for the horror person in your life. — Julie Sprankles

Jon Klassen is a Caldecott Medal winner who has absolutely never missed, and Abner and the Bubblegum Balloon is already generating serious buzz as one of the most anticipated picture books of the season. It has that signature Klassen deadpan humor, sparse text, and perfectly timed visual comedy that makes his books just as hilarious for the adults reading aloud as for the kids listening. If you have a child in your life who loved I Want My Hat Back or This Is Not My Hat, this is an immediate add to cart. The picture book that earns a permanent spot on the shelf and gets requested at bedtime on repeat! — Katie Garrity

#8100. Healed by a Dog Called Scar

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

When I hear those words, I wish they knew that, deep down, Scar is not just a dog to me. He is my entire world.

Scar is my amazing dog partner, my teammate, my source of happiness, and the reason I am who I am today. Looking back over the last six years, I truly cannot imagine where I would be without him.

Scar came to me during one of the most difficult chapters of my life. I was working in an incredibly unhealthy work environment that slowly chipped away at my confidence and mental health. Every day felt like a struggle, and I found myself constantly questioning my worth, carrying stress home with me, and struggling to see the light at the end of the tunnel. At 19 years old, it was too much, leaving me physically and mentally exhausted. I desperately needed something to lift me up and guide me out of such a hard place.

On March 1st, 2020, a little blue merle Australian Shepherd was born. He was the blessing I didnât know I needed. When he was only nine days old, I held him in my hands for the first time, and from that moment on, I knew this little guy would be my reason.

Scar gave me something to focus on besides the negativity surrounding me. I poured my heart into raising and training this incredible little puppy. From my weekly visits during his first couple of months to the training sessions in my kitchen and yard once I could finally bring him home, and every accomplishment that came out of it, I was constantly reminded that this dog was going to be my world.

As if raising a puppy was not challenging enough, Scar was a COVID puppy. Every service dog trainer knows that exposure to the world is one of the most important foundations of a confident working dog, and the world shut down shortly after bringing him home. All the critical and carefully planned socialization opportunities disappeared overnight. Stores were closed, public places were limited, and I couldnât run puppy classes or work. There were countless moments where I wondered if I would ever be able to give him everything he needed to succeed.

Instead of giving up, we adapted. Training during a pandemic required some serious creativity. I found new ways to expose him to sounds, environments, obstacles, and experiences while keeping us both safe. Making use of my parentsâ living room and backyard; every small outing was invaluable when opportunities were so limited.

Looking back now, those challenges only strengthened our partnership.

COVID wasnât the only challenge we had to overcome. Scar went through a traumatic incident at the vet that left him hesitant around men. As a service dog, he needed to be confident around all people. We spent weeks addressing his trauma. Now, not only does he work comfortably and confidently around men as a service dog, but he also works alongside them as a canine actor!

Scar has always been incredibly intuitive. There are moments when I do not even realize something is wrong, yet Scar already knows. From the look in those piercing blue eyes, itâs clear he always knows something. You can tell by his expression that he doesnât just perform tasks because itâs in his training; itâs what he wants to do.

If I am having a rough day, he finds a way to make me smile. Sometimes that means performing one of his trained tasks. Other times it means shoving a toy in my lap and insisting itâs time to play. And believe me: He is persistent when he wants something.

Scar is not just my service dog. He is also my very first sport dog. Before him, I had admired dog sports from afar, but could never have imagined how much dog sports would change both of our lives.

Together we have explored agility, AKC events, Trick Dog titles, Rally, FASTCAT, Barn Hunt, and countless other sports. Watching him work is one of my favorite things in the world. Fair warning: he loves to talk about itâ¦ A LOT! You might need earplugs when watching him compete in these sports, but thereâs no doubt he enjoys every minute of it, and thatâs what matters most to me. His enthusiasm is contagious. Every time he steps onto a course or enters a ring, he lights up, and my goal is (and has always been) to give him the best life.

Over the years, Scar has earned more than 50 titles across multiple dog sports and organizations. Every ribbon represents hours of practice and teamwork. Even when we donât go home with a ribbon, we always walk away having learned something together.

One moment that truly changed our lives was something completely unexpected: a simple task and one simple video. What started as a way to showcase one of his medical tasks â finding me a chair â quickly captured hearts all over the internet.

When I am not feeling well, one of Scarâs tasks is locating an available chair so I can safely sit down because getting up from the floor with my knee is not easy. He searches the surrounding environment, identifies a suitable object, and confidently leads me directly to it. Watching him point out chairs using his paw with such confidence is adorable, but it is also one of his many tasks as a service dog.

That video reminded people that service dogs perform tasks in countless unique ways depending on their handlerâs needs. It has prompted conversations about service dogswhile making people smile. Across the U.S., from Disney to local stores, people recognize him from that video. Itâs hard to wrap my head around, but Iâm glad I can share Scar (and what an incredible dog he is) with the world.

Beyond being a service dog and sport dog, Scar has also found success in the entertainment industry as an accomplished animal actor! Over the past couple of years, he has appeared in short films, commercials, promotional campaigns, model calls, and professional productions. Most recently, he has taken the stage as a cast member in a production of Annie, proving once again just how adaptable and talented he truly is. He never ceases to amaze me as I watch him under the bright stage lights, confidently working around large casts, loud music, crowds, and the constantly changing environment inherent to live theater. Most dogs specialize in one job, but Scar seems to thrive doing them all. He is incredibly special, and I admire him so much.

Despite carrying the name of a Disney villain, Scar has been nothing short of a hero in my life. He stood beside me during some of my hardest days. He has celebrated my happiest moments. He has been there through surgeries, chronic pain, medical appointments, school, life changes, career changes, and everything in between.

What makes Scar so extraordinary is not any single title, accomplishment, or viral video. It is who he is. He is incredibly intelligent and hardworking without ever making it look difficult or losing his playful spirit.

Scar is professional when it is time to work but transforms into the biggest goofball the moment he knows he can!

People often tell me how lucky I am to have such an incredible dog, but itâs not all luck. Itâs the hours Scar and I have spent training and building our relationship. But they are right about one thing: he is an incredible dog, and I am lucky to have the joy and privilege of giving him the best life possible.

To state it simply, life would not be the same without Scar, and I believe everyone deserves their own âScarâ in their lifetime.

#8099. Why Do I Get Dizzy When I Stand Up? Experts Say No, This Isn't Normal

“If something is repeatedly interfering with how you feel or function, you deserve a thoughtful evaluation.”

It happens when you get up from your desk at work, from playing on the floor with your kids, even when you get out of bed first thing in the morning. Lately, whenever you go from lying or sitting to standing, you get a little dizzy. You have to pause and close your eyes, maybe grab onto something solid, and wait a few seconds before taking off. So what gives? Why do you get dizzy when you stand up now, and is it normal?

Well, medical experts agree that getting dizzy every time you stand up is categorically not normal, and it’s worth making an appointment with your doctor to investigate why it happens to you. They say the answer is likely something easy to fix, and anything impacting your daily functioning is worth the investigation.

Adjusting your blood flow to your current activity level is one of those things our brain does all on its own that we don’t really appreciate fully until it goes wrong.

“When someone stands up, gravity pulls blood toward the lower half of the body, and the nervous system has to respond quickly to maintain blood flow to the brain. If that adjustment doesn’t happen efficiently, you can feel lightheaded, see spots, or feel as though you’re about to faint,” says Dr. Motisola Lewis, MD, internal medicine physician and founder of Lewis Medical NY.

For women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, dizziness upon standing can be a symptom of many different things.

“Some of the most common causes are dehydration, not eating or drinking enough, low blood pressure, anemia, blood loss, and medication side effects. In women in their 30s through 50s, I also think about heavy menstrual bleeding, hormonal transitions, and medications that can affect blood pressure or heart rate. Sometimes there is more than one contributing factor,” Lewis explains.

It’s also important to distinguish between dizziness and vertigo so you can accurately describe your experience to your doctor.

“If they feel lightheaded, faint, or like they might pass out, I would think about blood pressure issues, especially orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure with standing. Dehydration, medication side effects or interactions, blood sugar fluctuations, cardiovascular issues, and other medical conditions can also cause lightheadedness,” says Dr. Kim Bell, a doctor of physical therapy who specializes in dizziness, vertigo, balance problems, and fall prevention.

“If they describe more of a brief spinning sensation when they get up, I would also want to rule out benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV, which is the most common inner ear cause of vertigo. BPPV can cause momentary dizziness or spinning with position changes such as sitting up in bed or getting out of bed.”

If you’ve made an appointment with your doctor to discuss your dizziness, ask yourself a few questions and log the answers for a week or two before you go. Pay attention to what the dizziness feels like, what movement or position triggers it, and how long it lasts, Bell says. “Those details can provide important clues about the cause.”

If it happens once, OK, maybe you were just dehydrated. But if it happens frequently, no, that’s not normal at all, Lewis and Bell agree.

“I would not want someone to assume that their height, age, stress level, or tendency to ‘stand up too fast’ explains recurring dizziness without actually investigating the cause,” says Bell.

If you’ve ever had a doctor chalk up your dizziness to standing up too fast, anxiety, or literally just being too tall (this really happens), look for a second opinion.

“Women deserve to be heard before their symptoms are explained away. Many women are exceptionally good at pushing through discomfort. They get the children ready, go to work, care for their families, and carry on even when they don’t feel well. Sometimes they normalize their symptoms because they’ve been told that what they’re experiencing is just stress, aging, or something they have to live with. But if you're consistently dizzy when you stand, exhausted despite sleeping, experiencing a racing heart, or struggling to function the way you used to, it’s worth asking why,” says Lewis.

This doesn’t mean your dizziness is pointing to a rare or serious condition; usually the cause is something simple and totally treatable, Lewis adds.

If you’re experiencing certain symptoms along with dizziness, it warrants a more urgent assessment, Lewis says. Here are the symptoms that Bell and Lewis say would make them want to see you ASAP:

If you experience new neurological symptoms, including sudden weakness or numbness on one side, confusion, double vision, difficulty speaking, or a sudden severe headache, that’s your sign to head to your nearest emergency room, Lewis notes.

If you’ve heard about POTS lately, well, that’s because it’s becoming a lot more common.

All around the world, studies show health experts are diagnosing more people than ever before with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS: an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes your heart to beat faster than normal when you go from sitting or lying down to standing up. Unsurprisingly, dizziness upon standing is one of its hallmark symptoms. The condition can be caused by severe viral infections; public health experts believe the COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive number of previously healthy people to develop POTS.

While it might be in the zeitgeist right now, Lewis says POTS is not the most common explanation for dizziness upon standing. Women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s can have so much happening in their bodies that the dizziness may be the result of more than one factor as well — think sleep disruptions, hormonal changes, and iron deficiency.

If anything in your life, like getting dizzy when you stand, is interfering with how you feel or function, “you deserve a thoughtful evaluation” from your healthcare provider, Lewis says.

#8098. FBI Operation Summer Heat 2.0 Nets Thousands of Violent Crime Arrests

In four months, the violent crime initiative also seized enough fentanyl to kill 52 million people

The FBI and its law enforcement partners are announcing the results of Summer Heat 2.0, a four-month violent crime initiative that resulted in 8,927 arrests, the seizure of deadly fentanyl and cocaine, and 5,013 dangerous illegally possessed weapons taken off American streets.

“This year’s Summer Heat was our second straight nationwide offensive to crush violent crime all over the country, and the results were outstanding,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Even after last year’s unprecedented numbers, all 56 FBI field offices stepped up and delivered even higher numbers this year—arresting almost 9,000 subjects, up 3% from Summer Heat last year; seizing 63% more fentanyl; identifying or locating 1,410 children, 34% higher than last year; and recovering over 5,000 weapons, up 120% from 2025. Major cities across America saw increases as high as 80% in arrests compared to last summer alone. When this FBI elevated ‘crushing violent crime’ to one of our top priorities, we moved 2,000 FBI personnel out of Washington and permanently into the field—making the decisive call to go on offense. This FBI isn’t waiting for violent criminals, drug traffickers, and weapons dealers to devastate our communities any longer. As a result, under the Trump administration’s leadership, we have achieved the most prolific reduction in violent crime in U.S. history.”  Between June 1 and September 20, the FBI and its 56 field offices surged resources alongside state and local partners to execute federal warrants on violent criminals and fugitives, dismantle violent gangs and transnational criminal organizations, identify and rescue child victims, and resolve violent crime cases in Indian Country.

The FBI’s Summer Heat 2.0 initiative achieved additional victories with 687 kilograms of fentanyl seized: an amount equal to 52 million lethal doses. Of the 8,927 arrests, more than 5,900 arrests fell under the FBI’s violent crime and gang program.

A Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) takedown across two states, Operation Turf War, kicked off the FBI’s 2026 Summer Heat initiative. FBI Pittsburgh, in coordination with West Virginia’s HSTF, netted 32 narcotics and weapons-related arrests. In a separate effort in July 2026, FBI Los Angeles executed 17 federal arrest warrants and 49 search warrants in connection with Operation Hard Ball. The operation united FBI Los Angeles with law enforcement from Canada and Europe to investigate an organized crime group accused of a litany of criminal acts. And in yet another example of the success of Operation Summer Heat, FBI San Juan and its partners led Operation Taking Back West, which resulted in the indictment of 81 members of a violent criminal gang.   The FBI first launched the Summer Heat initiative for three months in 2025 to deploy a multi-pronged offensive to crush violent crime. The announcement of Operation Summer Heat 2.0 results follows on the heels of historic drops in crime across the U.S., according to the FBI’s 2025 UCR Summary of Reported Crimes in the Nation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As fall edges forward, strawberry patches can often look like they have finished their seasonal duties. The berries are long gone, creeping runners have tangled across walkways, and older foliage is beginning to bronze. It is tempting to simply walk away and leave the beds until spring. However, neglecting your patch in late autumn is one of the most common reasons for more disappointing crops the following year.

What happens to your strawberry plants in October has a massive impact on next year's crop. A few simple fall tasks now can help them get through winter in good shape, which directly leads to more berries that taste yummy next summer. Anyone who grows strawberries knows how much rides on the crown – the thick stem at the center of each plant, where new leaves and flowers start. It sits at the soil line, which makes it easy to damage in winter. Most of these fall jobs come back to protecting it.

Whether you cultivate June-bearers like Honeoye or Jewel, everbearing varieties like Ozark Beauty, or continuous day-neutral types like Albion, this next week is a critical window to protect strawbs. Time is short before the ground freezes solid. By taking a few quick steps now, you protect those delicate crowns and lay the foundation for a riot of sweet, juicy fruit next year. So don't skip these fall care essentials…

These strawberry tasks bridge the gap between active growing and total winter dormancy. Because strawberries have shallow root systems that rarely penetrate deeper than 6 inches (15cm) into soil, it’s good to check in with conditions both on and in the ground. Checking your patch's moisture, ambient temperature, and foliage health this month ensures plants enter dormancy with maximum energy reserves.

A steady cold at this time of year isn't always the biggest problem for strawberries. A sunny thaw followed by a hard freeze can heave plants right out of the soil and tear their roots. So where you live changes the following strawberry game plan a little bit. In colder USDA hardiness zones (zones 3-6), October is mostly about getting ready for winter and priming beds and containers before freezes strike. In warmer southern regions (zones 8-10) it can be a great time to plant new runners.

Strawberry care this month also varies according to whether you are growing in the ground or in containers. In-ground matted rows benefit from the relative continued warmth of surrounding earth, while strawberries grown in raised beds, terracotta jars, or vertical planting towers may face a tougher time now. Performing targeted checks on both border beds and container plants ensures that every strawberry crown remains healthy and protected through the cold months ahead.

Before you start these strawberry jobs, quickly check the soil with a good diagnostic tool like the budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon. This will help you to get a good sense of current root moisture and temperature levels ahead of any extra soil treatments or mulching extras. With that in hand, follow these simple steps…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One of the simplest ways to prime your strawberry plants is to quickly check for weathered, damaged or diseased foliage. This will eliminate overwintering pests and fungal pathogens before cold weather sets in. Walk your rows with sharp snips and trim away foliage that looks brown, decayed, or has reddish-purple spots (the telltale sign of strawberry leaf spot). Use spring-action snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips, available from Amazon, or Fiskars SoftGrip Handle Bypass Floral Hand Pruning Shears, from The Home Depot, to make any smaller targeted cuts.

Don’t leave the clippings on the ground, as pests can still overwinter in the old growth. Rake up the trimmings and get them off the bed, placing them in the trash rather than your compost heap. However, avoid aggressive cutbacks. The healthy green leaves are still feeding the crown, and June-bearing plants set next year's flower buds as the days get shorter. Save hard shearing for post-harvest renovation.

Another part of tidying up strawberry beds involves timely weeding. Weeds that get settled in during fall are usually harder to get rid of in spring, and they will actively compete with strawberries for water and nutrients. Remember, your strawbs have shallow roots, so avoid deep hoeing or aggressive tilling. After a spell of rain, pull the weeds by hand. Damp soil lets go of roots more easily. Work methodically around each crown, taking care not to accidentally loosen or heave plants from the soil.

Strawberry plants continue producing runners right up until the first hard frost. This can be exciting in terms of the potential for new plants, However, left unchecked, excessive runners can drain energy away from the mother plant. In established rows of June-bearers, you can keep a few runners and direct select healthy daughter plants into bare gaps. Pin them down using landscape staples or small soil mounds. Once the daughter roots, snip the connection with the mother.

Keep an eye on plant density, though. Thin any excess plants so that the crowns sit roughly 6-8 inches (15-20cm) apart. For everbearing and day-neutral varieties, it’s best to snip off all fall runners completely. Repeat-blooming cultivars produce higher spring yields when all that late-season energy stays focused inside the crowns. Day-neutral types make far fewer runners, and in cold regions a lot of them won't survive winter, though mulching them might give them a chance.

In warmer zones 8-10, October can be a good time to plant bare-root crowns and plugs. Work a balanced feed into well-drained, slightly acidic soil. A good organic option is Espoma Organic Berry-tone Fertilizer, available in budget-friendly packs from The Home Depot to condition your beds. Set new plants 12 inches (30cm) apart. Make sure the crown is at soil level, as a buried crown can rot. Keep a frost cloth handy for vicious cold snaps. In colder zones, it’s best to plant in spring.

Fall weather often brings more rainfall, prompting many of us to abandon our watering cans. However, rain is rarely sufficient for shallow-rooted strawberry patches. Because strawberry roots are shallow, they can dry out rapidly during crisp, windy afternoons. Keeping strawberry crowns in dehydrated soil as they enter winter can stress plants and invite winter kill. New plants are especially vulnerable, since their roots haven’t spread far yet. This task is so easy to keep tabs on. Your plants just need one deep weekly soaking, roughly an inch (2.5cm) of water per week.

Water your strawberries early in the day so the foliage can dry before nighttime chills. Use a soaker hose or watering wand if you can, and aim for the base of the plants. Moist soil holds thermal heat better than bone-dry earth. Keep watering until the ground freezes. For a light nutrient boost, add a diluted seaweed drench every 2 weeks until the ground is frozen solid. A splash of Neptune’s Harvest Fish & Seaweed Organic 2-3-1 Fertilizer, available from Walmart, is a great root tonic to help see your strawbs through winter.

Winter mulching is vital for strawberry survival, but timing is everything. Mulching strawberries too early in October, while daytime temperatures remain mild, can trap warmth and moisture against the crowns. This seeming act of kindness can create more problems, preventing plants from hardening off and inviting crown rots. So wait until the plants have been through several hard frosts and the leaves start to look gray or red, which usually lines up with a few nights around 20-25°F (-4 to -7°C). This signals that plants are dormant.

Once the ground begins freezing, spread a loose, airy 3 to 4-inch (8-10cm) blanket of clean, weed-free straw (such as oat, wheat, or barley) or clean pine needles over the entire planting bed. Straw bales cover plenty of ground. You can grab some Bell Nursery Straw Bales from The Home Depot for an airy yet cozy blanket over wintering strawberry beds. Skip fallen leaves, which can mat down into a soggy blanket and trap moisture. Unprotected crowns can die at around 15°F (-9C). Just wait for a real cold snap before tucking everything under straw.

Container-grown strawberries face higher winter risks than those in beds. Pots don't give the roots much protection, and in a hard freeze the soil inside can get nearly as cold as the air. This can expose roots to brutal freeze-thaw cycles that can crack containers and kill sleeping strawberry crowns. So once your container plants enter full dormancy in late October, extra protection is necessary in zones 7 and colder.

The easiest fix is to carry the pots into an unheated garage or shed for the winter. As long as temperatures remain around 25-40°F (-4 to 4°C), they will be fine. If indoor shelter is unavailable, push the pots together against a sheltered, south-facing wall. Surround the outside pots with some burlap or insulating bubble wrap, and mound loose straw over the crowns.

Before tucking pots away for winter, water and refresh the upper layer of potting soil with some organic compost. For a simple soil refresher, add a sprinkle of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Compost, available from Walmart, to your containers. Top-dressing winterized containers will help to prime your strawbs for spring growth.

October strawberry care is all about thoughtful, timely preservation. By cutting away the worst of the leaves, managing trailing runners, keeping roots well watered, adding a timely straw mulch, and protecting container-based strawbs, you can shield your plants from the harshest winter weather. Tackle these simple tasks today, and you look forward to an abundance of homegrown berries next year.

#8096. Can Trap-Neuter-Return Solve the Feral Cat Crisis?

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Trap-neuter-return, better known as TNR, is one of the main ways communities try to manage feral cat populations. The idea is relatively simple: instead of removing cats born outdoors or those that have reverted to a semi-wild state, cats are trapped, sterilized, vaccinated, and returned to the place where they were found.

But TNR is also the subject of an ongoing debate over animal welfare, wildlife impact, and public health. With a push to make October Feral Cat Awareness Month, and National Feral Cat Day coming up on October 16th, we thought it would be time to look at this in more detail.

The scale of the problem helps explain why TNR has become so widely used. Roughly 3.3 million cats enter US shelters each year, while the feral cat population has been estimated at as many as 100 million nationwide. With unspayed females capable of producing one to two litters a year, and uncastrated males able to father an immeasurable number of litters in their lifetime, sterilization is essential to stopping the cycle.

In the past, dealing with increasing feral cat numbers meant eradication. Not only is culling cats cruel, but it has also been proven, time and time again, to be ineffective, with new cats migrating into the area to fill the void left by those who have been removed or destroyed.

By sterilizing cats in a feral colony, population control happens gradually. There is less fighting, less roaming, and less disease spread. Populations naturally dwindle as the number of fertile cats is reduced.

A feral cat is humanely trapped, examined, vaccinated, and neutered before being marked with a small notch in its ear. The cat is then returned outdoors rather than placed for adoption, since genuinely unsocialized cats are often unlikely to adapt to life as pets.

Anyone considering TNR should ideally start by contacting a local shelter or TNR organization. Experienced volunteers may be able to handle the process themselves and will also know the local rules governing trapping and release.

For those doing it independently, a proper humane trap is essential, as is a legal location where there is a genuine concentration of cats. Local regulations vary, so checking with animal control or a wildlife agency beforehand is important.

Once baited, usually with wet cat food, traps need to be checked at least every 12 hours. Other animals, including raccoons, can sometimes be caught accidentally, and different rules may apply to releasing them. Cats should remain inside the trap during transport, and veterinary care needs to be arranged beforehand because not every clinic treats feral cats.

The basic argument for TNR is that sterilizing cats prevents them from producing more kittens. Over time, that can reduce the size of a colony and the number of feral cats entering shelters.

That matters for shelters already dealing with large numbers of animals. Fewer feral cats arriving can leave more resources available for cats and other animals that are suitable for adoption.

TNR also offers an alternative to simply removing cats from an area, something that can be difficult when dealing with large outdoor populations.

Some research has questioned whether TNR consistently reduces feral cat populations, since new cats can be introduced into established colonies and abandoned cats can add to the numbers. Tracking colonies accurately is also notoriously difficult.

Only an estimated 2 percent of feral cats are currently sterilized, compared with roughly 85 percent of owned pets, highlighting how much of the population remains outside the reach of traditional veterinary care.

Animal welfare groups, including PETA, argue that returning feral cats outdoors can amount to abandonment. However, in established feral cat colonies, relatively few can adapt to life in a home, but for those that can, rehoming is always the preferred option.

Public health is another concern. Maintaining vaccinations and preventive health across an unowned population can be extremely challenging. One study found that 92 percent of captured feral cats carried fleas. Feral cats have also been associated with typhus, plague, internal parasites, and toxoplasmosis, and, at roughly six times the rate of dogs, they are the domestic animal most frequently diagnosed with rabies in the US.

Perhaps the most contentious part of the TNR debate concerns wildlife.

The American Bird Conservancy has linked cats to the extinction of 40 bird species, 21 mammals, and two reptiles. Hundreds of additional species are affected by feral and outdoor cats more broadly.

Sterilization prevents reproduction, but it does not remove a cat's instinct to hunt, and a neutered cat can still kill birds, mammals, and reptiles, making population control only one part of the wider environmental debate.

Some evidence suggests that keeping cats well-fed with a high-protein diet may reduce their prey drive; however, this requires continued management of the colony.

Few researchers argue that TNR alone can solve the feral cat problem. Even supporters generally see it as one part of a broader approach that includes sterilizing owned pets and reducing the number of cats entering the outdoor population in the first place.

At the same time, critics point to the potential consequences for wildlife, public health, and the cats themselves.

That leaves TNR in an awkward position. It can reduce reproduction without necessarily eliminating the wider problems associated with free-roaming cats, but whether it is the most ethical approach ultimately depends on how the competing welfare concerns involving cats, wildlife, and people are weighed.

Ultimately, feral cats are a human-created problem, and it is up to us to work towards a solution. TNR may not be the only answer, but it has, in many cases, proven to be a humane and effective way to control feral cat populations.

#8095. 10 Make-Ahead Thanksgiving Sides That Genuinely Reheat Well

Assemble them ahead of time and Turkey Day will be a breeze.

Maybe you’re trying to avoid a spicy mother-in-law and want to be sequestered in the kitchen all day on Thanksgiving (and more power to you). But for most people, the idea of having your house full of family and friends and being trapped standing at the stove the whole time isn’t ideal. That’s where these make-ahead sides that actually reheat well come into play. You see, no one wants clumped-up, days-old, dried-out mashed potatoes on Turkey Day, nor do they want to be hand-mashing while everyone laughs and drinks in the living room. But with recipes like these, a happy medium is possible.

Sweet potato casserole is a must at every Thanksgiving feast. When else is it socially acceptable to serve a vegetable topped with marshmallows? All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes special notes of orange and brown butter, as well as a few notes about different ways to prep the recipe ahead of time and save yourself some work the day-of.

Just go ahead and whip up All The Healthy Things’ slow cooker mashed potatoes in advance; they’ll microwave beautifully, or fit right back into the slow cooker on “keep warm.” This way you can focus all your efforts on the turkey gravy.

Make Simply LaKita’s corn pudding ahead of time so you can use that oven space for other things on Thanksgiving. Her reheating instructions say you can put the whole dish back into the oven at 300 degrees, or just put individual portions in the microwave.

Who knew you could make stuffing ahead of time? Just follow Damn Delicious’ recipe up to step five (which is when you combine all the ingredients in the baking dish). Instead of putting it straight into the oven, let it cool and pop it in the fridge overnight, then bake when you’re ready to serve the following day.

Just like the stuffing, you can make this green bean casserole from Damn Delicious nearly to completion — just hold off on popping the breadcrumbs and fried shallots on top until you’re ready to bake it. Then, they’ll come out crispy and perfect and right on time.

Princess Pinky Girl’s scalloped potato recipe is perfect for planning ahead. You can bake it completely and reheat individual portions, assemble but wait to bake, or even bake it halfway and finish it off on the day of Thanksgiving dinner.

Damn Delicious’ make-ahead yeast rolls are perfectly plump and fluffy, ideal for spreading with butter or mopping up gravy (mmm). Her post explains that you can refrigerate the rolls overnight so they double in size before baking, or simply bake, freeze, and reheat, so you can make them much farther in advance.

Fried apples may not be a staple on every Thanksgiving table, but in the South, they often make an appearance at holiday meals. Simply LaKita’s recipe is simple and easy, and includes instructions for reheating the apples in the microwave or a skillet.

This mac and cheese recipe from Averie Cooks is incredibly easy and will definitely reheat beautifully. It’s so creamy and saucy, it won’t dry out like a premade baked mac tends to.

Whether you choose to reheat them in the microwave or the oven, Simply LaKita promises her candied yams come out tender and flavorful every time. You can make them up to two days in advance, so this could be one of your Tuesday evening preps.

Which of these recipes will you try this year? Personally, I’m eyeing that green bean casserole pretty hard...

#8093. 20 Buddy Shows To Watch After You Finish 'Friends' For The Umpteenth Time

Time to cue up your next comfort-watch obsession.

You will never, and I mean never, catch me shaming anyone over how many times they’ve binge-watched Friends. If anyone can recite Ross's meltdown from "The One Where No One's Ready" from heart, it's yours truly. If you handed me a pencil and sketch pad right now, I could probably draw a pretty decent rendering of Monica's apartment from memory. Friends, for so many of us, is like the TV equivalent of your softest sweatshirt; it's just something that makes you instantly feel better, something you want to slide into at the end of a long day. Alas, even the coziest rewatch eventually runs out of episodes, leaving you staring at the screen like Joey staring at a menu devoid of meatball subs.

The good news is that the things you actually love about Friends aren’t exclusive to our favorite funny New Yorkers (and that signature orange Central Perk couch). There are lots of truly incredible shows out there that’ve also nailed the buddy-comedy magic. So whether you're on the hunt for a replacement friend group or craving another workplace crew that feels like family, here’s what you can queue up next.

If You’re Looking for Another Friend Group to Adopt

I don’t want to ruffle any feathers here, but Living Single actually came out a full year before Friends… and yet it doesn’t get nearly as much love as it deserves. Watch it and try to deny the overlap: a core group of twentysomethings, a New York brownstone, romantic chaos to spare. Queen Latifah has even publicly hinted that NBC borrowed the concept; I'm just saying. Either way, Khadijah, Synclaire, Régine, and Max are an all-time friend group, and Kyle and Max’s bickering is will-they-won’t-they at its finest.

Obviously, right? Just swap the coffee shop for a dive bar and you’ve got New Girl. Jess, Nick, Schmidt, Winston, and Cece are so funny you’ll literally be crying from laughing (the best kind of tears). Plus, we can probably all agree that Nick and Jess give Ross and Rachel a serious run for their money. Bonus: True American is the Friends’ Thanksgiving football game for a new generation.

Happy Endings only got three seasons before ABC pulled the plug, so be aware of that going in. It’s expiration dating, if you will. And while that remains a crime, it just means you can binge the whole thing in one weekend... which you should, because Damon Wayans Jr.’s Brad and Eliza Coupe’s Jane are one of TV’s best married couples, full stop.

For many fans, this is likely the most direct descendant of Friends on the list: five pals, one bar booth, and a nine-season mystery to see who one of the group ends up with. People have many opinions about that finale, but you can’t argue that the journey to get there is pure comfort food.

Joan, Toni, Maya, and Lynn may have been a dysfunctional group of friends, but they loved each other fiercely and honestly through all the ups and downs. To this day, they remain the L.A. girl gang I wish I could have been a part of in my 20s (fine, I still do — Tracee Ellis Ross, let’s be best friends please). The series recently left Netflix, but you can stream all eight seasons on Pluto TV for free. Maybe if we all stream enough, they’ll give us some sort of reunion!

Derry Girls is kind of like an Irish coming-of-age version of our Central Perk crew. Hear me out. Erin, Orla, Clare, Michelle, and James (the "wee English fella") are a group of teens navigating Catholic school and family histrionics in '90s Northern Ireland. It's hilarious, but also surprisingly heartfelt. Plus, episodes are short enough to make it an easy rewatch.

As a workin’ mom myself, I can think of few shows more relatable than this raunchy and delightfully real series. Meet Kate, Anne, Frankie, and Jenny: a group of moms who took a mommy-and-me class together and then became part of each other's mom circle. They experience all the stuff that moms need someone to talk to about, from pumping mishaps at work to postpartum spirals and terrible bosses. And, yes, relationship snags and some truly questionable decision-making along the way. All seven seasons are ready, so you can binge straight through a long weekend if you're feeling froggy.

Camille, Tye, Quinn, and Angie are four college besties now navigating their 30s... in heels, uptown, with an extra spicy group chat. They show up for each other through the big friendship milestones, like meltdowns and messy exes, and whew, they do it all in style (prepare for serious wardrobe envy). Created by Girls Trip writer Tracy Oliver, it’s edgy and smart, not to mention wildly bingeable.

If one of the things you love most about Friends is the dynamic between Joey and Chandler, you cannot go another minute without tuning into Scrubs for J.D. and Turk. The bromance is beyond real (Zach Braff and Donald Faison are BFFs outside of the show, too). The fantasy sequences are undeniably some of the best to ever exist. And somehow this deeply funny show can turn on a dime and have you ugly-crying at any minute. Even better: The revival is back on ABC for another season, so this one’ll keep you busy for a while.

Abbi and Ilana’s friendship is a little bit of everything: supportive, chaotic, always a little too high. They’re two twentysomething women trying to make it in New York City and all that entails, between dating disasters and struggling to make rent. It’s raunchy, it’s feminist, it’s unapologetically millennial, it’s 100% worth your time.

Available to stream on Hulu and Paramount+

Yep, a show about a ride-or-die duo that is named Ride or Die. Prepare for a little disappointment right up front because, despite it being a No. 1 show for the streamer, Prime Video canceled this absolute gem after just one season. There’s still hope it’ll get picked up somewhere else, though, so go watch how brilliant Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer are as best friends on the lam… and then spam Prime Video with positive reviews.

When their husbands leave them for each other, Grace and Frankie are not exactly simpatico. You couldn’t find two more different women if you tried. But grief and growth and time have a funny way of making people see what’s right in front of them, and in this case, that leads to Grace and Frankie becoming best friends. Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin are perfection as this uptight/hippie odd couple.

Make no mistake: The central love story in Insecure is the friendship between Issa and Molly, and one of the best parts is how refreshingly honest and authentic the series portrays it. These are best friends who love each other, hurt each other, find their way back, rinse and repeat. It’s funny and it’s messy and it’s just so real.

Who would have thought that Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short would give us one of the best TV trios of our time? Yet here they are, three memorable characters who bond over true-crime podcasts and, well, actual murders in their building. Their cross-generational friendship feels totally natural thanks to their killer chemistry, which we’ll get even more of when Season 6 heads to London starting Dec. 8.

I would watch anything with Christina Applegate. I would watch anything with Linda Cardellini (speaking of, go watch her in Crystal Lake right now if you like horror). So, it just makes sense that I would be utterly obsessed with this series about two women who meet in a grief group and develop a ridiculously tight, beautiful, complicated friendship. It’s darker than anything you’ll see at Central Perk, but it’s got just as much heart.

Fair warning: This show will make you feel sick over the fact that you can’t have Shawn and Gus as friends in real life. Still, it’s worth watching Shawn fake psychic powers to solve crimes while Gus reluctantly (always reluctantly) tags along. Their rapid-fire riffs are unrivaled, and you’ll get tinges of Joey and Chandler’s rapport when you hear their ridiculous nicknames for each other. Eight seasons plus three movies means plenty to binge. Just don’t forget to look for the pineapple hidden in every episode!

Available to stream on Peacock and Prime Video

If You Want Work Friends Who Feel Like Family

Monica stans, rise up! Here, we get the local government version of our favorite Type A personality in Leslie Knope: organized, intense, and devoted to her people. Add in Ron Swanson, April and Andy, and the eternally optimistic Chris Traeger, and you’ve got a bang-up workplace comedy. Galentine’s Day alone earns it a spot on this list.

Available to stream on Peacock, Netflix, and Prime Video

If you want found family, you’ll find it at the 99th Precinct; they just all happen to be wearing badges. Much like Friends, the holiday episodes (specifically the Halloween heists) are must-watch TV, plus you get another epic bromance with Jake and Charles. It’ll break your heart a little to laugh at Captain Holt’s endless deadpanning knowing Andre Braugher is no longer with us, but binge-watching his brilliant performance is an homage.

Available to stream on Netflix, Prime Video, and Peacock

Let’s be so for real: If you’re the type who rewatches Friends annually, you most likely have logged at least a few laps through Dunder Mifflin. We couldn’t leave it out, though! Jim and Pam’s slow-burn romance is Ross and Rachel without the “we were on a break” baggage.

In this episode of Catster's Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole dive deep into the peculiar yet normal world of feline behavior, unraveling the mysterious reasons behind common cat habits. From unpacking why domestic pets bring home "gifts" like dead prey or hair ties to setting the record straight on why cats "make biscuits," they share what it truly means to listen to, understand, and care for our feline companions. Instead of advertising a one-size-fits-all approach to pet discipline, the conversation focuses on the importance of understanding a cat's instincts and body language. The hosts chat about how speaking a cat's natural language leads to better communication, proving that forcing a feline into a human mold rarely ends well.

Tune in to find out why your indoor or outdoor cat feels driven to bring home dead preyâor stolen household objects like hair tiesâeven when they are fully fed. Dr. Karyn breaks down the hardwired hunting instincts that persist despite domestication, explaining how cats view their owners as substitute family members to provide for. You will also learn about the true origin of kneading (or "making biscuits"), why it brings adult cats so much comfort, and why some male cats awkwardly take the habit a step further.

Plus, this episode sheds light on hilarious personal pet stories. You will find out what happened when Dr. Karyn caught her neutered cat making eyes at her while humping a cozy blanket, why traditional deterrents like spray bottles or double-sided tape often backfire into fun games, and how a simple, gentle "hiss" can instantly communicate boundaries to your pet!

Hunting Instincts Realities: Dr. Karyn and Nicole address why cats bring home dead animals or scavenged items, clarifying that hunting is an automatic survival drive with no time for logical processing, meaning even well-fed cats will pounce on instinct.

Klepto Cats & Treasure Hunting: The hosts reveal that some cats redirect their hunting drive entirely onto non-living household items, such as hair ties, bringing "treasure" home to their owners as part of their natural drive to provide for their substitute family.

The "Making Biscuits" Origin: Dr. Karyn explains that kneading originates from suckling behaviors in kittenhood; while grown cats no longer need to nurse, they carry the motion into adulthood because it triggers a cozy, endorphin-filled state of comfort and security.

Arousal and Humping Habits: The episode explores how kneading can sometimes lead to unexpected sexual arousal or humping in cats, noting that while humping is typically associated with dog dominance, cats display it purely as a cozy or quirky behavior rather than a social hierarchy tool.

Misinterpreting Body Language: Dr. Karyn clarifies that cat facial expressions and body language require full context; wide pupils can mean fight-or-flight adrenaline or catnip excitement, while a swishing tail can signal playfulness or an impending scratch.

Effective Boundaries Over Punishment: The hosts highlight why yelling, spray bottles, or double-sided tape fail to stop bad behavior, sharing Dr. Karyn's top tip of using a brief, clear "hiss" to instantly speak their language and set boundaries without causing distress.

#8090. My Kids Love My Toxic Boomer Mom. Why Does It Drive Me Nuts?:

I hate myself for fostering this relationship that feels monumentally unearned, but also I hate myself for resenting it so much.

My children have a special smile they reserve for their grandmother, a sort of twin upturning of the lips and cocking of the head. They love her unreservedly. When they were still little and living at home, the thought of a visit from her was like Christmas. They barely slept before she arrived on our doorstep bearing gifts and hugs and questions and, of course, her own special smile just for them. A similar smile lifting similar lips, a buttery glow of love encircling them all like halos. I have always stood just a little bit outside that circle, their smiles taking a decisive U-turn around my anxious frown.

I am the buzzkill in the room everyone tries to avoid.

It’s not like I don’t love my mom, and it’s certainly not as though I don’t love my children or want them all to love each other. On the contrary, I have spent two decades doing my best to enthusiastically encourage their closeness. I invited her to every school play, every soccer game, every music recital. We spent most of our holidays with her. Her walls are filled with framed photos of my children from me. Her cupboards stocked with mugs about the joys of being a grandmother. Now that they’readults, I update her on all of their accomplishments and downplay any of their struggles. I give her ample content for bragging on social media and long phone calls to her friends.

I hate it sometimes, though: The ease of their love for each other. The falseness of it. I hate myself sometimes for fostering this relationship that feels, in so many ways, monumentally unearned but also I hate myself for resenting it so much.

My mother was not this person with me when I was a child. She lied about everything. She did not hug me or tell me I was good or nice or loved. She parented only when we had an audience and otherwise, I was alone. All the time I was alone. I spent my childhood watching after her, catching glimpses of her as she moved past me and away from me like an accidental celebrity sighting. She was not cruel. She did not hit me or neglect my basic needs. Our home was full of nice furniture. Our fridge full of wholesome food. I had a closet full of clothes that fit me.

It was simply that motherhood was not for her. This was what she told me when I was eight years old. Being a mother was not what she expected, it was boring and annoying and thankless and I really did not bring anything to the table to change her mind. I was just a regular kid like all kids with regular grades and a regular haircut and a regular face. It was never enough to bring her on board.

My children, though, are enough for her. Grandmotherhood, it turns out, is very much for her. She loves the pageantry of it. The constant stream of adoration. She benefits greatly from their clemency, the way they smile indulgently at her obvious lies. Her deeply involved stories in which she is the hero of all things and I am a footnote in their lives if I am mentioned at all. Every moment of my own motherhood stripped away with a few careless sentences at the breakfast table, my face red with frustration and tongue-biting as she erases me from every story. As she slots herself into my absence. As she becomes center stage, yet again.

My children have chided me for getting upset about her lies. They tell me they know the truth, they remember their childhood full of me and us and our lives together where she was simply a benevolent guest. So what’s the harm in letting Gran tell a few harmless fibs. They tilt their heads. They look at each other with doting smiles full of affection. Oh Gran, they’ll say. You know how she is. Don’t let it get to you.

It makes me want to stomp my feet and scream like a petulant child. I want to tell them that yes, I know how she is. That my life has been shaped by “how she is.” That it’s not as easy for me to laugh off her lies, her manipulation, her careless erasure of me and my role as it is for them. They have been gifted with Gran-lite. The watered down, palatable version.

The truth is, they have the relationship I wanted for them. They get to know my unknowable mother in a way I never will. Uncomplicated, easy. Transparent. Someone who lies because she’s old, who is a bit selfish because her days are quiet. Someone who thinks the sun rises and sets on them. Something we have in common.

Maybe it’s simply jealousy. Maybe I wish, even at this late stage of the game, that my mother thought the sun rose and set on me too.

Maybe I wish I was in their little golden circle. All of us smiling at each other. No long, painful history always hiding in the shadows. No one to kill our buzz. Just easy love.

If you haven’t got around to planting spring-flowering bulbs yet, don’t panic because you can plant all these showstoppers in November. From tiny pastel-hued muscari to alliums the size of softballs, many-petalled tulips to intensely scented hyacinths, the range of bulbs to plant in November is just as exciting as those that need planting in September or October, so don’t feel you’re missing out for a second if you're slow off the starting block this fall.

Growing blooms from bulbs couldn’t be easier, because fall and winter rain will provide all the moisture they need. The secret to getting great results when planting bulbs in November is to sit them on a shallow layer of grit to improve drainage, so creating a drier environment to stop bulb bases rotting in wet winter soil. You could use horticultural grit but poultry grit does exactly the same job and costs a lot less. Just make sure you use a product that’s 100% crushed rock like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart, rather than the type made from oyster shells.

My bulb recommendations will brighten up your garden from February all the way into May and beyond, and return year after year. And I’ve skipped right past the common-or-garden varieties to bring you flowers in standout shades and shapes to create a colorful stir in your yard. Grow these beautiful bulbs in the ground, in raised beds or in pots – but do just grow them! Which of these striking bulbs to plant in late fall will skyrocket your spring garden next year?

November is the very best month to plant tulips. Waiting until temperatures have lowered reduces the risk of fungal disease tulip fire, and cooler temperatures mean bulbs are less likely to rot. Plant tulips in full sun, burying them at a depth that's three times the height of the bulb. Tulips need excellent drainage so dropping a ½-inch layer of grit into the planting holes first is a smart move. If you’re planting tulips in containers then mix a good handful of grit into the potting soil, too.

If it’s a while since you shopped for these spring flowers, you’ll soon find that tulips don’t have to look like tulips anymore! All these show-off varieties are fully hardy in zones 3-8, blooming in April and May when you can expect lots of curious neighbors asking what they are.

Spring-flowering crocus are incredibly hardy so can be planted in November but pick wisely for the best results. Botanical crocus flower early in January or February so have little time to grow roots from a November planting. Crocus vernus, however, blooms February to April, and their bigger bulb-like corms are tougher and store more energy.

While botanical crocus have tiny blooms, the goblet-shaped flowers of Crocus vernus grow to a far more noticeable 5 inches high. And, whether you want to welcome spring into your garden with pristine white petals or drifts of carnival color, there’s a variety to suit. Plant Crocus vernus at a depth that’s equal to three times the corm’s height, in sun or partial shade in zones 4-8, adding ¼ inch of grit to the bottom of each hole, and the bulbs will quickly naturalize. A favorite spot for these crocus is under deciduous trees where bare branches give them the early spring sunshine they need to flower well.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

These little lovelies only grow 18-24 inches tall but they really punch above their height with orchid-like flowers in saturated colors, and florists prize them highly. Dutch iris are better planted in November as any earlier and the bulbs can start sending up their green shoots prematurely, when the tender growth is quickly knobbled by cold weather.

Because these spectacular flowers sit atop a single slender stem, Dutch iris bulbs look better planted in groups, which makes them easier to bury, too. Dig a hole around 6 inches deep in full sun, mix a handful of grit into the soil, and add the bulbs 3 inches apart. In containers, you can pack them more closely at 2 inches apart.

Iris x hollandica bulbs are hardy in zones 5-9, but in zone 5 they benefit from a mulch of shredded leaves thrown over the top to keep them cozy. You can also plant these bulbs in zones 3 and 4 in pots in an unheated greenhouse, ready to move outside when the worst of the winter is over. Dutch iris is a little later to flower than most spring bulbs from May into June, providing a seamless transition into summer.

These ornamental onions are very relaxed when it comes to when they’re planted and, although most folk get their alliums into the ground in October, as long as the soil isn’t frozen solid, they’ll flourish from a November planting. There are dozens of allium varieties with flowers ranging from small pom poms to huge spheres, lasting for up to a month then drying into structural seedheads.

As the size of the bulbs ranges as much as the blooms, use the usual rule of thumb to plant bulbs at a depth equivalent to three times their height. All alliums need full sun, where they’ll thrive in zones 4-9, and be sure to line holes with a layer of grit. While there are alliums that flower in summer, all my recommendations are late spring varieties that bloom from April into June.

There’s one big reason why you should add hyacinths to your garden, and that’s their incredible scent. As the flowerbuds open, their perfume is fresh, reminiscent of cut grass. In full bloom, an intense and intoxicating floral fragrance takes over, warm with vanilla and spicy with clove. Then as the flowers fade, the aroma deepens and becomes more musky. The scent profile can differ by color, too, with purples and blues typically boasting the strongest perfume, while whites and pinks smell a little sweeter, and yellows and oranges spicier.

Emerging in late February, hyacinths add an extra dimension to crisp, cold spring days when their scent hangs in the air. Hardy in zones 4-8, hyacinths prefer to be planted once soil temperatures have dropped, so the bulbs remain dormant but still get the deep chill they need to flower. Choose a sunny spot and plant bulbs at a depth of three times their height, dropping a ½ inch layer of grit into the hole to prevent them rotting. Hyacinths also thrive in a pot, where you can pack bulbs so they’re almost-but-not touching for a fabulous fragrance cloud on a patio or front porch.

Don’t reach for the standard pink, white and blue colors as there are now all sorts of tempting hyacinth tones to choose from.

‘Delft Blue’ does naturalize but gently, and you easily prevent it from travelling far by snipping off faded flower spikes before they set seed. ‘Fantasy Creation’ has sterile flowers so only spreads very slowly through underground division. And Muscari latifolium has a clumping habit so will stay exactly where you put it. All are suitable for zones 4-8 and flower March or April into May.

The more bulbs you buy, the cheaper they get, so if you end up filling your borders with beautiful spring flowers, speed the planting with a labor-saving tool.

The diameter of this bulb planter adjusts to fit different-sized bulbs. It automatically releases soil and is marked with measurements to make getting the correct depth easy.

This long-handled bulb planter with a serrated base is sturdy enough to perform well even in hard ground, and the raised pedal makes it simple to release the excavated soil plug.

Let your drill do all the work with these garden auger bits that fit a standard ⅜” hex shank. The 1.6” bit is perfect for tulips while the 3.5” can handle the biggest allium bulbs.

Millennial Disney Channel stans, rejoice! CatConâ¢ - the worldâs largest event dedicated to the intersection of cat culture and pop culture, returns to the Pasadena Convention Center October 10â11 for its 11th year of feline fun, with cat-centric nostalgic art masterpieces, world-famous celebricats, unique brand activations, exclusive products from specialty small businesses, and more. We ask Nathan Kehn â aka @nathanthecatlady â what makes this event so special.

Picture the fun and spectacle of Comic-Con, the annual Pasadena event that celebrates comics, movies, television, gaming, celebrities, and cosplay. Now, imagine that, instead of Marvel, DC, Trekkies, or Star Wars, it's about cats. This is CatConâ¢.

The two-day immersive event brings together cat lovers from around the globe for exclusive product drops, interactive brand experiences, original art, internet-famous felines and creators, live entertainment, and hundreds of specialty vendors, all while helping more than 200 adoptable kittens find forever homes.

Proud cat Dad to Pickles, Ginger, Annie, Theodora, and new addition, 10-week-old Puzzle, Nathan has become a well-known face and beloved member of the social media community. His content, which started out as a lighthearted celebration of all things feline, has evolved into a powerful platform that brings much-needed attention to animal welfare, the stray cat overpopulation crisis, and the importance of trap-neuter-return (TNR) programs.
