While every bird feeder needs a few commercial staples, some bird-friendly nibbles may already be in your kitchen. Treat your birdies to these quick and nourishing scraps

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In late fall, bird feeders start emptying a lot faster. Black-capped chickadees make trip after trip to cache seeds in tree bark, while northern cardinals arrive at the crack of dawn and linger until dusk. As fall nights lengthen and temperatures plunge, small songbirds burn through a lot of stored body fat just to get through a long, cold night and maintain core body temperatures of 105°F (40°C) until sunrise.

Summer's bugs are mostly gone, and whatever is left on the coneflowers and dogwoods will be getting rapidly picked over as the weeks go by. So your local birds need all the help they can get. But you don't have to buy anything special or massively expensive to start feeding birds this time of year. Key kitchen scraps set out alongside the seed can give them a little extra boost in the next few weeks. Even a bruised apple or a few plain peanuts can help to keep them going.

Transforming a few everyday, wholesome kitchen leftovers into supplemental treats provides immediate, calorie-dense relief right when birds need it most. However, it’s important to be discerning and use the right scraps. Birds possess delicate digestive systems. Salty or moldy leftovers can make a bird sick, and a couple of common kitchen foods are toxic to them. So make sure you are topping up your feeding supplies with the right handy kitchen scraps – to help out hungry beaks on a budget.

If you’re offering your birdie pals these “cheep and cheerful” kitchen scraps (pun intended), just be mindful of cleanliness and portion control. Fresh scraps lack the protective husks of wild seeds, so they spoil rapidly when exposed to fall damp. Leftovers that sit out overnight can sour, harbor harmful bacteria, or attract nocturnal scavengers such as rats. Offer only modest quantities in the morning which birds will devour by early afternoon, and sweep away any uneaten remnants before dusk.

Keeping things clean is critical, as communal feeding areas can easily become hotspots for infections. Feeding trays and platform feeders need a scrub every week or so, and sooner after rain or heavy traffic. Soak feeder elements in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, then rinse and let them dry before refilling them. If you’re using a tube feeder, it’s worth investing in a long brush like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon, for a versatile bargain to speed up cleaning.

And don’t forget to keep your fresh water supplies regularly topped up in tandem with these kitchen scraps. Birds require plenty of clean drinking water to metabolize high-calorie foods, as well as bathing water to clean their feathers. As night frosts become frequent, it’s a good idea to install a birdbath de-icer or a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, also from Amazon, to protect your water.

Have fun watching your birds pick over these scraps. They aren’t intended to replace your regular bird feeds. But they can give some delightful added nourishment during these trickier transitional weeks. So put some of these out, a little at a time, and enjoy the birdlife putting the following leftovers to good use in these chilly fall mornings.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Those soft, bruised apples and pears lingering at the bottom of the fruit bowl make yummy supplemental treats for backyard birds. These sweet pomes deliver quick, easily digestible carbs and sugars, not to mention vital moisture. Fruit-eating species such as American robins, northern mockingbirds, eastern bluebirds, gray catbirds, and nomadic cedar waxwings will eagerly feast on fresh diced fruit.

Preparation is key: always cut apples and pears into small, bite-sized cubes (roughly a quarter-inch) to make them manageable for smaller bills. Make sure you remove all the seeds (or pips) out of the cores. Apple seeds contain a compound that can release cyanide. And any moldy pieces need to go in the compost. Fruit-eaters rarely visit seed tubes, so set the pieces on a sturdy, open platform feeder like the Kingsyard Platform Feeder from Amazon, which can house a healthy bird feast in comfort and safety.

When clearing out the pantry, there are usually some dry rolled oats or steel-cut oats sitting at the bottom of a canister. This can make a wholesome carbo boost for birdies. Uncooked oats supply fiber, minerals, and steady energy for ground-foraging birds. Mourning doves, dark-eyed juncos, song sparrows, and native towhees will all happily hoover up any scattered across a low ground tray or gravel border.

Just make sure they are raw, plain, and dry. Never set out leftover cooked oatmeal, as cooked porridge turns into a gummy paste. Furthermore, steer clear of instant flavored oat packets, which are loaded with refined sugars, salt, and artificial flavorings. Scatter only a handful at a time on dry days, as wet oats quickly sour and congeal. And make sure to supplement your oats with a hearty wild bird mix like the popular Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot.

Plain, unsalted peanuts might be the best thing in the pantry for birds preparing for winter. Raw or dry-roasted, unsalted nuts are packed with heart-healthy fats and dense proteins that small birds need to bulk up reserves ahead of winter. Peanuts, walnuts, pecans, and almonds also attract an enthusiastic crowd, including tufted titmice, black-capped chickadees, woodpeckers, and blue jays. Jays in particular will happily carry off whole shelled peanuts to stash in tree hollows and mulch beds.

Never offer nuts that contain added salt, spicy seasonings, sugar glazes, or chocolate. Birds have minimal tolerance for sodium and cannot process salty cocktail party leftovers. Crush or chop whole nuts into coarse pieces, so smaller songbirds like chickadees and nuthatches can eat them safely. And keep a lookout for any that smell musty or stale and remove quickly to prevent infection. The very affordable Round Peanut Bird Feeder from Amazon is a novel way of dishing up your nuts.

Rice has a reputation for swelling up and bursting birdie tummies. But this myth has been debunked by ornithologists. Plenty of wild birds (like doves and bobwhites) eat rice. However, from a nutritional standpoint, plain cooked rice is the superior choice for backyard songbirds. Steamed brown or white rice leftovers offer quick carbs that are easy for house sparrows, doves, rock pigeons, and common grackles to digest.

The rice must be cooked with zero butter, cooking oils, salt, soy sauce, garlic, or onions. Also, damp rice is susceptible to bacterial contamination, so only put out a few tablespoons at a time on cool mornings. Sweep away uneaten grains each day to keep your feeding station rodent-free. Rice is a tasty snack, but supplement with high protein treats. You can buy Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart.

Slightly squishy blueberries, raspberries, blackberries, or strawberries that might be lingering in the fridge crisper drawer are a scrummy treat for birds. In nature, wild berries are rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and simple sugars that provide instant fuel. Northern mockingbirds, eastern bluebirds, and American robins will find fresh berries irresistible as natural hedgerow fruit diminishes. And a flock of cedar waxwings may empty a tray by lunch.

Serve berries fresh and unseasoned, slicing larger strawberries into quarters. Only place small portions on a clean feeding platform early in the day, as high-moisture berries degrade rapidly. If you’re after a standing bird feeder that can hold fruits and keep them better protected from rain, the charming Ontala Metal Bird Feeder and Bath with Umbrella, available from Amazon, is great value and a real talking point. A word of warning if you are a dog owner: never substitute fresh berries with dried raisins or currants. They cause kidney failure in canines, even in tiny quantities.

When preparing dinner, set aside a small portion of plain baked, boiled, or steamed potatoes before adding butter, milk, or seasoning. Boiled potato is fine in small amounts if nothing's been added to it. It provides easy starch on freezing mornings. Starlings, common grackles, jays, and robins will happily pick apart soft potato cubes when natural insect foraging grounds become frozen and inaccessible.

Prep your bird-friendly spuds by chopping them into tiny, crumbly, pea-sized bits so they are easy for birds to ingest. However, never feed birds raw potatoes or any green-skinned bits. These contain solanine, which causes gastrointestinal distress and neurological damage in birds. And avoid french fries, salty potato chips, or buttery mashed potatoes. To supplement your potato with a “meaty” treat, hang out some suet. Placed in cages, like the More Birds Double Suet Feeder with Weather Guard from Amazon, this gives a nourishing fall boost to prime birds for winter chills.

This is prime pumpkin-carving season, leaving behind mounds of gooey seeds that are often destined for the trash. But fresh pumpkin seeds, butternut squash seeds, and raw sunflower seeds are nutrient powerhouses for backyard wildlife. They are loaded with raw fats, plant proteins, and magnesium, all of which cardinals, chickadees, titmice, nuthatches and blue jays need now.

Place the seeds in a colander, rinse away any stringy pulp and spread in a single layer on a parchment-lined baking sheet to air-dry for 24-48 hours. Leave them raw and unsalted. To help smaller beaks, run your dry seeds through a food processor for a few pulses to crack the husks. If you need to, you can grab a bag of National Audubon Society Black Oil Sunflower Seed from Lowe’s to bulk up these free treats as they are sure to go fast.

Some leftovers belong in the trash, however cold it gets. The theobromine in chocolate is toxic to birds. Avocado is another hard no, as it can cause heart damage and death. Salty snacks and cured meats need to stay inside, plus anything cooked with onion or garlic. Bread is a bit of a gray area, as it isn't harmful, but it fills a bird up without much fat or protein.

Bacon grease trips people up. It seems like a handy base for treats, but it's salty and carries preservatives. It also stays soft, and soft fat smeared on feathers can damage their waterproofing. For a safe birdie snack along similar lines, opt for suet cakes that are designed for the job. The double-basket Woodlink Suet Basket from Walmart holds two cakes, handy for when woodpeckers and nuthatches line up in the cold.

Making more of kitchen scraps feels great in terms of recycling, and it can also help you save a little on multiple bird food products. It also means you have a bit more cash freed up to treat yourself and your local birdlife to a pretty feeder. Plenty of options offer smart functionality and real-time footage of your feeding friends. These curated picks are some of the best for aesthetics, value for money and bird-friendly features, letting you feast your eyes on your feathered pals while they chow down.

Currently a whopping third off the normal price, this bargain smart feeder can identify over 6000 species of birds and can even distinguish males from females. Users love the easy assembly and sturdy build, as well as the garden-friendly mocha accents.

Combine function and visual elegance with this pretty 2-in-1 feeder and solar light. Perfect for cardinals, it has a classy vintage Mediterranean vibe, good drainage, and a lovely splashguard.

Crisp action shots, instant notifications, and 2K video are just a few attractions with this feeder camera, and it even tells you when to expect birdie visits for specific species. Great camera quality, super easy to use, and currently available at a 20% discount.

Supplementing your fall bird feeding with these kitchen scraps is a great way to reduce household waste while giving local wildlife a crucial calorie boost. Just remember they are designed to serve as supplements rather than replacements to your existing bird feeds. Make sure you offer a diverse natural diet this fall, and combine these scraps with fresh water, to keep your backyard birdies thriving and happy all season long.

Strategies for ditching the burnout, surviving the chaos, and rediscovering holiday magic.

Kids losing sleep during the holidays basically a rite of passage. But for moms with ADHD? By that point, the holiday sleep deprivation started weeks ago.

Here’s how mom-of-two Alba C. puts it: “[During the holidays] my mind races to the point that it can take me hours to fall asleep, or fall back asleep. I’ll have thoughts like, ‘Did I buy enough presents?,’ and ‘I have so many presents to wrap!’ Those thoughts start piling up, and that can put me in a moody state where I get irritated very easily.”

Nobody wants to be the holiday Grinch. But when you toss executive dysfunction into the mix with social obligations, family drama, and midnight present-wrapping marathons, the holidays become a brutal obstacle course for moms with ADHD.

“Mothers are often responsible for much of the invisible labor associated with the holidays, from coordinating family schedules, to purchasing and wrapping gifts, moving the Elf on a Shelf, making the ‘holiday magic,’ and keeping a pulse on everyone’s logistical and emotional needs,” explains neuropsychologist Dr. Jessica McCarthy. “For women with ADHD, these responsibilities can become especially overwhelming.”

So moms with ADHD, hear this: You aren’t failing at the holidays — they’re just intense. We talked to experts — and some moms who’ve been through it — to find out how to ditch the burnout, survive the chaos, and rediscover holiday magic this season. Here are some ways to cope.

The holidays amplify struggles with executive dysfunction like forgetfulness, task avoidance, or missing details, explains Dr. Ifeanyi M. Olele, a board-certified psychiatrist with Genesis Psychiatric Solutions. To ease holiday stress, he recommends delegating responsibilities to other family members and asking for help wherever possible.

“Moms shouldn't feel that they have to do everything themselves. If you have a spouse or partner, communicate and divide responsibilities. If there are teenagers or adult children in the house, ask them to help with some of the holiday preparations,” he says.

Holiday parties are where Jacquelyn D.’s ADHD symptoms — including sound sensitivity and social self-consciousness — feel the most intense. To avoid spoiling the party, the 47-year-old mom of two always comes prepared with an escape plan.

“I take a break when I need to, and don't feel bad taking a few minutes to regulate myself,” she explains. “I have some social masking techniques as well, like keeping conversations short and directed outward, and using checking on the kids as a reason to step away and get some fresh air.”

During the merriest season, many moms stay up late wrapping gifts, organizing events, or completing tasks they couldn’t get to during the day. Since sleep deprivation magnifies difficulties women with ADHD are already working hard to manage — like attention, working memory, impulse control, and emotional regulation — Dr. McCarthy advises that sometimes the most productive thing a mom can do is leave something unfinished, and go to bed.

“My advice is to treat sleep as a priority rather than something that happens after everything else is finished,” says McCarthy. “Set realistic cutoff times for holiday tasks, maintain consistent sleep routines when possible, and resist the pressure to sacrifice rest to meet unrealistic expectations.”

One of the biggest mistakes busy moms make during the holiday season is assuming that because there’s technically room on the calendar for another activity, they have the emotional capacity for it, explains Kristen Carder, an ADHD coach and author of You're Not in Trouble: The ADHD Guide to Building Healthy, Connected Relationships.

“If you know that an afternoon with extended family is going to be emotionally taxing, don't schedule another demanding activity immediately afterward. Build in downtime, protect your routines when possible, and pay attention to early signs of dysregulation.”

Amy H., an author and mother of eight, keeps her own ADHD symptoms in check by planning ahead. Her advice? Start your preparations early. Like, early, early.

“Start earlier than feels reasonable,” Amy recommends. “ If the prep is done early, December gets to be about the good stuff instead of the panic. Your future self will thank you — and so will everyone who has to live with that future self.”

While social media scrolls portrays picture-perfect holiday decor and flawless family photos, Emily M., a mom of five, reminds us that real life is rarely as immaculate as it appears through tiny screens — especially for moms with ADHD.

“When I feel myself starting to spiral and feel like I’m not enough, I look at my husband, my kids, and my friends, and I remind myself that I’m worthy even when I’m not perfect. Some days I have to come back to that over and over again, and that’s okay,” she says. “That is the practice.”

Learn more about how to handle your ADHD symptoms at https://www.reframeadhd.com/

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole tackle the controversial topic of scruffing, while also sharing some fun comparisons between cats, dogs, and toddlers. Instead of treating scruffing like an absolute taboo, the hosts break down why understanding a cat's specific boundaries can make quick vet visits or home care way less stressful for everyone. Dr. Karyn brings her cat, Sirill, onto the desk to show why a timid pinch fails, how a solid hold gives cats a sense of security, and how to quickly test if your cat is way too sensitive for the technique.

Get the real scoop on scruffing catsâincluding why total bans ignore harm reduction when you just need to safely pull out a thorn or trim nails in a pinch. Dr. Karyn breaks down the biggest mistakes pet parents make, explaining why delicately pinching a bit of skin only annoys your cat and how a full-hand hold actually provides better control and stability. Youâll also learn how to check your catâs tolerance before even trying a hold so you never accidentally upset a sensitive pet.

Plus, the hosts chat about research comparing how dogs, cats, and toddlers help others, debating whether cats are truly selfish or just super selective about their time. From winning over shy rescue cats to comparing dogs to needy toddlers and cats to moody teenagers, this episode offers a relaxed, relatable look at living with felines.

Rethinking the Scruffing Debate: Dr. Karyn and Nicole discuss how complete anti-scruffing rules miss the mark on practical care. They explain that learning safe restraint acts as harm reduction, letting you handle fast tasks like pulling out a thorn or trimming claws without having to resort to full sedation.

Test Sensitivity First: Before going in for a hold, Dr. Karyn recommends checking the neck area with gentle pets and tickles. If a cat flinches or pulls away (like her cat, Zelda), you should never try to scruff them.

Skip the "Pinch": The most common mistake people make is grabbing a tiny pinch of skin, which just annoys the cat and provokes a fight. Proper restraint needs a full, firm hand on the scruff so the cat feels secure and can't wriggle free.

Never Pick Them Up by the Scruff: The hosts emphasize that while a hand on the scruff helps keep a cat grounded, you should never lift or carry an adult cat this way.

Altruism in Pets vs. Toddlers: The conversation turns to research comparing toddlers, dogs, and cats. Studies show dogs and kids will help out even without a reward, while cats generally step in only when thereâs something clear in it for them.

Earned Love Feels Extra Special: Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how dogs offer constant, people-pleasing affection, whereas a catâs love feels like an earned privilege. That conditional nature is exactly what makes it so rewarding when a quiet cat finally comes over to snuggle.

#8053. Dogs on the Screen and in the Audience for Brad Pitt’s New Film

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

You know the drill. Keys in hand. Shoes on. One last look at your dog before you head out, and there they are, wagging their tail like maybe, just maybe, this time you are taking them with you.

Those hopeful eyes. That little head tilt. The expression that says, Excuse me, where exactly do you think youâre going without me?

And then you do the cruelest thing imaginable: you leave.

Sure, they have a perfectly comfortable sofa at home, but imagine settling into a movie theater seat, popcorn in hand, with your dog curled up beside you. Instead of leaving them behind, wondering where you went, you could reach down during the movie and give them a little scratch behind the ears.

Honestly, why have we been doing movie night without them all this time?

Apparently, someone in Miami had the same thought.

At a special screening of Brad Pittâs new movie, Heart of the Beast, at Silverspot Cinema in Downtown Miami on September 19, dogs were officially on the invite list.

The morning had all the ingredients of a proper dog outing: leashes in the lobby, photo ops, plenty of new butts to sniff, and a red carpet where the dogs seemed perfectly comfortable stealing the spotlight.

Then came the part that made this movie night different. The dogs got to go inside and watch the movie, too. And considering that Heart of the Beast is about the bond between a man and his dog, enjoying it in the company of dogs feels almost too perfect.

Heart of the Beast follows Special Forces officer James Belmont, played by Brad Pitt, and his combat dog, Odin, after a plane crash leaves them stranded in the Alaskan wilderness. Their survival depends on communication, trust, and their ability to work together.

The story centers on a relationship that many dog people will recognize, even if the circumstances are a bit more dramatic than the average Tuesday with a Labrador!

Directed by David Ayer and co-starring a German Shepherd named Uber, the movie is described as an adventure thriller centered on the bond between a man and his dog as they face the Alaskan wilderness together.

So while the movie tells the story of one extraordinary human-dog partnership, the Miami screening gave plenty of ordinary dog parents the chance to celebrate their own.

And really, that is part of what makes dogs such irresistible companions. They are not just waiting at home while life happens. They are woven into the little things: the walks, the errands, the road trips, the lazy Sunday mornings; even the occasional movie date.

As fun as dogs in the theater sounds, not every dog is going to be thrilled about it. Crowds, darkness, unfamiliar dogs, and those big cinematic sound effects can be a lot, especially for pups who are sensitive to noise.

Dogs hear much more acutely than we do, so a theater that feels exciting to us can feel pretty intense to them. Around 90 decibels can be uncomfortable for some dogs, and sudden bursts of sound can be especially startling.

A pup who settles happily beside their person? Perfect.

A pup who starts panting, pacing, hiding, or searching for the exit? That is probably their polite way of saying, âI vote for the sofa.â

And honestly, that is okay. Dog-friendly should mean dog-comfortable, not dog-compulsory.

The movie promotion had another very good reason to put dogs in the spotlight.

Ahead of the filmâs September 25 theatrical release, Brad Pitt teamed up with organizations including Wags & Walks Nashville to bring adoptable rescue dogs along to some of the movieâs promotional events.

At a Big Dog Adoption Event in Nashville, Pitt and animal coordinator Andrew Simpson spent time with dogs looking for homes. And at the filmâs global premiere in Franklin, Tennessee, adoptable dogs from Wags & Walks got to join Pitt on the red carpet.

And letâs face it, standing beside Brad Pitt is only going to improve a dogâs chances of finding a new home! Itâs the kind of exposure that can give a little rescue dog a better chance of being noticed. Someone who has never considered adopting might spot one of those faces, click to find out more, and suddenly find themselves filling out the adoption paperwork.

And that is perhaps the most impactful part of all this movie promotion.

The movie gives us a story about the bond between a man and his dog. For these rescue dogs, the hope is much simpler: to find their person, go home, and become someoneâs dog. If Brad Pittâs star power helps a few of these dogs find their forever home, that has to be worth more than any gold statuette.

For the dogs who got to tag along in Miami, they got the kind of movie night most dogs can only dream about: their person right beside them, plenty of new smells to investigate, and a whole theater full of things to sniff. Add a little popcorn to the mix, and honestly, what more could a dog ask for?

A spider plant with browning leaves at this time of the year is a desperate cry for help – here’s what to do to save your airplane plant, pronto!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your spider plant has brown leaf tips this fall, you should take action, fast. Brown leaf tips on a spider plant are like the warning lights on your car dashboard: they alert you to a problem that, if you don’t do something about it, is likely to get far worse. In fall, dying leaf tips are a common houseplant complaint, but it’s vital to work out what the problem behind this symptom is so you can set it right and bring your Chlorophytum comosum back to full health.

Don’t worry, though. A spider plant with brown leaf tips is easily fixed if you act soon enough, so great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. The localized damage you see as brown leaf tips on a spider plant isn’t life-threatening in its own right, but it could be pointing to a problem that is potentially fatal. So, taking swift action if you spot browning leaf tips is an important part of fall houseplant care.

Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your poorly spider plant with browning leaves.

First off, take a closer look at your spider plant’s dead leaf tips. Is there a clean, sharp line between the brown and the green leaf parts, or can you see a thin yellow section between them? Is the browning just at the tip of the leaves or are there any dark patches near the center or base of those leaves? Do the brown areas feel dry or mushy to the touch, and is the discoloration a dull greyish, blackish brown or a warmer, redder brown? The answers to these questions will help to inform your diagnosis.

In fall, there are four likely culprits behind a spider plant's browning leaves, and your foliage examination will help you work out which it is. Remember, your houseplant may be stressed by more than one issue so may show more than one type of damage.

Turning on a home’s heating system in fall is a common reason why spider leaf tips turn brown in fall. This is the likely cause if the damaged foliage feels dry and crispy, and there’s a sharp line between the green parts and the discolored leaf tips, or a very narrow, clean yellow line separating them. When the heat gets turned on, the air in your home rapidly loses its humidity and in these drier conditions, moisture can evaporate from a spider plant’s leaves faster than roots can replace it. As a spider plant primarily loses most moisture from its leaf tips, that's where the damage shows first.

When days start to shorten, spider plants dramatically slow their growth rate, so need to drink far less water. If you haven’t adjusted your watering routine to suit, the plant is likely getting more water than it can use. Roots are likely stressed as they’re sitting in wet, soggy soil, and this damage shows up as yellowing leaves and a blurry-edged yellow halo-like zone separating the green and brown leaf parts. This damage can appear anywhere on the leaf and, if the patches feel mushy and extend into the center or base of the leaf then those houseplant roots have started to rot.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Spider plants hail from tropical climates so if yours is sitting on a windowsill or near an external door where it's regularly blasted by cold air, it will likely struggle as temperatures drop outdoors. If this is the problem, then leaves will become floppy, dull and pale, and any foliage that’s touching a glass window pane will rapidly turn brown or black, often overnight, and feel soft and limp.

Spider plants are tough houseplants but they don’t cope well with tap water that’s high in fluoride and chlorine. And while this is a year-round problem, when a spider plant is dealing with fall-induced environmental stress on top of this chemical stress, the issue can quickly become obvious.

Spider plants pull water – and any fluoride and chlorine in it – to their leaf tips, where much of the water evaporates, leaving a concentration of chemicals. This causes browning that starts at the very tip of the leaf and creeps down the outside edges. A distinctive reddish-brown tint is another diagnostic clue to tap-water chemicals being the cause. The discoloration on the outer, older leaves will be worse than on the inner, younger leaves which haven't been sucking up the chemicals for as long. Brown leaf tips will feel dry and crispy, you may see a narrow yellow line between the green and brown parts, and there might be a crusty white residue on the soil or inner rim of the pot.

All these problems are easily fixed with the right spider plant care.

Check your spider plant isn’t sitting too close to a radiator, heat vent or in a current of warm air. Moving it to a more humid room such as a bathroom will help it recover, or stand the pot on a shallow tray of water and pebbles such as this Bonsai Humidity Tray from Lowe’s, or make your own with an old plant saucer and pea gravel like this Landscape Rock from Walmart. Make sure the pot base sits on top of the pebbles rather than in the water – you’re simply using the water to humidify the air as it evaporates.

Stop watering immediately, let the soil dry out and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry, or take out the guesswork with a moisture meter like this from Amazon.

If you suspect root rot, slide the pot off and if there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp pruners or scissors to snip off any rotting roots that are dark in color, mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your spider plant with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot.

Move your plant to a spot with bright but indirect sunlight – a room with an east- or west-facing window is ideal.

Switch to using harvested rainwater or distilled water. Don’t use regular filtered water because while a filter removes chlorine, fluoride slips right through. A gallon jug of distilled water costs just over a dollar from Walmart and will keep your spider plant watered for 3 months, and rainwater is even cheaper! It’s also a wise idea to repot your spider plant into fresh potting soil to remove any build-up of chemicals sitting around the roots, or flush or leach the existing soil by pouring rain- or distilled water through.

Trim damaged leaf tips with sharp scissors, cutting at an angle to mimic the pointed shape of the foliage.

Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

#8048. What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

Bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

Unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

Impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.

#8047. The Resentment of Being the Parent Who Can Never Clock Out

Maybe it’s a lack of freedom, unequal responsibilities with a partner, or both, but you’re big mad.

You had a certain expectation for what new motherhood would look like: Friends and family stopping by, your partner playing peek-a-boo with the baby, and even yourself feeling calm, patient, and present when the baby cries.

Reality might look a bit different, though. You blink, and your partner heads back to work, reading a newly cracked novel on the commute. Your friend drops by with pastries, then jets off to a yoga class. Everyone’s gone but you and the baby.

You’re at home, wading through a pile of burp cloths and hoping the baby naps long enough for you to choke down a sandwich. If you’re feeling a little ragey about that, you’re not alone. In one 2022 cross-sectional survey, nearly a third of new moms reported feeling intense anger.

But who are you actually angry with, and are you even mad, or — let's be brutally honest for a second — just jealous of their freedom and spontaneity? What’s really going on is likely more complicated than that, but there are things you can do things about it besides screaming into a pillow.

Anger is often underrepresented in research on the postpartum period, and tends to fly under the radar when moms get screened for perinatal depressive and anxiety disorders, as it can occur without elevated depressive symptoms, says Christine Ou, Ph.D., lead author of the aforementioned survey, assistant professor at the University of Victoria in Canada, and founder of the school’s Parent-Child Lab. “So asking only about depression may miss mothers who are struggling [with anger],” she says.

In a 2018 review, which Ou co-authored, researchers found that several factors contributed to moms’ anger, including a feeling of powerlessness and a misalignment between expectations and reality.

But you can also feel angry simply because having a newborn is hard. Moms were often mad because “their needs were compromised, and they were exhausted or stressed,” says Ou, as to why many new moms reported feeling anger. That’s pretty par for the course during the newborn haze, but being stuck at home — especially without help or breaks — can intensify those emotions.

Babies can bring a lot of joy, but staying at home around the clock with one is no picnic. First, newborns operate on an unpredictable schedule and demand constant supervision, making it feel like a logistical nightmare to get out of the house. Compounding that, mothers have historically been cast as the ‘default parent,’ says Paige Bellenbaum, L.C.S.W., founding director of The Motherhood Center, a clinic in New York City that provides care for women with postpartum depression (PPD). In traditional families, they’re “the ones physically with the baby most of the day and night, carrying most of the mental and emotional load, and managing the logistics, often while preparing for their own return to work,” says Bellenbaum.

Even if parents split duties pretty evenly within their own orbit, external factors can still throw that balance off. Take the fragmented, inadequate, and deeply unequal parental leave in the US: Often the dad or non-birthing partner ends up returning to work first. When that happens, the parent who remains at home “may feel envy, anger, or a sense of abandonment,” says Bellenbaum. Being home day in and day out with a baby can be isolating, even if you do get help from family or well-meaning visitors, she adds.

It's not just one person returning to work that creates this isolation. Reliable childcare can cost as much as your monthly mortgage these days, which means many birthing parents may make the tough but economical decision to stay home with the baby. “Everyone else can come and go, while she remains responsible for the baby, with no real opportunity to step away,” says Ou.

You could argue that the parent who’s heading into the office doesn’t necessarily want to be away from their family nor view it as an “escape.” Nevertheless, they “get to step back into their former life, stopping for coffee on the way into work, using the bathroom when they need to, and feeling useful and connected to the outside world,” says Bellenbaum. Plus, heading back to work can restore elements of their pre-baby life they may have been missing, like adult conversation, structure, control, and a sense of mastery and accomplishment, she adds. Meanwhile, the mom at home takes a 30-second shower and sings Wheels on the Bus for the 40th time in a row.

It’s normal to feel a lot of emotions in the postpartum phase — joy, frustration, rage, loneliness, anxiety, sadness, gratitude, you name it, says Ou. But that mix can make it hard to figure out exactly what you’re feeling.

While postpartum anger can happen independent of PPD, the two are clearly linked. For instance, Ou’s survey found that anger and PPD can also occur at the same time; in fact, those who screened positive for depressive symptoms had almost four times the odds of reporting intense anger. (But the survey couldn’t establish which came first.)

It’s not surprising: Imagine telling people you’re feeling trapped in your house — and no one seems to care. “When the circumstances behind a mother’s anger don’t change, when she remains overwhelmed, unsupported, or unheard, she may start to feel helpless or hopeless, which could contribute to depression,” says Ou. Maybe your partner acknowledges the struggle but doesn’t actually change anything, or you don’t feel comfortable or safe expressing your anger. Both can contribute to the development of PPD.

You might feel guilty for feeling trapped in the first place. After all, aren’t moms supposed to want to soak up as much time as possible with their babies? And, in a country where parental leave isn’t guaranteed, isn’t it a privilege to be at home with your newborn? Despite these arguments being flawed — they’re ignorant of the realities of newborn needs and nonexistent help for moms — this narrative can put a lot of pressure on moms, or even make you feel like you’re not doing right by your child. “Guilt and shame about being angry can add to that distress, potentially contributing to or worsening depressive symptoms,” says Ou.

First, know that it’s normal to be angry or irritable—period. But if you notice yourself getting worked up, take stock of how often you get angry, and how mad you get. If anger is frequent, intense, difficult to manage, or affecting your relationships or everyday life, that warrants a discussion with your doctor, says Ou. As is “feeling scared by your anger, or that you have little control over your reactions,” she adds. Postpartum Support International offers a peer support group for postpartum anger and rage, which may be a potential resource.

A screening from your healthcare provider can also be helpful since it may factor in other symptoms like crying and sadness, changes in sleep or appetite, a lack of interest in the baby, a sense of hopelessness or helplessness, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, according to Bellenbaum. “When these are present along with the anger, PPD may be at play,” she says.

However, getting professional help is not a replacement for making changes in your home and routine, if needed, stresses Bellenbaum. These tactics can help.

Since anger often stems from a lack of equality, it helps to start by looking at the division of labor in a partnered relationship. “Who gets more opportunities to sleep?” says Ou. “Who can leave without making arrangements? Who notices what needs doing, and who is responsible for making sure it happens?” Assessing this together allows you both to see who’s shouldering more of the work. “When that load is shared more equitably, resentment tends to ease, and a sense of shared responsibility emerges,” says Bellenbaum.

If and when you identify the areas of inequality, the partner should take “more ownership of tasks, night shifts, and the mental planning, not just ‘helping’,” says Bellenbaum, who recommends a card-based system called Fair Play that helps partners rebalance household work and divide invisible mental labor (like remembering to schedule doctor appointments). “Instead of splitting every chore 50/50, each partner takes full ownership of specific responsibilities, divided in a way that both people feel is fair,” she says.

“Genuine off-duty time means someone else is fully responsible for the baby,” says Bellenbaum. In other words, mom’s not on standby. She’s not listening for cries or manning the monitor, and she’s also not checking her phone or expecting a call because her partner feels the baby “wants mommy,” she explains. That can be hard, especially if the mom is afraid to leave the baby or feels guilty about being away, but it’s a worthwhile exercise for everyone. Otherwise, it “can make it harder for her partner to learn to care for the baby on their own,” she says.

Non-partnered parents need breaks, too. “Friends and family can bring food, do laundry, or hold the baby for half an hour,” says Ou. Run errands alone one evening while the baby stays home with a loved one. “A grocery run might be a chore, but it can also mean getting out of the house, being alone, and deciding what happens next without having to respond to a baby and their needs,” she says.

If a new mom in your life is dealing with anger or isolation, there are ways you can support her. Instead of asking what she needs, be specific and offer choices, like "I can do some laundry for you or bring over food for you. Which would help more?” says Bellenbaum.

If going out with friends or on a date night feels like too much for the mom, that's okay. "Separating from the baby is hard, and it often takes small steps before big ones,” says Bellenbaum. In this case, offer to watch the baby while she goes for a walk, go grocery shopping with her while you push the stroller, or hold the baby at the salon while she gets a haircut.

The bottom line? Feeling angry because your world feels small right now doesn’t make you a bad mom. “You can love your baby and resent having so little freedom over your own time,” says Ou. “Both things can be true.” It just means you need more sleep, a conversation with other adults, or an hour or two out of the house, and having those needs met only makes you a better parent to your baby.

#8046. A Change of Scenery Should Be Part of Your PPD Recovery

When the walls start closing in, a shift in your surroundings can help.

Even 13 years later, Graeme Seabrook can still vividly remember how she felt when she got home from the hospital with her newborn son.

“It was like a gray wall had come down between me and the world, and everybody else was on the other side,” she says. “I was on this side with this tiny baby who depended on me for everything. And I felt all-consuming rage, like 24/7; nothing made me happy. Nothing made me even peaceful. It was really hard to sleep. Breastfeeding was torturous. It was scary.”

Seabrook, now a mom of two, says she felt claustrophobic in her two-bedroom home in Charleston, SC, where she lived at the time.

“It felt like I didn't have any air in that house because there was baby stuff everywhere,” she says. “I had no place to go. I had no way to get out. And even when I tried to, my anxiety was so bad that I couldn't leave.”

Seabrook was ultimately diagnosed with postpartum depression (PPD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and, with treatment, was able to emerge from the fog. She now lives in Colorado and created Whole Human Mama, an online support space for moms.

But you don’t need a diagnosis to know what it’s like to feel trapped. It’s common for new moms to feel stuck at home, even without PPD, says Catherine Monk, Ph.D., psychologist and division chief of Women’s Mental Health in the Department of Obstetrics & Gynecology at Columbia University.

Postpartum brings on a dramatic lifestyle shift. During pregnancy, you may still be going to work, meeting friends for coffee, and generally living on your time. Once the baby arrives, your world gets a lot smaller, and it’s often just you and the baby following the same routine day in and day out.

“Feeling trapped in one's house or apartment … can just really amplify the stuckness of the mood,” says Monk. Plus, if you’re already in the thick of PPD, getting out of the house, or even off the couch, can feel impossible.

But even the littlest of wins can make a big impact on how you feel, says Monk. This isn’t about uprooting your life or your comfort zone. A small change of scenery can do wonders to improve your mood.

You know how a smell can take you back to your grandmother’s kitchen? The same can happen with certain environments. Memory research has long shown that the brain connects memories with places, and memories bring emotions with them, says Monk. Now picture a new mom whose whole day happens in the same couple of rooms (probably covered with burp cloths, diapers, and breast pads). It makes sense that emotions would get tangled up in those surroundings.

Taking care of a baby means routines come alongside chaos, says Monk. “People's worlds can start to feel centered in maybe the bedroom or a baby's room or the living room,” she says. “People can get quite planted and rooted.”

Science has also looked into whether how a home looks and feels can alter your mood. A 2011 study of about 2,100 mothers found that moms whose homes were crowded or noisy had slightly higher odds of screening positive for depression. A small UCLA study in 2010 also showed that women who described their homes as cluttered and full of unfinished projects reported feeling down as the day went on, while those who described restful, relaxing spaces reported feeling less down.

A natural solution for getting out of the house is going outside, and it works. Spending time in nature, whether that’s hiking a trail or simply taking in the scenery, could help you feel better, says Gina South, M.D., M.S., associate professor of emergency medicine at Penn Medicine, who studies how nature affects mental health.

“There is something very specific about nature that we connect to at a very deep level that impacts our brains and our experience,” says South.

One reason lies in something called fractals, or repeating geometric patterns found organically in nature. Consider a tree: The trunk splits into big branches, which split into smaller branches, which split into twigs, and those twigs split into leaves with leaf veins — all those splits follow a similar pattern.

Research shows our brains can process these patterns with little effort, which may ease mental fatigue, reduce psychological stress, and improve attention, says South. In fact, a 2015 study found that healthy adults who took a single 90-minute nature walk showed lower activity in the region of the brain associated with rumination than those who walked just as long on a busy road.

In her own randomized controlled trial, South and her co-authors surveyed the mental health of residents living near vacant lots in Philadelphia before and after some of these lots were planted with grass and trees. Those living near the new green spaces reported fewer feelings of depression and worthlessness than those near the untouched areas. “It showed that if you change the environment, it could change the trajectory of someone's mental health,” she says.

Getting outside is also associated with socialization and physical activity, both of which have been shown to improve mood, says South. “Those social connections are very important for mental health, for depression, including for postpartum depression where people can feel isolated and [that they have] low social support,” she says.

So what exactly counts as “being in nature”? It can be taking a walk by a green space, sitting at a park bench, going to a nearby lake, or even as simple as stepping out to your backyard for five minutes.

“Include nature in your toolkit,” says South. “Going outside is not going to prevent [or treat] depression, so it’s also important to talk to your physician. It's so hard to change behavior; it's so hard sometimes to get out of a rut, but start small.”

Even if you desperately want to get out of the house, planning an outing with a newborn — even if it’s just a walk around the block — can be overwhelming. If the thought of getting outside paralyzes you with worries about blowouts and meltdowns, there are ways to change your environment without leaving home.

Create a list of things that please you, even if they seem silly or insignificant, suggests Monk. They can be as simple as drinking tea in a special mug, eating a meal at the dining table instead of the couch, taking 15 minutes to call a friend, feeding your baby in a different room, or lighting your favorite candle. Small actions can break up your routine and remind you this stage isn’t forever, she says.

If you feel like you have nowhere to escape in your own home, just taking a step to transport your mind can help shift your mood, says Monk. This can look like opening up a book, streaming a favorite TV show, listening to music or a podcast, she says. These are “things that can both be distracting [and] focus the mind elsewhere but are taking an action,” she says. “That underscores, ‘Oh, I can do things to help myself feel better.’”

Determined not to feel trapped again, Seabrook created a place that she could call her own when she was pregnant with her second child. She transformed her screened-in back porch into a colorful, cozy oasis, which served as a visible reminder that she was going to be OK, she explains.

“That was my safe space,” she says. “I had a scheduled C-section, and I knew when we were going to the hospital that morning that I had that [space] to come home to no matter how bad it got.” She didn’t experience PPD with her second birth, but that porch still became her favorite place in the house.

This tactic has now become her go-to advice for postpartum moms who feel boxed in. Simply put: Claim a spot, she says.

“And it needs to be clear of baby stuff …. It doesn't have to be a big spot. It could be a chair,” says Seabrook. “If there is enough room, make it a room. You're worth that. Who you were, who you are now, and who you are going to become — you need space for all of that.”

#8043. If Life With Dogs Were a Movie, These Would Be the Outtakes

Meet Dave Coverly, creator of the popular cartoon panel, âSpeed Bumpâ, which appears internationally in hundreds of publications, including The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and the Detroit Free Press. His work was named âBest in Newspaper Panelsâ by the National Cartoonists Society in 1995, 2003, 2014, and 2021. He is also the principal cartoonist for Bark (formerly BarkBox) and illustrator for Ranger Rick magazine.

We sit down with Dave to learn the story behind his charmingly wry comic, and find out how, 32 years down the road, inspiration in the ordinary keeps his content relevant and relatable.

The path to becoming a professional cartoonist always starts in childhood â pretty much every kid likes to draw, right? And I was no different. But as kids get older, they tend to get more particular about how good their drawings look, and thatâs where frustration sets in. They tend to move on to other hobbies. Where a cartoonistâs path diverges from that of wiser, more sensible humans is that we love the process of creating more than we chafe at the frustration. Believe me, there is frustration. One misconception about artists is that we do it because it comes easy to us, but the general truth is that most of us put in long hours because we want to be good at what we already love.

I taped rejection letters to the wall above my drawing table for motivation. At the time, though, my panels didnât have a title, so when my breakthrough finally happened, I needed to name it. I submitted a list of possible titles to Creators, and Speed Bump was the unanimous choice. Fortunately, that was my top choice, too. Iâd like people to perhaps slow down just for a second when they read my work since Iâm rarely going to hit you over the head with the joke.

My second favorite title was The Wide World of Stretch Pants.

Animal humor has always been a part of my work. I was slightly obsessed with Ranger Rick magazine growing up, and spent loads of time drawing the critters they featured. I discovered thereâs something inherently funny and absurd about talking animals, not to mention itâs the most fun way to trigger the imagination. What would a giraffe order at a restaurant? What does a dolphin dream about? That was how I discovered how much fun cartooning was â and that the crazier you make it, the less perfect it needs to be.

Iâve always had a dog until very recently, and had two hilarious knuckleheads as a kid: Shag and Tigger. They were actually father and son, and I didnât need a DNA test to prove it â Shag got out one day, and the neighborhood kids on bikes came by to let me know he could be found down the street at Queenieâs house, where they were in the front yard together. Letâs just say Shag was living up to his name. Then Queenie begat Tigger.

I grew up in a small lake community, but Shag was found by my grandpa just living on the streets of Detroit. He was pretty feral â Shag, not my grandpa â and impossible to train, but also a total sweetheart. They slept in the garage, and in the morning weâd often find him sleeping on top of the car. Tigger, on the other hand, preferred to sleep behind the toilet. And he wasnât a small dog.

In any case, I believe these two funny mutts had as much influence on my work as any other cartoonist.

Great question! Cats and dogs are obviously very different, but they have one really big thing in common: their own unique personalities. Thatâs what makes both perfect for cartoons â most of us already treat them like little furry people anyway, right? Itâs just their behaviors that set them apart.

Dogs tend to be goofier, cats tend to be cooler, and they show affection in their own ways, too. Pets generate a lot of material because almost everyone knows a dog or a cat. Even if they donât have one (or many) themselves, the odds are a reader will recognize why the cartoon is funny (hopefully!).

One of my most popular cartoons is a sign that says âBeware of Avant-Guard Dog,â and the dog in the yard is wearing black and a beret and holding a sign simply saying WOOF. The idea started as a pun, but I think one of the reasons readers seem to like it so much is that it plays against type. The dogâs sensibility is quite cat-like, making it even more absurd.

My new book is a full-color collection of the âbest ofâ my dog cartoons from the last decade, and thereâs only one cartoon per page so that they can be seen in a larger format, which was important to me. I put a lot of effort into the art and the details, things that are often lost when the cartoons are shrunk down to an illegible size, so I wanted readers to be able to fully enjoy that aspect of the cartoons. Also, the friend who colors my panels, Ron Raff, is a genius, so whether you think the jokes are funny or not, youâll see that they look gorgeous and consistent throughout!

It was difficult but fun to choose which cartoons made the cut, too. Some are simply personal favorites; others were chosen based on readersâ reactions and how much love they got online. Feedback is extremely helpful, by the way â sometimes it feels like Iâm drawing these alone in my belfry studio and tossing them into a black hole, so hearing from people which ones they liked really makes my day.

There are two aspects to dog cartoons: The first and most obvious is that they really arejokes about dogsâ behavior in general â how they eat, how they might react in different settings, why they lick themselves, bathroom habits, etc etc. Thereâs a lot of material there! The second aspect is what generates even more material, and thatâs when dogs are reflecting human behavior, or simply behaving like a human.

Many of the dog cartoons are really about us, and heaven knows people will never stop providing fodder for jokes. Dogs â and animals in general â are a good buffer between the joke and the point of the joke. A good example in the book is a dog shaking a toy in his mouth, and a woman next to him is saying, âBad dog! Drop Mommyâs voodoo doll! Bad dog!â In the background, her husband (presumably) shakes back and forth like the toy. At some level, the cartoon is about the coupleâs relationship, right? But itâs framed by a typical and humorous dog action weâve all seen before. Just not with a voodoo doll, haha.

I would say simply that our question is also the answer: love. I try to approach my cartoons the same way I approach dogs in real life; from a standpoint of love, affection, admiration, and a little bit of gratitude that they exist.

There have been too many to count over three decades! I drew a cartoon years ago of a man walking his dog in heaven, but the leash is attached to the dogâs halo. A few weeks later, I received a card in the mail from a woman whose dog had just passed awayâ¦only a month after her husband. She said she cried with happiness thinking of the two of them like that, and it made her heart feel lighter. How incredibly moving is that? I think of that often: when I share a cartoon, the reader brings their own life experiences to it and then weâve made a two-way connection. That connection is my favorite part of the gig.

My only hope is that my cartoons help people simply see the world in a different way for a few seconds. I want them to laugh with others and not at others; see that absurdities are universal and that when we recognize ourselves or others in a cartoon, weâre really just acknowledging that weâre all connected.

And then I hope they cut them out and slap them on their fridges.

The best place to find all my work and links is my site: www.speedbump.com, and anyone should feel free to reach out, follow, etc on Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/speedbumpcomic/) or Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/davecoverly)

If youâre a skywriter, aim for the west side of Ann Arbor. Iâll look out the skylight in my belfry studio.

#8042. 16 Easy Christmas Recipes For A Crowd That'll Sleigh Their Appetites

You have to feed the people, but it doesn’t have to be hard.

The best part of the holidays is being together with your family, all of them, in one place (yes, it can also be the worst part, but we’re not talking about that right now). But when everyone has flown in and unpacked, you do have to keep them fed and happy. Part of the joy of having a house full of people is cooking and baking together — hello, holiday memories. When you have a small army to feed, you and your crew of cooks need some Christmas recipes to feed a crowd. These entrees and sides will yield large amounts of food to fill up your holiday table and stash in the fridge so guests can reheat them at their leisure.

Did someone say fresh garlic bread? Grab a premade pizza dough from your local grocery store to simplify the process, a la this recipe from Damn Delicious, and then watch your family members flock to the kitchen as the smell of baking bread and garlic waft through the house.

Salads are a great dish to feed a crowd because you can size it up as much as you need to, as long as you have a big enough serving bowl. This one from Averie Cooks is delicious as an appetizer or part of a larger winter spread. It’s got apples, pears, walnuts, pomegranate, and feta, all doused in an easy sweet balsamic vinaigrette.

You just recovered from brining and roasting an entire turkey a few weeks ago, so we need not go there again. Damn Delicious’ recipe for sheet pan chicken thighs and stuffing will give you all that herby, wonderful seasonal flavor with way less work involved.

If you need a 9x13-sized vegetarian main or side dish, try Foodie Crush’s spinach and ricotta baked pasta. It’s easy to make and easy to bulk up with the protein of your choice. Personally, I’d grab a rotisserie chicken at the store to shred and toss in with everything else.

Averie Cooks’ mashed potato recipe involves caramelized onions and plenty of cheese — hell to the yeah. If you want to simplify it, though, just skip the onions and follow the instructions for getting perfectly tender, mashable potatoes in your slow cooker. She’ll tell you exactly how much broth, half-and-half, and sour cream to add to get the perfect texture.

Pork loin is one of those meats you probably don’t make often on a random weeknight, so it feels a little extra special served around the holidays. Laughing Spatula’s recipe will show you how to stuff it with seasonal deliciousness — apples, cranberries, and pecans — for a meal your family will request again next year.

Seven ingredients (most of which are pantry staples you for sure already have) and 15 minutes of prep — that’s all you need to make Foodie Crush’s candied sweet potatoes.

You could definitely order a honey-baked ham and be done with it, but if you’re game to make your own, Damn Delicious’ version is surprisingly simple. The 8-pound ham yields about 12 servings, for reference, which you could scale up or down depending on your crowd.

If you’re unfamiliar, cottage pie is kind of like shepherd pie’s easier-to-make cousin. Shepherd’s pie is traditionally made with lamb, while cottage pie is beef-based. This recipe from Our Love Language is Food will teach you how to make a delicious, comforting cottage pie in 30 minutes, and get that cheesy mashed potato crust on top juuust right.

Beans are the perfect filling food for a crowd. They’re super cheap, loaded with protein and fiber, and they hold so much flavor. Foodie Crush’s 15-bean soup looks delicious and comforting, and would be perfect served with a big, easy salad and some bread (and reheated later when the errant house guest gets hungry).

Some dishes from Thanksgiving do deserve a comeback tour, and that includes green bean casserole. Family Fresh Meals’ version comes together in the slow cooker with nearly zero effort on your part and without so much as even taking up space in the oven. It’s a Christmas miracle.

You need carbs for an army, you say? Princess Pinky Girl’s slow cooker macaroni and cheese is the easiest and the cheesiest on the internet.

If you need to make a side dish for a crowd, a massive sheet pan or two of roasted veggies will always get the job done. You could choose broccoli, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, or, in the case of this recipe from Budget Bytes, butternut squash.

Want to whip up one or two easy desserts that’ll feed a crowd? Simply LaKita’s no-bake eggnog cheesecake recipe is just a matter of measuring and mixing, and letting the cheesecake set in the fridge for a few hours before serving. You will catch your relatives sneaking bites at midnight in their Christmas jammies.

You no longer have the energy to make another thing. That’s OK. Family Fresh Meals’ Little Debbie Christmas tree cake dip requires but a whisper of effort. You just need to food-process or mash everything together and stick it in the fridge to set for an hour, and I promise, the people will lose their minds over this stuff.

Princess Pinky Girl’s cherries in the snow recipe will yield a no-bake, light and fluffy cake dessert that serves 12. It only takes about 15 minutes to assemble (you’ll get to tear up some angel food cake for the base, which is therapeutic), and it looks so pretty on the table with that bright red cherry topping.

*Siiiiigh.* Time to go buy yet another box of Christmas tree cakes.

This article was originally published on Dec. 15, 2025

#8041. 19 Easy, Cheap Christmas Baking Recipes Loaded With Holiday Magic

‘Tis the season for sweet treats that don’t require 87 niche ingredients to make.

What’s affordable is different for every family. For the purposes of this story, let’s assume you keep sugar, flour, butter, and some basic baking seasonings (like cinnamon) on hand.

Ina Garten’s rich, gooey brownie pudding recipe went viral earlier this year; this recipe is Feel Good Foodie’s take on hers. It’s less expensive because it omits the liqueur and subs in vanilla extract for vanilla bean paste, but you still get that custard-like center with crispy edges like Ina intended.

Laughing Spatula’s cranberry bars would be a great dessert to take to a holiday gathering at work or with friends. The bulk of the ingredient list relies on pantry staples, so you’ll just need to grab sour cream, a bag of fresh cranberries, and some vanilla extract if you’re out.

White chocolate chips, sweetened condensed milk, peppermint extract, and some candy canes — that’s all it takes to whip up Averie Cooks’ white chocolate peppermint fudge. Her post has great tips for first-time fudge-makers, like how best to store it so it stays fresh and how long to let it set before venturing that first slice.

Growing up, we made Rice Krispie treats for every holiday. You can add festive sprinkles, a colorful icing drizzle, or mix in something like crushed candy canes and white chocolate chips. You can even add food coloring to the marshmallows when you melt them and then shape the Krispies into whatever you want — gingerbread men, little trees, or snowmen. If you’ve never done it before, Budget Bytes explains the whole process of making your own Rice Krispies treats thoroughly.

Eggnog lovers, this one’s for you: an eggnog poke cake courtesy of Princess Pinky Girl. Again, this recipe relies on a boxed cake mix base, so you don’t need to have any flour or sugar on hand to pull it off. (Side note: her red velvet Christmas poke cake looks amazing too.)

I love how easy and cozy dump cakes are, especially when you eat them warm out of the oven with a scoop of ice cream on top. Family Fresh Meals’ recipe uses canned apples for affordability and a boxed vanilla cake mix for ease.

Something about this cake looks expensive, but you could bake far pricier cakes than this one. Budget Bytes’ recipe breaks down the cost per serving to make this fluffy, tender cake that also has a satisfying nutty crunch.

No dessert sounds cozier to me than a warm brown butter snickerdoodle fresh out of the oven (you know your whole house is going to smell amazing after baking these). All The Healthy Things’ recipe relies on pantry staples you likely already have, and if you do need to pick up a few things — cream of tartar or a new box of baking soda — they’re all pretty cheap.

A genuinely good cake that requires no eggs, milk, or butter? Believe it. Budget Bytes’ recipe is a take on a chocolate cake recipe from the Great Depression when such food items were scarce, but perhaps more than ever, families just needed a little sweet treat to get through the day.

Brb, I need to go buy marshmallows and Rice Krispies ASAP.

#8040. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.
