#8014. Let’s Be SMART – Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

The Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. organization is a Public Charity registered in the State of New York under the 509 (a) (2) Status and under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 501 (c) (3); tax ID number is 20-4051556. We are also a registered non-profit organization in Greece.

Website: https://www.letsbesmart-greece.org

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

To start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. #8012. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! My Elderly Dog is Drinking and Urinating A Lot! (October 19, 2026)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

She received her degree from the University of Guadalajara, Mexico.

Her passions are animal welfare and preventive medicine, and has skills in the fields of nutrition, microscopy, clinical pathology, diagnostic imaging, and endoscopy. Paola frequently contributes pet care insight to various media outlets like PetMD, The Daily Record, Parents.com, etc.

Paola is also an animal behaviorist with extensive experience in positive reinforcement animal training.

Before the recycling goes out, pull a few things aside. Cardboard boxes, old sheets, milk jugs, and more can carry plants through a light frost for free.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Frost warnings in October can seem to arrive with barely a day's notice. One evening, the forecast dips toward freezing while the peppers are still loaded and the fall lettuce is finally filling out. Good frost protection on a night like that doesn't have to come from a garden center.

Before buying frost cloth, take a look in the recycling bin. Last week's delivery boxes, milk jugs, and newspapers can protect plants from frost for a night or two, and the old bedsheet in the linen closet will cover a whole bed of peppers.

There's a limit to what cardboard and cotton can do. They'll carry plants through a light frost, the kind that whitens the lawn at dawn and is gone by mid-morning, but not a freeze that sits in for days. First frosts are often followed by weeks of mild weather, though, and getting tender crops past that one night can stretch the harvest.

So why does a thin bedsheet make any difference? On a clear, calm night, the soil gives off the heat it soaked up during the day, and with no clouds overhead, that warmth drifts up and away. Covers catch some of it on the way out. Drape yours loosely so the edges reach the ground, and the stems have some air space – Home Depot sells steel grow tunnel hoops with a row cover for lifting fabric over a whole garden bed.

Once the air warms above freezing in the morning, the covers need to come off, or they'll trap heat and moisture around the plant. Plastic is the riskiest material here. Wherever it presses against leaves, it carries the cold straight through, so it belongs on a frame or over a fabric layer, never directly on foliage. An analog outdoor thermometer, like this one from Walmart, hung near the garden, makes the morning check easier, though air at ground level can run a few degrees colder on still nights.

Stash these as they come through the house, and keep them dry until a frost advisory goes out.

Flip a box over the plant at dusk. If the cardboard presses on the tips of a young shrub or pepper plant, go up a size and fold the flaps inward so the edges rest on the soil. Container herbs can go under one too. Set a brick on top if there's any wind in the forecast, since an empty box weighs next to nothing. Cardboard also blocks every bit of light and turns soft in heavy dew. It needs to come off first thing in the morning.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A queen-size flat sheet will stretch over a good length of border. Save pillowcases for the odd small plant. By morning, a cotton sheet is often heavy with dew, and stakes or tomato cages pushed into the bed first keep that weight off tender stems. Rocks along the hem will hold it, or you can snap a few row cover clamps from Home Depot onto the stakes. A tarp over the top helps on rainy nights, as long as none of that plastic touches leaves.

Cut the bottom off a gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it becomes a mini cloche for a seedling or a young head of lettuce. That's the same idea behind the reusable plastic cloche from Walmart, though a rinsed jug costs nothing. Press the open edge an inch or so (2.5cm) into the soil to keep it from blowing over, and leave the cap on for cold nights. Twist the cap off on sunny days to let heat escape – a sealed jug in full sun warms up fast.

On a frosty night, the roots in a patio pot sit only a pot wall away from the cold air, while roots in the ground have soil all around them. Bubble wrap taped around the outside of the pot, below the rim, gives them a layer of trapped air to slow heat loss. Since the wrap never touches the plant, it can stay on through a stretch of cold weather, and pots pushed together against a sheltered wall hold their warmth a little better.

If you can't save up enough bubble wrap for your plants, then it's worth picking up a roll of Amazon Basics bubble wrap.

If there's newspaper around the house, spread a few sections several layers thick over low, tender plants and young vegetables, or roll one sheet into a cone for a single seedling. Weigh the corners with rocks or a scoop of soil. Once the dew soaks in, paper loses much of its insulating value. Take it off in the morning and let it dry. On wetter nights, a polypropylene frost blanket, like this one from Home Depot, holds up better.

Rake the leaves into a pile and leave them there for now. Once the soil has cooled in late fall, a few inches heaped around a tender perennial will insulate its crown and roots, though they won't help the foliage. Spread too early, and a leaf layer keeps the ground warm and can give voles a spot to settle in. Shred the leaves with a mower first or a leaf mulcher, like this Worx one from Amazon – the pieces stay loose and drain well – and leave a small gap around each stem so the crown doesn't sit wet all winter.

Slide a whole toilet paper tube, or a third of a paper towel tube, over a seedling or young transplant and push it about an inch (2.5cm) into the soil. That little collar stops cutworms such as the black cutworm (Agrotis ipsilon) from chewing through the stem at the soil line, and it takes some of the bite out of a cold wind, too. Tubes won't do much against frost by themselves, though, so pair them with a milk jug or newspaper on cold nights.

Boxes in the garage and old sheets in the closet can carry a garden through those first chilly nights. Pull the covers each morning, fold them up, and they'll be ready the next time the forecast drops. With a little luck, a few more peppers will ripen before the season wraps up.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8009. HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

That's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

As the growing season winds down, some plants benefit from a final tidy-up. But knowing what to cut – and what to leave alone – is crucial.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While the cold weather and dropped leaves of November make it seem as if the gardening season is over, there’s still one task left: pruning. Certain plants benefit from a pre-winter trim, while others shouldn’t be touched with pruners until next year.

Some perennials should be cut back all the way right now, while other types of plants, like fruiting vines and certain shrubs, can be touched up more lightly. Exact timing for these tasks depends on your location, weather, and the plant.

Here, we’ll outline some late fall pruning basics and list some of the plants you can tidy up or trim back now, before winter fully takes hold. We also share which plants are better trimmed next season.

Peonies are notoriously susceptible to fungal diseases. The deciduous foliage will die back in fall and, if left in place, can allow fungal spores to overwinter and reinfect plants next year. Trim back foliage once the leaves have yellowed or browned, or earlier if they look diseased.

November is the right time for this chore in many places, but if you garden in a warmer climate, the timing might be later. Remove all of the foliage without cutting it too close to the plant’s crown.

Another herbaceous perennial common in many gardens, hostas die back in fall. Clearing away the spent foliage tidies up beds, makes spring cleaning easier, and prevents many pests and diseases from overwintering and spreading. Cut leaves back to the base without getting too close to or cutting into the crowns. As long as leaves are still green, keep them in place to collect energy. Wait until they die back.

Gardeners are often tempted to cut back the leaves of these early bloomers soon after flowering, but it’s important to wait. The green leaves continue collecting energy to store for next year’s flowers. As long as they are healthy, keep the leaves in place until they start dying back in fall. November is a typical time for pruning bearded irises in many gardens. Cut the fans back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As with irises, you don’t want to trim back leaves just because the plants have finished flowering. Let healthy, green leaves stay in place to gather energy. For many gardeners, daylily leaves will be ready to cut back by November. In warmer climates, you might not trim them back until December. Cut daylily leaves back to a few inches above the ground.

Summer-fruiting raspberries develop fruit on canes that are two years old. Once they’re done fruiting, these older canes use up energy that the plant could be using on new canes and next year’s fruit. Identify the older, woodier canes that fruited this year, and trim them back to the ground.

You’ll also see newer, greener canes. Do not cut these back, or you’ll lose next year’s berries. Tie them together or to a support, like a fence, to protect them from winter winds.

Grapevines need regular pruning to maintain their size and structure and to support abundant fruit production. Timing is important. The vines should be dormant, so they don’t lose too much sap or sprout fresh growth. You also don’t want to prune too late, after hard freezes turn vines too brittle to make clean cuts.

When you find the right time to prune your grapevines, remove dead, damaged, or poorly positioned vines and canes. Identify healthy, young vines and trim around these. Don’t remove all older wood, especially the main trunk and arms.

Lavender hedges that are cold-hardy, like English lavender, benefit from a late fall or early winter trim to maintain their shape and health and protect them from winter weather. Too much material left on the plants can accumulate snow and ice that damage the crowns. Trim these lavenders back by about a third before the real freezing weather begins.

Pro gardeners can't get enough of Felco pruners – and these scored top in our testing.

This handy sharpener keeps pruners in top condition for clean cuts.

This telescopic tool is brilliant for trimming trees and tall climbers – no ladders required.

While these are examples of plants you can and should tackle this time of year, there are also plants that should not be trimmed now.

As a good general rule, you can trim back damaged, dead, or diseased stems and branches from any plant at any time of year. However, harder maintenance pruning needs careful timing. These plants are examples of those that can take a hard trim as winter is about to set in. Most importantly, know which plants and varieties you have and what the best practices are for these before you begin any pruning project.

Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

#8006. Trick or Treat? These Halloween Hazards Can Be Hellish For Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly important on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

#8005. “Love to the Point of Invention” – Injured Kitten with a Tiny Toy-Car Wheelchair Finds His Forever Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Some kittens steal your heart with their big eyes. Others win you over with their playful antics. And then there's Gelato, a tiny kitten who needed a wheelchair and ended up getting one made from Hot Wheels cars. Yes, really. Human ingenuity and humane creativity to the rescue!

Becoming more mobile in a Hot Wheels wheelchair might seem like a dream come true, but today, Gelato has even more reasons to celebrate: Heâs found his forever home.

Gelato arrived at Cincinnati Animal CARE in Ohio as a stray kitten with a lower-back injury that left him unable to use his hind legs normally. The shelter team wanted to help him move around, but there was a rather inconvenient problem. The wheelchairs they had available were too big for his tiny body.

Now, anyone who has lived with a kitten knows that, besides being irresistibly cute, they can be remarkably determined little creatures. They want to explore everything, investigate every corner, and get involved in whatever their humans are doing. Being unable to move around easily can limit those everyday experiences for the tiny fur balls.

Fortunately, Gelato had people in his corner who weren't about to let his small size stop him from exploring the big world.

The shelter's lead veterinary technician, Mallory Smith, came up with a wonderfully resourceful solution. She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Gelatoâs improvised mobility device is a perfect example of how animal medical care personnel go above and beyond to help patients in need.

Gelato's homemade wheelchair was a clever solution to an immediate problem. However, a makeshift device is not necessarily the best long-term option for a growing kitten with mobility challenges.

Help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

Gelato got lucky the moment someone refused to give up and asked, "How can we make this work?" This first lucky chance opened him to new opportunities from a wider effort to help one small animal have a better chance at life. Itâs impressive how sometimes sharing an animal's story can make all the difference. A social media post can connect shelters with people who have the skills, resources, or homes that animals need.

Giving Gelato a way to move around was an important first step. And there was another milestone waiting for him: a loving family of his own.

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. She understood that caring for cats with special needs could involve extra responsibilities, adjustments, and plenty of patience.

In other words, she wasn't going into this adoption without knowing that life with a disabled cat can look a little different. Cat lovers are abundant, but those experienced in caring for disabled felines? Not quite as plentiful.

Hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his new home sleeping in her arms.

Absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the company of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation plan.

These are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

Gelato will continue receiving therapy in the hope that he may regain some use of his hind legs, but for now, his recovery is uncertain. Spinal injuries vary, and a cat's prognosis depends on several factors, including the extent of the damage and the neurological function that remains.

But Gelato doesn't need a guaranteed recovery to deserve a happy future. He's got somewhere to go, someone to cuddle, and absolutely no need to prove that he can walk to earn his place in the family.

His new family is ready to love and support him, whether or not he ever walks on his own. Hollandsworth put it beautifully: to her, Gelato is already perfect just the way he is.

There is a lot of wisdom in that simple sentiment. We can hope for progress, celebrate small improvements, and pursue appropriate treatment without making an animal's worth depend on how much they recover. Loving others, whether animals, people, or even ourselves, for who they are, exactly as they are, is what we call true love.

Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A plant frost jacket is such a simple, straightforward way to keep plants alive and well over winter, and modern designs with drawstring bases and ventilating zips make it easier than ever to use them. When winterizing a garden, zippered plant jackets don’t only protect tender beauties like banana plants and tree ferns but can help to stop sensitive souls like olive trees from dropping their leaves in a cold snap, shield citrus trees from the occasional frost if you garden in zone 9, and prevent palms from rotting.

Fleece plant covers are also incredibly useful to cocoon early-blooming shrubs like camellia and magnolia if a frost hits just as they’re setting their buds, so you can save the flower show. Young fruit trees, too, can benefit from this extra layer to stop their thin bark splitting in freezing winter conditions, and a plant cover can shield all sorts of other plants from damage caused by snow, sleet and strong winds.

So, if you're getting ready to winterize plants as you prepare your garden for the onset of cold weather, plant jackets should be part of your plan. Not all fleece plant covers are created equal, however, so if you want them to actually work, you need to take a close look at their weight rating. The material used to make frost jackets comes in different weights and, just like comforters offer various levels of warmth, that directly impacts how well it will protect plants in winter, but also the more sunshine it'll block.

Horticultural fleece is a non-woven material typically made from polypropylene, and its weight determines how much protection it offers your plant, measured in grams per square meter (gsm) or ounces per square yard (oz/sq yd). Check the label or online description to find the rating. Any good-quality frost jacket will state the rating and the higher the number, the more insulation it will provide but also block more sunlight.

Armed with this knowledge, you can choose the exact right level of protection for whatever plant you’re winterizing in your USDA zone. While you need to ensure your plant is getting the right level of cold protection, you also need to cater for its sunlight needs.

Because these plants are dormant through winter in colder zones, they don’t need sunlight so you can safely use an ultra heavy-weight fleece to protect them. The fleece alone won’t be enough to protect banana plants (Musa basjoo) and tree ferns (Dicksonia antarctica) from the deep chill of colder zones but are still useful as a cover once you’ve packed layers of insulating straw around the plant. Not only will the fleece form a great barrier against wind and rain but it’ll keep the straw in place and that wrapped plant looking tidy.

Made from 95gsm or 2.8oz/sq yd non-woven material, these plant covers have rounded tops for a good fit and come in green, beige or white in four sizes: 31" x 25", 47" x 39", 71" x 47" and 94" x 79".

Because deciduous shrubs drop their leaves in fall, they don’t need any sunlight over winter to survive so you can safely zip them up in a heavy or ultra heavy-weight plant jacket, depending on the level of protection needed in your zone. This thicker material will also keep snow from weighing down and snapping brittle winter branches. Do choose a design with a zipper as well as a base drawstring so you can regularly open up the zip on milder days to let air circulate.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In 60gsm or 1.77oz/sq yd non-woven fabric, these zippered plant jackets are made of a minimum 50% recycled material and come in four sizes: 23" x 23", 39" x 31", 71" x 47" and 83" x 71".

Hardy shrubs that flower early in the spring such as camellias and magnolias are typically tough enough to survive most winters without a jacket, but their flowerbuds are quickly killed by a late frost or cold snap. Throw on a medium- or heavy-weight plant jacket overnight to save those new buds from the frost.

Evergreen plants such as conifers still need sunlight and fresh air to survive through winter, so a medium-weight fleece is your best bet for general winterizing if your aim is to shield a hardy plant from snow, hail and wind damage. If you’re planning on leaving it on permanently through winter, use a medium-duty fleece for more tender evergreen olive and citrus trees and certain palms, too.

However, if you live in a colder climate you’ll need the increased protection of a heavy- or ultra heavy-weight fleece for these more tender plants. Either use this as an extra layer to throw on over the top of the permanent medium-weight layer in severe weather or, if you use this as the mainstay cover, you’ll need to keep unzipping it to allow sunshine and air in during milder daytime temperatures.

Most medium-duty fleeces are designed without a zipper but that’s not a problem: because the thinner material lets more air and sunlight through, they can safely be left in place.

Made of 32gsm or 0.95oz/sq yd breathable material, this medium-weight plant cover has a drawstring base and is available in three sizes: 32" x 32", 55" x 48" and 72" x 72".

No fleece jacket can generate heat, it can only insulate from the cold, so how you use it has a huge impact on how effectively it protects your plant in winter. Choose a design with both a drawstring and a zip as this not only makes the jacket quick and easy to pop on, but allows you to fit it closely and avoids the wind ripping it off.

Wherever possible, peg the plant jacket to the ground to catch any heat rising upwards. Soil holds onto considerable warmth from the sun, so make use of this natural radiator. Use bricks or stones to weigh the jacket base down, or peg it to the ground with landscape fabric pegs, choosing a product with gaskets to prevent the fabric tearing like these Galvanized Landscape Pins from Amazon.

Similarly, if you’re winterizing a plant in a container, use a frost jacket that’s big enough to fit around the pot, too, as this will protect the roots as well as trap any heat from the soil. Roots in planters are very vulnerable to freezing temperatures so consider wrapping the pot with bubble wrap first.

To prevent moisture building up under the cover and causing mold, make sure you buy a jacket marked as breathable, and open the zip on mild days to allow air to circulate.

While you don’t want to squash a plant into a cover, it’s a wise idea to fit the jacket around the plant to prevent it flapping in the wind and metal greenhouse clamps such as these from Amazon are invaluable to gather loose material or clip a jacket to existing plant supports.

Measuring 8’ x 8’ to fit bigger shrubs and trees, this ultra heavy-weight 80gsm or 2.4oz/yd cover comes with ties and stakes so it can be pinned securely to the ground in exposed gardens.

These ultra heavy-weight zippered covers are made from 75gsm or 2.2oz/sq yd patterned fabric and are available in a green or grey print in sizes 32"x24", 47"x32", 71"x47" and 83"x71".

Shaped for wide, bushy shrubs, this heavy-weight plant cover made of 50gsm or 1.5oz/sq yd fabric measures a generous 7' x 7' and is also available in an 8' square size.

#8003. What Makes a Lucky Dog? | Heroes of the Pet World

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â

Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

Three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7999. Late Summer Through Fall in Susan’s Minnesota Garden, Part 1

Hi GPODers! Today we’re welcoming back longtime contributor Susan from St. Paul, Minnesota (Zone 5a). Susan has shared her garden with us many times over the years, and today she’s taking us through some of her favorite moments from late July into October. If you’ve missed her previous visits, you can revisit last year’s gardening season at the 45th parallel. For now, let’s see what she’s been growing!

Still looking back: Here are some photos from late July to October.

Back garden, late July: I had a huge ‘Montana Aureomarginata’ hosta (Hosta montana ‘Aureomarginata’, Zones 3–8) in the front garden, where it received too much sun. My husband dug it up for me, and I divided it into three clumps, one of which is pictured above. The bluish hostas are ‘El Niño’ (Hosta ‘El Niño’, Zones 3–9), and the hydrangea is ‘Little Quick Fire’ panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘SMHPLQF’, Zones 3–8).

A second clump of ‘Montana Aureomarginata’ was replanted in the front garden, but in a shady spot under a white cedar (Thuja occidentalis, Zones 2–7).

Speaking of hostas, this is one of my favorites; even the almost pinkish flowers are pretty. The similarly colored companion is Chinese astilbe (Astilbe chinensis, Zones 4–8).

Grape-leaf anemone (Anemone tomentosa ‘Robustissima’, Zones 4–8) glows in the late-afternoon sun.

Front garden with end-of-summer gold and fuchsia: Garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia cvs., Zones 3–9), and a daylily blossom (Hemerocallis ‘Autumn Gold’, Zones 3–9; Sutton, 1952, not the more recent one) missed by the deer.

I was doing some planting in a redone, seldom-visited corner of the garden when I thought I spotted a piece of trash. It turned out to be a lone stalk and blossom of Japanese lily (Lilium speciosum ‘Album’, Zones 5–8) that had somehow escaped the scarlet lily beetle ravages and that I, too, had missed in my cutting-down frenzy. I have hope that the others will have survived.

According to Old House Gardens, this is a wild ancestor of ‘Casa Blanca’. OHG last offered it in 2012, and it is now considered “commercially extinct in the Netherlands.”

The painted lady butterflies love curly onion (Allium senescens ‘Glaucum’, Zones 4–8) as much as I do. Its long-lasting blooms perk up the late-summer, early-fall garden.

‘Autumn Joy’ stonecrop (Hylotelephium ‘Herbstfreude’, Zones 3–9) is a dependable fall bloomer, beloved by pollinators.

Another fall bloomer that attracts many pollinators is black cohosh, also known as bugbane (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8). This photo was taken on September 22, but other clumps of it are still blooming more than a month later.

‘Sun King’ Japanese spikenard (Aralia cordata ‘Sun King’, Zones 3–9) is prized for its golden foliage, but it also develops small but interesting flowers and fruits late in the season.

Thank you for sharing another look at your garden with us, Susan! I especially loved the surprise lily. Finding a flower you thought you’d lost is always exciting, especially after dealing with pests!

We have more photos from Susan to share soon, so stay tuned for Part 2!
